If q_+=z/\|z\|_2 has angle 	heta_+ to x_j, then  egin{aligned} 	an	heta_+ &= rac{\|w\|_2}{|\alpha/(\lambda_j-\mu)|}\ &\le rac{2\epsilon\,|\lambda_j-\mu|}{g\alpha}\ &=O(\epsilon^3). \end{aligned} Since \sin	heta_+\le	an	heta_+,  oxed{\sin	heta_+=O(\epsilon^3)=O(\sin^3	heta).} The mechanism is now explicit: an eigenvector error of size \epsilon produces a shift error of size O(\epsilon^2), and the inverse step reduces the relative unwanted component by this additional factor. The result is an error of size O(\epsilon^3).The theorem is local: a random starting vector is not asserted to enter this neighborhood in every case. It also concerns exact arithmetic; rounding and the accuracy of the shifted solves limit the improvement observed in a numerical implementation.

title: HW 3
NMI Midterm Study Plan
text: The midterm is Monday, November 2, 2026. This plan runs from October 19 to November 1 and matches 56 hours of NMI review on the calendar. The first three days are lighter to allow for other coursework due October 21. Breaks, homework for other courses, and class meetings are additional.The syllabus confirms a written exam with closed books and notes, and says homework problems will likely appear. The strongest preparation is therefore to solve the written homework independently, reproduce the main proofs, and trace the lecture algorithms on paper. The priorities below reflect the lecture coverage and homework; they are not predictions of the exam’s point distribution.Give the most repeated practice to these topics.QR and least squares: projection geometry, the normal equations, classical versus modified Gram-Schmidt, Householder QR, applying the implicit factors, and QR existence and uniqueness. These recur throughout Lectures 5-8 and HW3.LU, pivoting, and numerical error: elimination, triangular solves, the identity PA=LU, packed storage, small pivots, growth, conditioning, and the componentwise error estimate. These connect Lectures 1-6.Cholesky and Schur complements: positive definiteness, positive pivots, block elimination, the block inverse, eigenvalue and pivot bounds, and the Cholesky-QR relationship. These are the core of Lecture 9 and HW3 Questions 1-3.The spectral material scheduled before the exam: power and inverse iteration, Rayleigh quotient iteration, Schur factorization, orthogonal iteration, unshifted and shifted QR, SVD, polar decomposition, and low-rank approximation. These also need dedicated study time; their exact exam coverage should be confirmed on Brightspace.Give a shorter first review to detailed binary encoding, hardware timing examples, the different Cholesky loop arrangements, and the HW3 bonus minimax question. Know column-major storage, why blocking helps, basic operation counts, and one correct implementation of each main algorithm. Return to additional details after the core problems are reliable.Lectures 1-10 are currently in this repository. For later material, the plan uses the topic and class date in the syllabus: Schur factorization on October 14, orthogonal iteration on October 19, unshifted QR on October 21, shifts on October 26, and SVD on October 28. Collect those notes as they become available and use any announced exam cutoff to adjust the last topic blocks. Post-midterm topics such as Arnoldi, Lanczos, Krylov methods, and FFT are outside this plan.Use each topic block for learning and practice together.Recall the previous material, then follow the assigned lecture derivation and one worked example.Solve matching problems on paper before opening their solutions.Reconstruct the central proof or algorithm from memory; correct and redo missed steps.Calendar blocks are organized by topic and last no more than three hours. Keep coding to short checks after the paper calculation. Revisit missed questions on later days.Day by day planDay and dateFocused hoursStudy in this orderPractice and completion target1 - Mon Oct 191Triangular systems and elimination. Revisit uniqueness and operation counts during the later mixed review.3 - Wed Oct 211Least-squares geometry and normal equations. L5 §§5.2-5.10; L8 §§8.2-8.5. Distinguish an elimination pivot from its Cholesky square root.7 - Sun Oct 256Eigenvalue iterations and Schur factorization. Trace fixed-shift inverse iteration and Rayleigh quotient iteration. Derive the second-order Rayleigh quotient error and outline the local cubic argument. State the Schur theorem and reproduce the proof given in Lecture 11.8 - Mon Oct 264.5Orthogonal iteration and the unshifted QR algorithm. October 19 and 21 notes. Derive A_{k+1}=Q_k^*A_kQ_k and explain why eigenvalues are preserved. Explain the connection between accumulated orthogonal factors and orthogonal iteration. Finish study early enough to be rested for Monday.Use these as the core exam readiness checks.Compute and explain PA=LU, including row swaps, triangular solves, packed storage, and cost.Derive least-squares optimality, the normal equations, and the QR solution; explain the condition-number drawback of normal equations.Distinguish CGS from MGS and reproduce the lecture’s loss-of-orthogonality example.Construct a Householder reflector, choose its sign, and apply implicit Q and Q^* in the correct orders.Prove Gram-matrix positivity and Cholesky existence; explain the positive-diagonal uniqueness convention, including the complex case.Derive block LU, the Schur determinant and inverse identities, the SPD bounds, and the Cholesky-QR connection.Derive power and inverse iteration convergence factors and explain the Rayleigh quotient’s accuracy and local convergence assumptions.Explain Schur form, QR similarity, orthogonal iteration, shifts, deflation, and the iteration costs taught in class.Use SVD for norm, rank, conditioning, polar decomposition, and the low-rank approximation result covered before the exam.A topic counts as learned when you can solve a fresh question and reconstruct its central argument without help. title: 01 Mid-Point Method
text: 01.1 Formula DerivationThe derivative approximation: \begin{aligned} f(t_i, u_i) &= \frac{dy}{dt} \Big|_{t_i} \approx \frac{y(t_{i+1}) - y(t_{i-1})}{2\Delta t} + \mathcal{O}(\Delta t^2) \end{aligned} Update formula: \begin{aligned} u_{i+1} &= u_{i-1} + 2\Delta t f(t_i, u_i) \end{aligned} 01.1.1 Initial ConditionsInitial Condition Calculation: Given y_0 \begin{aligned} u_2 &= y_0 + 2\Delta t f(t_1, u_1) \end{aligned} Predictor-Corrector Steps: \begin{aligned} u_1^* &= y_0 + \Delta t f(t_0, y_0), \\ u_1 &= y_0 + \frac{\Delta t}{2} (f(t_0, y_0) + f(t_1, u_1^*)) \end{aligned} 01.1.2 Two-Step MethodHigher-order method that improves accuracy using information from two previous time steps.The method achieves second-order accuracy due to the central difference approximation. *** # Absolute StabilityWe consider the test equation: \begin{aligned} \frac{dy}{dt} &= -\lambda y, \quad y(0) = y_0 \end{aligned} where \lambda > 0.01.2 DiscretizationThe numerical update formula is: \begin{aligned} u_{n+1} &= u_{n-1} - 2\Delta t \lambda u_n \end{aligned} Rearranging: \begin{aligned} u_{n+1} + 2\Delta t \lambda u_n - u_{n-1} &= 0 \end{aligned} 01.2.1 Iterative ComputationStarting with initial conditions (y_0, y_1): \begin{aligned} u_2 &= y_0 - 2\Delta t \lambda y_1, \\ u_3 &= y_1 - 2\Delta t \lambda u_2, \\ u_4 &= u_2 - 2\Delta t \lambda u_3, \\ u_5 &= u_3 - 2\Delta t \lambda u_4 \end{aligned} This formulation helps analyze the stability of the numerical scheme by checking whether the sequence u_n grows or decays as n \to \infty.01.3 Stability Analysis of the Numerical SchemeWe assume a solution of the form: \begin{aligned} u_i &= C \beta^i \end{aligned} 01.3.1 Substituting into the Recurrence Relation$$ $$ This is a characteristic equation for the recurrence relation. And solving for \beta, \begin{aligned} \beta &= \frac{-2\Delta t \lambda \pm \sqrt{(2\Delta t \lambda)^2 + 4}}{2} \end{aligned} To ensure stability, we require: \begin{aligned} |\beta_0|, |\beta_1| &\leq 1. \end{aligned} 01.3.2 General SolutionSince the recurrence relation is second-order, the general solution is: \begin{aligned} u_i &= C_0 \beta_0^i + C_1 \beta_1^i. \end{aligned} From the initial conditions:$$$$ which can be solved for C_0 and C_1.01.4 Stability ConditionFor stability, the roots \beta_0, \beta_1 must satisfy: \begin{aligned}|\beta_0 \beta_1| &= 1.\end{aligned} From the characteristic equation: \begin{aligned}\beta_0 \beta_1 &= -\frac{1}{\beta_1}. \end{aligned} Ensuring |\beta| \leq 1 determines the absolute stability region.01.5 Finite Difference Approximation and Stability Analysis01.5.1 Finite Difference Approximation \begin{aligned} \alpha u_{i+1} + \beta u_i + \sigma u_{i-1} + \delta u_{i-2} &= (\alpha + \beta + \sigma + \delta) u_i + \mathcal{O}(\Delta t^5) \end{aligned} 01.5.2 Time Discretization \begin{aligned} \frac{du}{dt} \Big|_{t_i} &= \frac{u_i - u_{i-1}}{\Delta t} + \mathcal{O}(\Delta t^2) \end{aligned} 01.5.3 Stability Analysis \begin{aligned} \alpha + 4\beta &= 0, \\ \alpha &= -4\beta, \\ 4\beta - 2\beta &= 1 \Rightarrow \beta = \frac{1}{2}, \quad \alpha = -2. \end{aligned} These constraints ensure numerical stability and proper convergence of the finite difference scheme. ### Taylor Expansions Applying Taylor expansions to express the function values at different time steps: \begin{aligned} & \alpha\left[u_{i+1}=u_i-\left.\frac{d u}{d t}\right|_{t_i} \Delta t+\ldots\right] \\ & \beta\left[u_{i+2}=u_i-\left.\frac{d u}{d t}\right|_{t_i} 2 \Delta t+\ldots\right] \\ & \gamma\left[u_{i+3}=u_i-\left.\frac{d u}{d t}\right|_{t_i} 3 \Delta t+\ldots\right] \\ & \delta\left[u_{i+4}=u_i-\left.\frac{d u}{d t}\right|_{t_i} 4 \Delta t+\ldots\right] \end{aligned} Summing these expansions, we obtain the system of equations, \left\{\begin{aligned} -\alpha-2 \beta-3 \gamma-4 \delta & =1 \\ \alpha+4 \beta+8 \gamma+16 \delta & =0 \end{aligned}\right.

title: 9.1 边值问题的近似
text: 1.1 Set-up: String with fixed endpoints我们可以写 \begin{align} -\frac{d^2u}{dx^2} &= f(x), \quad x \in (0,1) \\ u(0) &= \alpha, \quad \frac{du}{dx}(0) = \beta \end{align} 记w = \frac{du}{dx}，那么 \frac{dw}{dx} = f(x)。因此，我们知道\frac{d}{dt} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} w \\ u \end{bmatrix}9.1.1.1 定义边值问题（boundary-value problem）的定义为 > [!definition|*] > \begin{align} -\mu\frac{d^2u}{dx^2} &= f(x), \quad x\in (0,1), \quad \mu > 0 \\ u(0) &= \alpha, \quad u(1) = \beta \end{align} > ## 1.2 泊松方程（Poisson Equation） 此类方程的二维形态为：\begin{align} -\left(\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2}\right) &= f(x,y) \\ u|_{\text{boundary of }\Omega} &= 0 \end{align}用拉普拉斯算子来表示：\left(\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2}\right) = \Delta u, \quad \text{where }\Delta = \nabla^2 u = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_i^2}所以，广义的泊松方程可以写为[!definition] A general (n-dimentional) poisson equation is written as \Delta u = f(\mathbf{x}) where \mathbf{x}=(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\dots x_{n}).1.3 Back to the String Example: How can we get a BVP?考虑以下经典力学中很常见的弦的能量泛函（energy functional）：J(u) = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 \mu\left(\frac{du}{dx}\right)^2 dx - \int_0^1 f \cdot u \, dx \quad \text{(Energy of string)}Boundary condition: u(0) = u(1) = 0.作为自然界的基本趋势中，最小作用量原理解释了自然系统倾向于采取能量消耗最小的路径或状态，也就是说，自然会沿着\min J(u)的路径发展。最简单的方法是直接用 欧拉-拉格朗日方程（Euler–Lagrange equation）搞定，但是这毕竟是个数学课，那么我们用最暴力的原始方法解决：大致思路为：把 u 加入扰动（perturbation）变成 u+εv：u_{\epsilon}(x) = u(x) + \epsilon v(x)J(u+εv) 进行显式展开：J(u + \epsilon v) = J(u) + \epsilon \underbrace{\delta J(u; v)}_{\text{一阶变分}} + \frac{1}{2} \epsilon^2 \underbrace{\delta^2 J(u; v)}_{\text{二阶变分}} + \cdots在变分法或力学的语言里：通常是指在能量或作用量（action）等泛函意义下的驻点（stationary point）：也就是对任意“小扰动” εv，该函数 u 都使得泛函的一阶变化量为 0。求导，来找J的最小值\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{J(u + \varepsilon v) - J(u)}{\varepsilon} = 0, \quad \varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}显然易见： \begin{align} &\frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 \mu\left(\frac{du}{dx} + \varepsilon\frac{dv}{dx}\right)^2 dx - \int_0^1 f(u+\varepsilon v) \, dx - \frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 \mu\left(\frac{du}{dx}\right)^2 dx - \int_0^1 f \cdot u \, dx \\ &= \frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 \mu\left(\frac{du}{dx}\right)^2 dx + \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2\varepsilon \int_0^1 \mu \frac{du}{dx} \cdot \frac{dv}{dx} \, dx + \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon^2 \int_0^1 \mu\left(\frac{dv}{dx}\right)^2 dx \\ &\quad - \int_0^1 f \cdot u \, dx - \varepsilon\int_0^1 f \cdot v \, dx - \frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 \mu\left(\frac{du}{dx}\right)^2 dx - \int_0^1 f \cdot u \, dx \\ &= \varepsilon \int_0^1 \mu \frac{du}{dx} \cdot \frac{dv}{dx} \, dx + \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon^2 \int_0^1 \mu\left(\frac{dv}{dx}\right)^2 dx - \varepsilon\int_0^1 f \cdot v \, dx\end{align} 这实际上正是欧拉–拉格朗日方程最早的“原始变分法”推导，也正是 E-L 方程的来龙去脉。只不过 E-L 方程把这个过程“公式化”了，让我们不必每次都展开一大堆项、再分部积分去凑出那个通用形式。然后\frac{J(u+\varepsilon v) - J(u)}{\varepsilon} = \int_0^1 \mu \frac{du}{dx} \cdot \frac{dv}{dx} \, dx + \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon \int_0^1 \mu\left(\frac{dv}{dx}\right)^2 dx - \int_0^1 f \cdot v \, dx极限为：\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{J(u+\varepsilon v) - J(u)}{\varepsilon} = \int_0^1 \mu \frac{du}{dx} \cdot \frac{dv}{dx} \, dx - \int_0^1 f \cdot v \, dx = 0一个“平衡解”（equilibrium solution）。9.1.2.1 变分形式或弱形式（Variational/Weak）:由此我们得到了一个泛函的“变分条件”：[!claim|*] \int_0^1 \mu \frac{du}{dx} \cdot \frac{dv}{dx} \, dx - \int_0^1 f \cdot v \, dx = 0分部积分: \begin{align} \int_0^1 \mu \frac{du}{dx} \cdot \frac{dv}{dx} \, dx &= \mu\left[\frac{du}{dx}v\right]_0^1 - \mu\int_0^1 \frac{d^2u}{dx^2} v \, dx \\ &= -\mu\int_0^1 \frac{d^2u}{dx^2} v \, dx \end{align} Since v(0) = v(1) = 0\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{du}{dx}\right) = \frac{d^2u}{dx^2}\int \frac{dv}{dx} \, dx = v边界项因为BC而消失，所以弱形式\rightarrow强形式:-\mu\int_0^1 \frac{d^2u}{dx^2} v \, dx - \int_0^1 f \cdot v \, dx = 0-\int_0^1 \left(\mu\frac{d^2u}{dx^2} + f\right) \cdot v \, dx = 0We want it to be true \forall v. So, it must be: \mu\frac{d^2u}{dx^2} + f = 0我们得到一个常见的附带边界条件的强形式常微分方程(ODE)。[!claim|*] We obtain a Boundary Value Problem (BVP): \begin{align} \mu u''(x) +f&= 0 \\ u(0) &= u(1) = 0 \end{align} Assumption: u is at least C^2.1.4 两种表述边值问题（BVP）的方式寻找函数 u，使得对所有满足 v(0) = v(1) = 0 的 v，均有 \int_0^1 \mu \frac{du}{dx} \cdot \frac{dv}{dx} \, dx \;=\; \int_0^1 f \cdot v \, dx \Rightarrow u 只需保证“一阶可微”\Rightarrow 通常采用 有限元法 (Finite Element)寻找函数 u，使得 \begin{aligned} -\mu \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} &= f, \quad x \in (0,1),\\ u(0) &= 0,\quad u(1) = 0 \end{aligned} \Rightarrow u 需要至少“二阶可微”\Rightarrow 通常采用 有限差分法 (Finite Difference)

title: 9.2 有限差分法
text: 2.1 边值问题（BVP）的有限差分:[!claim|*] Consider the Boundary-Value Problem: \begin{align} -\mu\frac{d^2u}{dx^2} &= f, \quad x \in (0,1) \\ u(0) &= u(1) = 0 \end{align} with discrete points: 0 = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_{N} = 1\quad\Longrightarrow \quad-\mu\frac{d^2u}{dx^2}(x_i) = f(x_i)2.2 推导二阶中心差分近似法2.2.1 Poisson 微分方程对与任意一个离散的点x_{i}，我们首先在网格点 x_{i+1} = x_i + \Delta x 和 x_{i-1} = x_i - \Delta x 处对函数 u(x) 进行泰勒级数展开： \begin{align} u(x_{i+1}) &= u(x_i) + \frac{du}{dx}(x_i)\Delta x + \frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2u}{dx^2}(x_i)\Delta x^2 + \cdots \\ u(x_{i-1}) &= u(x_i) - \frac{du}{dx}(x_i)\Delta x + \frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2u}{dx^2}(x_i)\Delta x^2 + \cdots \end{align} 当我们将这两个方程相加时，由于奇数阶导数项的符号相反，它们会相互抵消： \begin{align} u(x_{i+1}) + u(x_{i-1}) &= 2u(x_i) + 2\left(\frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2u}{dx^2}(x_i)\Delta x^2\right) + 2\left(\frac{1}{24}\frac{d^4u}{dx^4}(x_i)\Delta x^4\right) + \mathcal{O}(\Delta x^6) \\ \\ &= 2u(x_i) + \frac{d^2u}{dx^2}(x_i)\Delta x^2 + \frac{1}{12}\frac{d^4u}{dx^4}(x_i)\Delta x^4 + \mathcal{O}(\Delta x^6) \end{align} 接着, 我们重新整理方程以分离出二阶导数项（舍去高阶项）\begin{align} \frac{d^2u}{dx^2}(x_i)\Delta x^2 &= u(x_{i+1}) + u(x_{i-1}) - 2u(x_i) - \frac{1}{12}\frac{d^4u}{dx^4}(x_i)\Delta x^4 + \mathcal{O}(||\Delta x||^6)\\ \frac{d^2u}{dx^2}(x_i) &= \frac{u(x_{i+1}) + u(x_{i-1}) - 2u(x_i)}{\Delta x^2} - \frac{1}{12}\frac{d^4u}{dx^4}(x_i)\Delta x^2 + \mathcal{O}(||\Delta x||^2) \\ &\approx \boxed{ \frac{u(x_{i+1}) + u(x_{i-1}) - 2u(x_i)}{\Delta x^2}} \end{align}记 u_i = u(x_i) 与 f_i = f(x_i). 因此我们得到微分方程[!claim|*] -\mu\frac{d^2u}{dx^2}(x_i) = -\mu\frac{u_{i+1} + u_{i-1} - 2u_i}{\Delta x^2} = f_i截断误差（Truncation Error）为 \mathcal{O}(\Delta x^2)这证实了该近似是二阶精度 （second-order accuracy）2.2.2 构建线性系统用这种离散化方法推导出一个线性方程组（linear system）:Au = fwhere A is given by:A = \frac{\mu}{\Delta x^2} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & & \\ -1 & \ddots & \ddots & & \\ 0 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\ & & \ddots & \ddots & -1 \\ & & & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} 2.3 What is the Accuracy of FD?9.2.3.1 矩阵A的关键性质 (Key Properties of Matrix A)从差分离散化得到的matrix A有几个重要性质：正定性 (Positive Definiteness)：x^TAx > 0 \quad \forall x \neq 0 \Longrightarrow solvable。对称性 (Symmetry)：Symmetry \Longrightarrow \forall \,\lambda \in \mathbb{R}特征值性质 (Eigenvalue Properties)：Non-singular条件数关系 (Condition Number Relation)：A的最小特征值与最大特征值之比与Δx成正比，即\frac{\lambda_{min}}{\lambda_{max}} \propto \Delta x9.2.3.2 误差当我们解离散系统（Au = f）时，精确解u_{ex}与近似解u之间存在误差，所以Au_{ex} \neq f。精确关系实际上为：[!claim|*] Au_{ex} = f + T where T_i = C(x_i)\Delta x^2 is truncation error其中C(x_i)与四阶导数相关：C(x_i) = C\frac{d^4u}{dx^4}(x_i)9.2.3.3 误差方程 (Error Equation)若定义误差e = u_{ex} - u，则 Ae = T\Longrightarrow e = A^{-1}T因此||e|| = ||A^{-1}T|| \leq ||A^{-1}|| \cdot ||T||9.2.3.4 收敛性证明 (Convergence Proof)为了证明方法收敛，需要满足两个条件：1. 稳定性：A^{-1}有界 (Boundedness of A^{-1}) 2. 一致性：截断误差趋零 (Truncation Error Tends to Zero)[!lemma|*] Conditions to show convergence: ||A^{-1}|| < \infty \quad \text{and} \quad ||T|| \to 0 \quad \text{as} \quad \Delta x \to 09.2.3.4.1 关于 \|A^{-1}\| 的有界性矩阵的条件数定义为：\kappa(A) = \|A\| \cdot \|A^{-1}\|=\frac{\lambda_{max}}{\lambda_{min}}\frac{\lambda_{min}}{\lambda_{max}} \propto \Delta x \longrightarrow\kappa(A) \propto \frac{1}{\Delta x}hence, ||A^{-1}|| is bounded, regardless of \Delta x.9.2.3.4.2 关于T的一致性因为截断误差范数\|T\| \sim \Delta x^2，所以\|T\| \to 0 \,\,\text{as}\,\, \Delta x \to 0这也意味着：\|e\| \to 0 \,\,\text{as}\,\, \Delta x \to 0因此，该有限差分方法是收敛的 (convergent)虽然\kappa随 \Delta x 变化，但 \|A^{-1}\| 的增长被 \|T\| 的更快减小所抵消。9.2.3.5 实际意义？该有限差分法随着网格间距 (grid spacing) 减小而收敛到精确解收敛速率 (convergence rate) 是O(\Delta x^2)，即二阶精度 (second-order accuracy)误差主要受控于四阶导数的大小和网格间距的平方这解释了为什么在实际计算中，当我们将网格间距减半时，误差大约会减小到原来的四分之一这种数学证明为我们使用有限差分法求解微分方程提供了理论保障，确保了在足够细的网格下，数值解 (numerical solution) 会以可预测的速率接近真实解 (exact solution)。

title: 9.3 对流-扩散方程
text: 3.1 对流-扩散方程对流-扩散方程是一种描述物质或热量在流体中同时受到对流（也称为平流）和扩散作用影响的偏微分方程。这个方程在流体力学、传热学和物质传输等领域有广泛应用。 \begin{align} -\mu\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \beta\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} &= f \\ \text{diffusion} \quad & \text{advection} \end{align} u(0) = u_L, \quad u(1) = u_R3.1.1 离散化过程：9.3.1.1.1 一阶导数：对流项 （Advection）9.3.1.1.1.1 泰勒展开（向前）$$ $$9.3.1.1.1.2 泰勒展开（向后）u(x_{j-1}) = u(x_j) - \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}(x_j)\Delta x + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}(x_j)\Delta x^2 - \frac{1}{6}\frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial x^3}(x_j)\Delta x^3 + \frac{1}{12}\frac{\partial^4 u}{\partial x^4}(x_j)\Delta x^4 + \mathcal{O}(||x||^5)我们取(forward) - (backward)两者差值u(x_{j+1}) - u(x_{j-1}) = 2\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}(x_j)\Delta x + \frac{1}{3}\frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial x^3}(x_j)\Delta x^3 + \mathcal{O}(||\Delta x||^5)接着\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}(x_j) = \frac{u(x_{j+1}) - u(x_{j-1})}{2\Delta x} - \frac{1}{6}\frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial x^3}(x_j)\Delta x^2 + \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{||\Delta x||^4}{2}\right)9.3.1.1.2 二阶导数：扩散项（Diffusion）这都还不会吗？退群吧。9.3.1.1.3 对流-扩散离散方程[!claim|*] Final numerical solution: -\mu\frac{u_{i+1} - 2u_i + u_{i-1}}{\Delta x^2} + \beta\frac{u_{i+1} - u_{i-1}}{2\Delta x} = f_j with second-order accuracy: \sim \mathcal{O}(\Delta x^2)3.2 例子：精确解与数值解在对流主导问题中的差异我们现在考虑一个特殊情况的对流-扩散方程，其中源项（Source Term）为零，具有以下边界条件： \begin{align} -\mu\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \beta\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} &= 0 \\ u(0) &= 0 \\ u(a) &= 1 \end{align} 3.2.1 精确解这个方程的精确解是：u_{ex} = \frac{e^{\frac{\beta}{\mu}x} - 1}{e^{\frac{\beta}{\mu}a} - 1}这个解的特点是：当比值 \frac{|\beta|}{\mu} \gg 1 时（即advection远大于diffusion），解在边界 x=a 附近会形成一个陡峭的边界层。这被称为对流主导问题（advection-dominated problem）。在对流主导的情况下，解在大部分区域接近于0，只在接近 x=a 的小区域内快速上升到1。这对数值方法的解法是很大的麻烦。3.2.2 数值解当我们使用标准的中心差分（central difference）方法离散化这个方程时：-\mu\frac{u_{i+1} - 2u_i + u_{i-1}}{\Delta x^2} + \beta\frac{u_{i+1} - u_{i-1}}{2\Delta x} = 0重新整理这个方程：\left(-\frac{\mu}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{\beta}{2\Delta x}\right)u_{i+1} + \left(\frac{2\mu}{\Delta x^2}\right)u_i - \left(\frac{\mu}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{\beta}{2\Delta x}\right)u_{i-1} = 0数值实验表明，当 |\beta| 较大时，数值解会出现不一致，非物理的振荡。为什么呢？9.3.2.2.1 数学解释为了理解这一现象，我们可以对差分方程进行深入分析。我们假设差分方程的解具有形式 u_j = C\rho^j，其中 C 是常数，\rho 是待定参数。将这个假设代入到差分方程中：\left(-\frac{\mu}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{\beta}{2\Delta x}\right)C\rho^{j+1} + \left(\frac{2\mu}{\Delta x^2}\right)C\rho^j - \left(\frac{\mu}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{\beta}{2\Delta x}\right)C\rho^{j-1} = 0消去 C 并整理：\left(-\frac{\mu}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{\beta}{2\Delta x}\right)\rho^2 + \left(\frac{2\mu}{\Delta x^2}\right)\rho - \left(\frac{\mu}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{\beta}{2\Delta x}\right) = 0这是关于 \rho 的二次方程，它有两个解 \rho_1 和 \rho_2。差分方程的一般解是这两个特解的线性组合：u_j = C_1\rho_1^j + C_2\rho_2^j其中 C_1 和 C_2 是由边界条件确定的常数。9.3.2.2.2 振荡解的条件根据二次方程的性质，两个根的乘积等于常数项与二次项系数的比值：\rho_1\rho_2 = \frac{-\left(\frac{\mu}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{\beta}{2\Delta x}\right)}{\left(-\frac{\mu}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{\beta}{2\Delta x}\right)} = \frac{1 + \frac{\beta\Delta x}{2\mu}}{1 - \frac{\beta\Delta x}{2\mu}}这里引入了一个重要的无量纲参数，称为网格佩克莱数（Grid Péclet number）：\text{Pe} = \frac{|\beta|\Delta x}{2\mu}佩克莱数表示对流传输与扩散传输的相对强度。当 \text{Pe} > 1（即 \frac{|\beta|\Delta x}{2\mu} > 1）时，我们有 \rho_1\rho_2 < 0，这意味着两个根一正一负。当一个解包含负的幂时，会导致解在空间上呈现振荡特性，这与物理直觉相违背，因为扩散过程应该是平滑的。9.3.2.3 物理解释与改进方法9.3.2.3.1 为什么会出现振荡？物理角度看：信息主要沿着流动方向传播。Central Difference 方法对上游和下游的信息给予相同权重，所以对流主导的情况下不合适，除非极细的网格才能准确解析。即使数值方法在数学上具有二阶精度，其准确度依旧是要取决于特定的物理问题中。理解数值方法的稳定性条件才可以选择合适的求解策略。9.3.2.3.2 解决方案？网格细化：最直接的方法是减小 \Delta x，使 \text{Pe} < 1。但这会大大增加计算成本。迎风方法：（详细见下文）使用偏向上游的差分格式，如前向或后向差分，取决于 \beta 的符号。例如，当 \beta > 0 时，可以使用： \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}(x_j) \approx \frac{u_j - u_{j-1}}{\Delta x}人工扩散：增加一个数值扩散项，使有效的佩克莱数小于1。高阶格式：使用更高阶的差分格式，如QUICK、TVD或ENO/WENO方案，这些方法可以更好地捕捉强梯度区域。3.3 另一种方法：迎风法（Upwind Method）3.3.1 信息流动分析 (Information Flow)就像刚刚的对流主导问题，现实中经常存在明确的物理信息流动方向，使得这个问题本质上是非对称的。对于对流项（advection），当流动方向已知时 > [!assumption|*] > \beta > 0，meaning that the information flows from left to right.我们可以使用式子：[!claim|*] \beta\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \approx \beta\frac{u_i - u_{i-1}}{\Delta x} \quad (\beta > 0) \quad \text{(upwind)}这种差分格式考虑了信息流动的方向，使用”上游”的节点来计算导数，而不是像中心差分那样平等对待上下游节点（注意这个只有一阶精度）。3.3.2 迎风法的稳定性分析 (Stability Analysis)接下来，我们来证明迎风方法是稳定的。将迎风差分重写为：\beta\frac{u_i - u_{i-1}}{\Delta x} = \beta\frac{u_{i+1} - u_{i-1}}{2\Delta x} - \beta\frac{u_{i+1}}{2\Delta x} - \beta\frac{2u_i}{2\Delta x} + \beta\frac{u_{i-1}}{2\Delta x}整理一下上式：= \beta\frac{u_{i+1} - u_{i-1}}{2\Delta x} - \frac{\beta\Delta x}{2} \cdot \frac{u_{i+1} - 2u_i + u_{i-1}}{\Delta x^2}这个表达式可以分解为两项：中心差分项 (Central mean): \beta\frac{u_{i+1} - u_{i-1}}{2\Delta x}二阶导数近似项 (Approximation of 2nd derivative): -\frac{\beta\Delta x}{2} \cdot \frac{u_{i+1} - 2u_i + u_{i-1}}{\Delta x^2}这说明迎风方法等价于对原始方程进行中心差分，但增加了一个额外的扩散项（人工扩散，artificial diffusion）。9.3.3.3 等价表述：扰动方程 (Perturbed Equation)因此，我们可以将原始问题的迎风方法看作是下面这个扰动方程的中心差分解法：-\left(\mu + \frac{|\beta|\Delta x}{2}\right)\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \beta\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0对这个扰动方程应用中心差分近似：-\mu\frac{u_{i+1} - 2u_i + u_{i-1}}{\Delta x^2} + \beta\frac{u_{i+1} - u_{i-1}}{2\Delta x} = 0这正是原始问题的迎风解法。换句话说：对扰动问题使用中心差分 (Central for Perturbed) = 对原始问题使用迎风差分 (Upwind for Original)[!claim|*] \text{Central (Perturbed) }= \text{Upwind (Original)}这个等价关系揭示了迎风法的本质：它隐含地向原始方程中添加了一个数值扩散项。这个额外的扩散项是迎风法能够抑制数值振荡的关键原因。9.3.3.4 佩克莱数分析 (Péclet Number Analysis)回顾一下佩克莱数的定义：\text{Pe} = \frac{|\beta|\Delta x}{2\mu}。对于扰动系统，扩散系数变为 \mu^* = \mu + \frac{|\beta|\Delta x}{2} = \mu(1 + \text{Pe})。扰动系统的佩克莱数为：\text{Pe}^* = \frac{|\beta|\Delta x}{2\mu^*} = \frac{|\beta|\Delta x}{2\mu(1+\text{Pe})} = \frac{\text{Pe}}{1+\text{Pe}} < 1 \quad \forall |\beta| \text{ 和 } \Delta x这表明无论 |\beta| 和 \Delta x 的值如何，扰动系统的佩克莱数永远小于1，因此迎风方法始终是稳定的。9.3.3.5 一致性分析 (Consistency Analysis)当 \Delta x \to 0 时，\mu^* \to \mu，扰动方程趋近于原始方程，这保证了方法的一致性。对于扰动系统，我们使用了二阶精度的中心差分方法，但对于原始问题，由于引入了人工扩散项，它只是一阶精度的方法。9.3.4 详细解释与物理意义迎风方法的核心思想是考虑物理信息的传播方向。在流体流动中，当某点的特性（如温度、浓度）受到上游点的影响更大时，迎风方法使用上游点来计算导数，从而更好地反映物理现实。从数值分析的角度看，迎风方法引入了”人工扩散”(artificial diffusion)，增强了数值方法的稳定性。这种人工扩散恰好能够抵消中心差分在高佩克莱数情况下产生的数值振荡。然而，这种稳定性是以精度为代价的——迎风方法的精度降低到一阶（误差与 \Delta x 成正比），而中心差分是二阶精度（误差与 \Delta x^2 成正比）。这在数值方法中是一个常见的权衡：更高的稳定性往往伴随着更低的精度。在对流主导的问题中，稳定性通常比高精度更重要，因为不稳定的解会产生严重的非物理振荡，使结果完全无用。因此，对于高佩克莱数流动，迎风方法尽管精度较低，但往往是更实用的选择。更高阶的方法，如TVD (Total Variation Diminishing)、ENO (Essentially Non-Oscillatory) 和 WENO (Weighted Essentially Non-Oscillatory) 方案，试图在保持稳定性的同时提高精度，但它们的实现更为复杂。Our previous computation relies on symmetry. However, there is a clear physical information flow. So, this problem is asymmetric in reality. We don’t want as fancy as \sim \mathcal{O}(\Delta x^2) solutions, but we can use a \sim \mathcal{O}(\Delta x) method.\beta\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \approx \beta\frac{u_i - u_{i-1}}{\Delta x} \quad (\beta > 0) \quad \text{(upwind)}Now, let’s show (upwind) is stable.\beta\frac{u_i - u_{i-1}}{\Delta x} = \beta\frac{u_{i+1} - u_{i-1}}{2\Delta x} - \beta\frac{u_{i+1}}{2\Delta x} - \beta\frac{2u_i}{2\Delta x} + \beta\frac{u_{i-1}}{2\Delta x}= \beta\frac{u_{i+1} - u_{i-1}}{2\Delta x} - \frac{\beta\Delta x}{2} \cdot \frac{u_{i+1} - 2u_i + u_{i-1}}{\Delta x^2}Central mean \quad Approx. of 2nd derivativeSo, we can consider the equation: -\left(\mu + \frac{|\beta|\Delta x}{2}\right)\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \beta\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0Apply a central approximation: -\mu\frac{u_{i+1} - 2u_i + u_{i-1}}{\Delta x^2} + \beta\frac{u_{i+1} - u_{i-1}}{2\Delta x} = 0Upwind solution of the original problem.Recall Péclet: Pe = \frac{|\beta|\Delta x}{2\mu}. Then, \mu^* = \mu(1 + Pe).Péclet of this perturbed system: Pe^* = \frac{|\beta|\Delta x}{2\mu^*} = \frac{|\beta|\Delta x}{2\mu(1+Pe)} = \frac{Pe}{1+Pe} < 1 \quad \forall |\beta| \text{ and } \Delta xSo, this upwind method is always stable.Consistency: when \Delta x \to 0, \mu^* \to \mu.For the perturbed system, we have a 2nd order approach, but with the original problem, it is only a 1st order method.3.4 Design a Better Method\mu^{smart} = \mu(1 + \Phi(Pe))s.t.\Phi(Pe) \to 0 \quad \text{as} \quad \Delta x \to 0Pe^{smart} = \frac{|\beta|\Delta x}{2\mu^{smart}} < 1Our upwind method takes \Phi(Pe) = Pe \sim \mathcal{O}(\Delta x). But can we take some \Phi(Pe) \sim \mathcal{O}(\Delta x^2)?\Rightarrow Scharfetter-Gummel Method: \Phi(Pe) = Pe - 1 + \frac{2Pe}{e^{2Pe} - 1}\Phi(Pe) \uparrow\Phi(Pe) = Pe\Phi(Pe) \sim \mathcal{O}(\Delta x)The worst case order of Scharfetter-Gummel is \sim \mathcal{O}(\Delta x^2).Scharfetter-Gummel is also a special \Phi(Pe) that produces exact solutions.

title: 9.4 4.1 二维（2D）偏微分方程问题
text:
9.4.1 椭圆型4.1.1 问题设定我们考虑一个二维空间的问题，记为区域 \Omega。边界记为 \partial\Omega。方程一般形式如下： -\mu \Delta u +  eta \cdot 
abla u = f,\quad 	ext{在}\ \Omega 内边界条件为： u(\partial \Omega) = d \quad (	ext{给定的数据})这里的符号解释（见上一章）： eta：表示”风”或者对流的方向和强度\mu：扩散系数f：外力或源项因此，上面的方程可以展开写成：-\mu \left( rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} +  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2}ight) +  eta_x  rac{\partial u}{\partial x} +  eta_y  rac{\partial u}{\partial y} = f(x,y)4.1.2 简化情形（只有扩散，没有风）首先考虑更简单的情况，忽略对流（即“关掉风”），变成纯扩散问题：-\mu\left( rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} +  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2}ight) = f(x,y)4.1.3 离散化方法（有限差分法）用有限差分法来数值求解：假设空间被划分为一个网格，每个网格点用坐标 (i,j) 来表示位置：在x方向的间距为 \Delta x在y方向的间距为 \Delta y则对于二维的拉普拉斯算子，常用的中心差分格式为： rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}\approx  rac{u_{i+1,j}-2u_{i,j}+u_{i-1,j}}{\Delta x^2} rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2}\approx  rac{u_{i,j+1}-2u_{i,j}+u_{i,j-1}}{\Delta y^2}代入扩散方程得到：-\mu rac{u_{i+1,j}-2u_{i,j}+u_{i-1,j}}{\Delta x^2} -\mu rac{u_{i,j+1}-2u_{i,j}+u_{i,j-1}}{\Delta y^2} = f(x_i,y_j)4.1.4 形成线性代数方程组所有网格点的未知数u_{i,j}放到一个向量中（向量记为u），这样就可以把离散后的方程写成一个矩阵方程：A u = b这里：A 是系数矩阵（稀疏、对称、正定，简称SPD）u 是未知量向量（所有网格点的解）b 是已知项的向量（源项f和边界条件的组合）4.2 时间相关问题：抛物型（Parabolic）考虑的问题形式： rac{\partial u}{\partial t}-\mu rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}=f,\quad x\in(0,1),\quad 0<t<T初值与边界条件为：初值：u(x,t=0)=u_0(x)边界条件：u(0,t)=u_L(t),\quad u(1,t)=u_R(t)9.4.2.1 半离散化方法（空间离散，时间连续）我们首先只对空间（x）做离散化，得到： rac{d u_j(t)}{d t}-\mu rac{u_{j+1}(t)-2u_j(t)+u_{j-1}(t)}{\Delta x^2}=f_j(t)记：向量形式：u(t)=[u_1(t),u_2(t),...,u_n(t)]^T源项向量：f(t)=[f_1(t),f_2(t),...,f_n(t)]^T系数矩阵：A= rac{\mu}{\Delta x^2}	ext{tridiag}(-1,2,-1)于是问题变成常微分方程（ODE）的系统形式： rac{d u}{d t}-A u=f9.4.2.2 时间离散化（ODE方法）接下来我们对时间进行离散化，采用两种方法：9.4.2.2.1 方法1：显式欧拉（Explicit Euler, FE）将时间导数在时间点t_n近似为： rac{u^{n+1}-u^n}{\Delta t}=f^n+A u^n解得：u^{n+1} = (I+\Delta t A)u^n+\Delta t f^n显式方法容易计算，但稳定性有限，时间步长不能太大。9.4.2.2.2 方法2：隐式欧拉（Implicit Euler, IE/BE）另一种方法是在时间点t_{n+1}处求导： rac{u^{n+1}-u^n}{\Delta t}=f^{n+1}+A u^{n+1}解出隐式方程：(I-\Delta t A)u^{n+1}=u^n+\Delta t f^{n+1}这个方法更稳定，但需要在每个时间步解一个线性系统。9.4.2.3 关于矩阵性质的总结：A 为SPD矩阵（对称正定）当 A 和 b 是与时间无关时，通常我们更喜欢隐式方法，因为可以分解矩阵一次（如LU分解）并反复使用，加快计算速度。9.4.3 总结一下：以上涉及了两类偏微分方程问题：椭圆型（空间二维）问题，通过空间离散化直接得到线性方程组；抛物型（空间一维+时间）问题，先对空间离散变为ODE，再对时间离散使用ODE数值方法（显式/隐式欧拉方法）进行求解。以上步骤逐步解释了问题如何从连续形式变成数值可求解的离散形式。  egin{align} -\mu\Delta u + \vec{ eta} \cdot 
abla u &= f \ u(\partial\Omega) &= 	ext{data} \end{align} Write it out:  egin{align} -\mu\left( rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} +  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2}ight) +  eta_x rac{\partial u}{\partial x} +  eta_y rac{\partial u}{\partial y} &= f(x,y) \ u(\partial\Omega) &= d \end{align} 4.1 Only Consider Diffusion. Turn off Wind:To form a system: (i,j) 	o k.Au = b.A is symmetric, SPD.4.2 Turn on the Wind. UpwindWith upwind, the pts are not good.5. 抛物型（Parabolic）问题（时间相关问题）  egin{align}  rac{\partial u}{\partial t} - \mu rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} &= f, \quad x \in (0,1) \quad 0 < t < T\ u(0,t) &= u_L(t), \quad u(1,t) = u_R(t) \ u(x, t=0) &= u_0(x) \end{align} Discretization along x: semi-discretization: u_j(t) \approx u(x_j, t).  rac{du_j}{dt} - \mu rac{u_{j+1}(t) - 2u_j(t) + u_{j-1}(t)}{\Delta x^2} = f_j(t) = f(x_j, t)So, we form system Au = f.A =  rac{\mu}{\Delta x^2}	ext{Triad}(-1, 2, 1), \quad u(t) =  egin{bmatrix} u_1(t) \ \vdots \ u_n(t) \end{bmatrix}, \quad f(t) =  egin{bmatrix} f_1(t) \ \vdots \ f_n(t) \end{bmatrix}Then, we have a system of ODE:  rac{du}{dt} - Au = fWe can now do time discretization and use ODE methods.EE/FE: u^n = u(t^n), \quad \left. rac{du}{dt}ight|_{t^n} \approx  rac{u^{n+1} - u^n}{\Delta t} = f^n + Au^nu^{n+1} = u^n + \Delta t Au^n + \Delta t f^n = (I + \Delta t A)u^n + \Delta t f^n = (I + \Delta t A)^n u_0 + \Delta t f^nIE/BE: \left. rac{du}{dt}ight|_{t^n} =  rac{u^n - u^{n-1}}{\Delta t} = f^n + Au^nu^n - u^{n-1} = \Delta t f^n + \Delta t Au^nu^n - \Delta t Au^n = \Delta t f^n + u^{n-1}(I - \Delta t A)u^n = u^{n-1} + \Delta t f^n \quad \leftarrow 	ext{A linear system to solve}I - \Delta t A is SPD and A is time-independent. So, we may favor direct method (as we can store A = LU and reuse it) over iterative methods.To discuss stability, set f = 0:EE is conditionally stable: Let \lambda_i be eigenvalues of A.\Delta t <  rac{2}{|\lambda_i|} \quad 	ext{for stability}Further, A =  rac{\mu}{\Delta x^2}	ext{triad}(1, -2, 1), ho(A) \sim  rac{c}{\Delta x^2}. So,\Delta t <  rac{2}{|\lambda_i|} \leq  rac{2}{ho(A)} =  rac{2}{c}\Delta x^2So, if we decrease \Delta x by 2, to have stability\Delta t_{new} <  rac{2}{c}\left( rac{\Delta x}{2}ight)^2 =  rac{\Delta t_{old}}{4} \quad \Rightarrow 	ext{we need finer intervals for time}IE is unconditionally stable.Def. (	heta Methods).  rac{u^{n+1} - u^n}{\Delta t} = 	heta Au^{n+1} + (1-	heta)Au^n + 	heta f^{n+1} + (1-	heta)f^n, \quad 	heta \in [0,1]EE: 	heta = 0 \quad \mathcal{O}(\Delta t) \quad explicit \quad conditional stabilityIE: 	heta = 1 \quad \mathcal{O}(\Delta t) \quad implicit \quad unconditional stabilityCN: 	heta =  rac{1}{2} \quad \mathcal{O}(\Delta t^2) \quad implicit \quad unconditional stabilitySuppose f = 0. Then,  rac{u^{n+1} - u^n}{\Delta t} = 	heta Au^{n+1} + (1-	heta)Au^nu^{n+1} - u^n = \Delta t 	heta Au^{n+1} + \Delta t(1-	heta)Au^n(I - \Delta t 	heta A)u^{n+1} = (I + \Delta t(1-	heta)A)u^nWe essentially solve a linear system in each iteration.5.1 Thm (Stability and Order of 	heta Methods)	heta methods are unconditionally stable for 	heta \geq  rac{1}{2}. Otherwise, it is conditionally stable for 	heta <  rac{1}{2} and the stability condition for parabolic problem is \Delta t < c\Delta x^2.Meanwhile, the method is order 1 for 	heta 
eq  rac{1}{2} and order 2 for 	heta =  rac{1}{2}.Although the 	heta method is 2nd order in space, the order of error is dominant and determined by the order in time.CN is the most vulnerable to lack of regularity and sensitive to non-smoothness.6. Hyperbolic Problems6.1$ $Exact solution: u(x,t) = u_0(x - \alpha t)6.2 Example: Modeling Density of Pollutantu: pollutant, x: displacement of boat, t: time.$$ $$x(t) = x_0 + at \Rightarrow characteristic curvesu(x,t) = u_0(x-at). Solution to  egin{cases}  rac{dx}{dt} = a \ x(0) = x_0 \end{cases}Consider u(x(t),t):  rac{du}{dt} =  rac{\partial u}{\partial t} +  rac{\partial u}{\partial x} \cdot  rac{dx}{dt} =  rac{\partial u}{\partial t} + a \cdot  rac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0.6.3 Similar Problems:Conservation law  rac{\partial u}{\partial t} +  rac{\partial q(u)}{\partial x} = 0q(u) = v(u) \cdot u with v = v_{max}\left(1 -  rac{u}{u_{max}}ight)\Rightarrow  rac{\partial u}{\partial t} + v_{max}\left(1 -  rac{u}{u_{max}}ight) rac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0. title: Quiz 4
text:
1 Solutions for Quiz 41.1 Question 1For a given problem, we know that the solution belongs to H^2(\Omega). We use finite elements of order 2. What is the expected order of convergence in the norm of H^1(\Omega). Is this an optimal choice? Motivate your answer.1.1.1 Solution:Based on approximation theory for finite elements, we can analyze this using the relationship between the solution regularity, the polynomial order, and the expected convergence rate.For a solution u \in H^2(\Omega) and using order k Lagrange interpolation (where k=2 in this case), we can refer to the following relationship for error estimates:If we construct a table of convergence rates based on solution regularity q and polynomial order k:q k123111121223123Here we’re looking at the case where q=2 (solution in H^2) and k=2 (quadratic elements).For this combination, we expect order of convergence O(h^1) in the H^1(\Omega) norm.This is not optimal. The optimal convergence rate would be O(h^2) in the H^1(\Omega) norm, which would require the solution to be in H^3(\Omega) when using quadratic elements.For a solution in H^2(\Omega), we only achieve first-order convergence in the H^1 norm with quadratic elements, which is the same rate we would get with linear elements. Therefore, using quadratic elements is not computationally efficient for this problem.1.2 Question 2Explain why in advection-dominated problems in 2+ D, adding artificial viscosity to stabilize the solution is not optimal.1.2.1 Solution:In advection-dominated problems where the convection term significantly outweighs the diffusion term, we often encounter numerical instabilities. Consider the extreme case where the velocity field is highly anisotropic, such as: eta =  egin{bmatrix} 1000 \ 0 \end{bmatrix}In this scenario, using the upwind method with artificial viscosity is not optimal because:The advection-diffusion equation takes the form: -\mu^*  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} - \mu^*  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} +  eta_0 \cdot  rac{\partial u}{\partial x} = fThe key issue is that \mu^* (artificial viscosity) doesn’t help stabilize the problem in the y-direction. The only thing we need to do is to regularize the x-direction, which can be written as:-\mu^*  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} - \mu  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} +  eta_0  rac{\partial u}{\partial x}More generally, we can write: \mu \int_\Omega 
abla v \cdot 
abla u + \int_\Omega  eta 
abla u \cdot v +  rac{\mu}{2} \int_\Omega ( eta \cdot 
abla u)( eta \cdot 
abla v)  rac{1}{| eta|^2} = \int_\Omega f vThis shows that artificial viscosity adds diffusion isotropically (in all directions), whereas the instability primarily occurs in the direction of the flow. This makes the method unnecessarily diffusive in directions perpendicular to the flow, degrading solution accuracy where stabilization isn’t needed.1.3 Question 3True or False?1.3.1 a) If we solve an advection-diffusion problem with the condition that the convection dominates the diffusion (||β|| >> μ) with the finite element method, the solution does not oscillate: T ___ F ___Answer: FWhen convection dominates diffusion, standard finite element methods will produce oscillatory solutions unless stabilization techniques are applied.1.3.2 b) If we solve a reaction-diffusion problem with the condition that the reaction dominates the diffusion (σ >> μ) with the finite element method, the solution does not oscillate: T ___ F ___Answer: F (ATO-1), u = fThis is stable. Unlike advection-dominated problems, reaction-dominated problems may not show oscillations but can exhibit sharp boundary layers. The finite element solution doesn’t typically oscillate in the same way as advection-dominated problems.1.3.3 c) When we do Mass Lumping, the matrix with entries \int_0^1 \varphi_i \varphi_j dx we obtain is diagonal: T ___ F ___Answer: TIn mass lumping, all terms become one term in the diagonal. The mass matrix, which normally has entries from the integral of basis function products, is approximated by a diagonal matrix through the lumping process.

text: 2.1 12.2 22.1 Poisson Equation2.1.1 The Poisson Equation and the Finite Element DiscretizationThe Poisson equation is a partial differential equation (PDE) used in modeling, e.g.: steady-state heat conduction, electrostatics, gravitational fields.Problem: Find u such that -\Delta u=f \quad \text { in } \Omega, \quad u=0 \quad \text { on } \partial \Omega Weak Form: Find u \in V_{h} such that \int_{\Omega} \nabla u \cdot \nabla v \, d\Omega=\int_{\Omega} f v \, d\Omega \quad \forall v \in V_{h} Algebraic Form: after discretization, solve the linear system A x=b 2.1.2 Basic FE Steps (2-5 in MFEM)Discretize the computational domain (meshing) ⇒ external meshing softwareDerive the weak form for your PDE problemAssemble global systemApply boundary conditionsSolve the linear systemPost-processing and visualization ⇒ ParaView, GLVis, VisItImplemented in tutorial_emory_01.cpp in the example folder, and original tutorial at https://mfem.org/tutorial/fem/.2.2 Convergence Analysis2.2.1 Convergence AnalysisVerify numerical accuracy by computing errors against the exact solution: \left\|u-u_{h}\right\|_{L^{2}}, \quad\left\|u-u_{h}\right\|_{H^{1}} Evaluate convergence rates as the mesh is refined: r \approx \frac{\log \left(e_{h_{2}} / e_{h_{1}}\right)}{\log \left(h_{2} / h_{1}\right)} Expected behavior for polynomial order p: \left\|u-u_{h}\right\|_{L^{2}}=O\left(h^{p+1}\right), \quad\left\|u-u_{h}\right\|_{H^{1}}=O\left(h^{p}\right) Implemented in tutorial_emory_01_convergence.cpp in the example folder, and original tutorial at mfem-convergence-xsdk.2.3 Partial AssemblyHigh-order FEM ⇒ large, dense matricesPA avoids global matrix assemblyApplies element operators on-the-flyFaster, memory-efficient, GPU-friendly A=P^{T} G^{T} B^{T} D B G P Implemented in tutorial_emory_01_pa.cpp in the example folder.

title: 2. Transport equation
text: 2.1 Evans §2.1 — Transport equationLet b\in\mathbb R^n be a constant velocity and let g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be the initial data: \begin{cases} u_t+b\cdot Du=f(x,t), & (x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty),\\ u(x,0)=g(x). & \end{cases} The operator \partial_t+b\cdot D differentiates in the space-time direction (b,1).2.1.1 CharacteristicsTo find the value at a fixed endpoint (x,t), trace its characteristic backward. Let X(\tau)=x-(t-\tau)b,\qquad 0\leq \tau\leq t. Then X'(\tau)=b, X(t)=x, and the characteristic meets the initial plane at X(0)=x-tb. Along this curve, \frac{d}{d\tau}u(X(\tau),\tau) =Du(X(\tau),\tau)\cdot X'(\tau)+u_t(X(\tau),\tau) =b\cdot Du+u_t =f(X(\tau),\tau). Integrating from 0 to t gives the characteristic formula \boxed{ u(x,t)=g(x-tb)+\int_0^t f\bigl(x-(t-\tau)b,\tau\bigr)\,d\tau. } Equivalently, the integrand may be written as f(x+(\tau-t)b,\tau).2.1.1.1 Homogeneous equationIf f=0, the value of u is constant along each characteristic: \boxed{u(x,t)=g(x-tb).} Thus the initial profile is translated with velocity b without changing shape. The characteristic lines satisfy x-tb=\text{constant}. 2.1.2 Slides 4–5 correction[!danger] Do not use the formula shown incorrectly in the recording Wrong: z(s)=u(x+sbt,t+s) Correct: z(s)=u(x+sb,t+s).For the correct path, with s\in[-t,0], z'(s)=b\cdot Du(x+sb,t+s)+u_t(x+sb,t+s). Also, z(0)=u(x,t),\qquad z(-t)=u(x-tb,0)=g(x-tb). Hence u(x,t)-g(x-tb) =\int_{-t}^{0}f(x+sb,t+s)\,ds, which becomes the boxed formula after setting \tau=t+s.The erroneous x+sbt has derivative tb with respect to s, so it produces z'(s)=tb\cdot Du+u_t, not the transport operator b\cdot Du+u_t; at s=-t it also lands at the wrong point x-t^2b.2.1.3 Quick checks and regularityFor f=0, u_t=-b\cdot Dg(x-tb) and Du=Dg(x-tb), so u_t+b\cdot Du=0.If g\in C^1 (and f is sufficiently regular), the formula gives a classical solution.For rougher, locally integrable data, the same formula is interpreted distributionally as a weak solution; lack of smoothness is transported rather than smoothed out.Memory aid: to compute u(x,t), go backward by tb to the footpoint x-tb, then accumulate the source f forward along that line.

title: 1.1 Data and Solution
text: 0.1 Basic ConceptWe think of a physical problem (the actual physics in a perfect world) as a map that takes data \to solution, and a numerical problem as an approximation of that map (and of the data).0.1.1 Three MappingsA physical map P (exact, continuous, infinite-dimensional reality) is formulated as \underbrace{d}_{\text{data}} \;\longmapsto\; \underbrace{u}_{\text{solution}} = P(d) data d: initial conditions, boundary conditions, or source termssolution u: the true, continuous function that solves the PDE.On computer, we must discretize the problem so the continuous map can be handled by the algorithm.A numerical map N is formulated as:\underbrace{ d_h }_{\text{approx. data} } \longmapsto \underbrace{ u_h }_{\text{numerical sol.} } = N(d_h)mesh step h: discretization size parameter/step sizeapproximated data d_{h}: the projection or restriction of the continuous data d onto a finite-dimensional discrete spacenumerical solution u_h: the exact solution to the discrete algebraic system of equations (e.g., A_h u_h = d_h)A perturbed numerical map N_{\text{perturb}}, by definition, is formulated as \underbrace{d_h + \delta_h}_{\text{perturbed data}} \;\longmapsto\; \underbrace{u_h + \varepsilon_h}_{\text{perturbed numerical sol.}} So the diagram is comparing: \begin{align} \text{data space: } & d, \;d_h,\;d_h+\delta_h \\ \text{solution space: } & u,\; u_{u},\; u_{h}+\epsilon_{h} \end{align} with the mappings P, N, and N_{\text{perturb}} connecting them.0.1.2 Three Fundamental PropertiesTo evaluate the relationship between these maps, or bridge the gap between the physical reality (P) and the numerical execution (N), we ask 3 most important questions for numerical PDEs:0.1.2.1 ConvergenceDoes u_h \to u when h \to 0?Convergence measures the distance (error) between the true physics and our numerical approximation. By definition, a method is convergent if, as the mesh is refined (h \to 0), the numerical solution approaches the true physical solution (u_{h}\to u).0.1.2.2 ConsistencyDoes N \to P when h \to 0?Consistency checks the local accuracy of our discrete equations, the map N, in relations to P. In other words, do our discrete equations accurately mimic the continuous differential equations?.We test this by plugging the exact solution u into the discrete operator A_h. The resulting residual is the Truncation Error \tau_h. ### 0.1.2.3 StabilityDoes \varepsilon_h \to 0 when \delta_h \to 0?Stability is about sensitivity to perturbations. If you slightly nudge the data (d_h + \delta_h), does the solution ripple slightly (\varepsilon_h) or explode?The operator N must be uniformly bounded with respect to h. In linear algebra terms, we use condition number of matrix A_h to measure that behavior.0.1.3 The Fundamental linkFor well-posed linear problems, you don’t need to prove convergence directly (which is hard because we usually don’t know u). Instead, we use the Lax Equivalence Theorem:[!theorem|] Lax Equivalence Theorem For linear, well-posed problems, we have the equivalency: \text{Consistency + Stability} \iff \text{Convergence}

title: 1.2 Functional Analysis
text:
This section covers basic concepts in functional analysis, such as Lebesgue Spaces, Distributions, Sobolev SpacesSince a PDE can be viewed as an operator mapping data to solution, numeric replaces the infinite-dimensional space by a finite-dimensional subspace, so we need:notions of size (norm),notions of closeness (metric),notions of limits (completeness),notions of orthogonality/projection (Hilbert),and generalized derivatives (distributions) to make sense of weak solutions.In PDE, we need the weak (variational) formulation because the classical formulation asks for derivatives that often don’t exist, and because numerics (especially FEM) naturally lives in an integral/inner-product world. In the following notes, we will build the language used to write PDEs in a weak/variational form, and use them to analyze numerical methods (FEM, DG, FV) later.0.1 Basics of Functional AnalysisIn previous section, we think of PDE as a “problem operator” P:\ d \longmapsto u = P(d), where d is the data (forcing term, boundary values, initial condition, coefficients) and u is the solution. Functional analysis provides the right spaces X where this mapping is well-defined and stable.[!definition|1.2.1] Functional A functional is \mathcal{F}(\cdot): X 	o \mathbb{R}. Let f(x), g(x) \in X. A functional is linear if \mathcal{F}(\lambda f(x) + \mu g(x)) = \lambda \mathcal{F}(f(x)) + \mu \mathcal{F}(g(x)) Interpretation. A functional takes a function and returns a number (think: “measurement”). Linearity means the measurement respects superposition.[!example|1.2.2] A functional For example, \int_a^b f(x)\,dx is a functional.Why it matters. Weak formulations are built out of integrals of the solution against test functions; those are functionals.[!definition|1.2.3] Form A form is a(\cdot,\cdot): X 	imes X 	o \mathbb{R}, where f, g \in X. A form is bilinear ifa(\lambda f_1 + \mu f_2, g) = \lambda a(f_1,g) + \mu a(f_2,g)a(f, \lambda g_1 + \mu g_2) = \lambda a(f,g_1) + \mu a(f,g_2)Remark. A bilinear form takes two functions and returns a number.[!definition|1.2.4] Space A space is a set with operations defined. If X is a space, thenf \in X \Longrightarrow \lambda f \in Xf,g \in X \Longrightarrow \lambda f + \mu g \in XRemark. This is the “closed under linear combinations” property (vector space idea). It’s needed so we can add trial functions, scale solutions, etc.0.2 Metrics, completeness, and norms0.2.1 Why do we need a distance?To talk about convergence of numerical methods, we need a notion of “u_h 	o u”. That requires a distance or metric, and usually we obtain it from a norm.[!definition|1.2.5] Distance A distance is d(\cdot,\cdot): X 	imes X 	o \mathbb{R} such that  orall\, f,g,w \in Xd(f,g) = d(g,f) [symmetry]d(f,g) \ge 0 and d(f,g)=0 \Longleftrightarrow f=gd(f,g) \le d(f,w) + d(w,g) [triangle inequality]A space with a distance is a metric space.[!definition|1.2.6] Completeness Let (X,d) be a metric space. Let f_n be a sequence in X and f be a candidate limit.The sequence is convergent if d(f_n,f)	o 0 as n	o +\inftyThe sequence is Cauchy if d(f_n,f_m)	o 0 as n,m	o +\inftyIn general, 1 \Longrightarrow 2, but 2 
ot\Longrightarrow 1. Indeed, d(f_n,f_m) \le d(f_n,f) + d(f,f_m) by triangle inequality.If in a metric space, 1 \Longleftrightarrow 2, then the metric space is complete.Why completeness matters in PDE. If a method produces a Cauchy sequence of approximations, completeness guarantees a limit exists in the same space. That’s crucial for existence arguments and for convergence proofs.[!definition|1.2.7] Norm A norm is \|\cdot\|_X: X 	o \mathbb{R} such that\|f\|_X \ge 0 and \|f\|_X = 0 \Longleftrightarrow f=0\|\lambda f\|_X = \lambda \|f\|_X\|f+g\|_X \le \|f\|_X + \|g\|_XA space is normed if a norm is defined. A normed space is also a metric space: d(f,g) = \|f-g\|_X Comment. Most numerical error estimates are statements like \|u-u_h\|_X \le C h^p. That only makes sense after we choose a norm \|\cdot\|_X.[!definition|1.2.8] Banach Space A Banach space is a complete normed space.Comment. Banach spaces are the natural setting for fixed-point theorems and stability results.0.3 Inner products, Hilbert spaces, and orthogonality0.3.1 Why inner products show up in FEMGalerkin methods are built from orthogonality conditions like (u-u_h, v_h)=0. That requires an inner product structure.[!definition|1.2.9] Scalar Product (\cdot,\cdot)_X: X 	imes X 	o \mathbb{R} is a symmetric bilinear form such that(f,g)_X = (g,f)_X(f,f)_X \ge 0 and (f,f)_X = 0 \Longleftrightarrow f=0\left|(f_1,f_2)_Xight| \le (f_1,f_1)_X^{1/2}(f_2,f_2)_X^{1/2} [Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality]A scalar product induces a norm: \|f\|_X^2 = (f,f)_X So, a space with a scalar product is automatically normed.Key point. Inner product \Rightarrow norm \Rightarrow metric \Rightarrow talk about convergence.0.3.2 Example 1.2.10[!example|1.2.10] A standard estimate from the scalar product  egin{aligned} (f_1+f_2,f_1+f_2)_X &= (f_1,f_1)_X + 2(f_1,f_2)_X + (f_2,f_2)_X \ &\le \|f_1\|_X^2 + 2\|f_1\|_X\|f_2\|_X + \|f_2\|_X^2 \ &= (\|f_1\|_X + \|f_2\|_X)^2 \end{aligned} (Here the inequality step uses Cauchy–Schwarz on (f_1,f_2)_X.) Taking square-roots yields \|f_1+f_2\|_X \le \|f_1+f_2\|_X+\|f_2\|_X.Note (typo fix in words only). The last line should read: \|f_1+f_2\|_X \le \|f_1\|_X + \|f_2\|_X, which is exactly the triangle inequality for the induced norm.[!definition|1.2.11] Hilbert Space A Hilbert space is a Banach space equipped with a scalar product.Practical takeaway. Hilbert = “complete + inner product”. Most FEM theory lives in Hilbert spaces (especially L^2, H^1, H_0^1).[!definition|1.2.12] Orthogonality The angle between two functions is defined as \angle(f_1,f_2):\ \cos(\varphi) =  rac{(f_1,f_2)}{\|f_1\|\|f_2\|} =  rac{(f_1,f_2)}{(f_1,f_1)^{1/2}(f_2,f_2)^{1/2}} Two functions are orthogonal to each other \Longleftrightarrow (f,g)=0. We denote f \perp g.Interpretation. Orthogonality means “no component in that direction,” just like vectors in \mathbb{R}^n.0.4 Orthogonal Projection (Galerkin principle)When we approximate in a subspace X_L, the best approximation is obtained by orthogonal projection (in a Hilbert space). This is the geometric heart of the Galerkin method.0.4.1 Find the Best ApproximationLet X_L \subset X, where X_L is “small.” X_L and X are both Hilbert spaces.We want to find the best approximation f_L of f in X_L. So, we need to find f_L s.t. (f - f_L, v_L) = 0 \quad  orall\, v_L \in X_L What this condition means.f-f_L is the error.The condition says the error is orthogonal to the whole approximation space X_L.This uniquely characterizes f_L as the orthogonal projection of f onto X_L.This is an extension of the Pythagorean Theorem. If g_L \in X_L:  egin{aligned} \|f-g_L\|^2 &= (f-g_L,f-g_L) \ &= (f-f_L + f_L-g_L,\ f-f_L + f_L-g_L) \ &= \|f-f_L\|^2 + 2(f-f_L,f_L-g_L) + \|f_L-g_L\|^2 \ &= \|f-f_L\|^2 + \underbrace{2(f-f_L,f_L-g_L)}_{=0,\ 	ext{orthogonality}} + \|f_L-g_L\|^2 \ &= \|f-f_L\|^2 + \|f_L-g_L\|^2 \ &\ge \|f-f_L\|^2 \end{aligned} Conclusion. Among all g_L \in X_L, the minimizer of \|f-g_L\| is f_L. So “best approximation” = “orthogonal projection”.0.5 Lebesgue Integration and L^p spaces0.5.1 Why we switch to L^pMany PDE solutions are not classically smooth. We need spaces that:allow functions with limited regularity,still make integrals meaningful,provide norms used in stability/error estimates.[!definition|1.2.13] L^p Spaces L^p(a,b) = \left\{\, f:\ (L)\int_a^b f^p\,dx < +\infty ight\}, \quad 	ext{with } p=1,2,\ldots,\in \mathbb{N} Here, (L) indicates that the integration is done in Lebesgue sense. L^p(a,b) is the collection of functions that can be integrated in interval (a,b) in the Lebesgue sense without blowing up.These are Banach spaces with the norm \|f\|_p = \left(\int_a^b |f|^p\,dxight)^{1/p} Interpretation.L^1: integrable functions (area under curve finite).L^2: square-integrable (energy finite) — the most common in PDE/FEM.Similarly, L^\infty(a,b) = \left\{\, f:\ 	ext{bounded (up to all-measurable intervals) in }(a,b)ight\} is also a Banach space with norm \|f\|_\infty = \max_{(a,b)} |f| Comment. Strictly speaking, L^\infty uses the essential supremum (ignores measure-zero sets), but the above matches the typical intuition.Specially, L^2(a,b) or L^2(\Omega) with \Omega \subset \mathbb{R} is a Hilbert space:  egin{aligned} (f,g) &= \int_a^b f g\,dx \ \|f\|_2 &= \left(\int_a^b f^2\,dxight)^{1/2} = (f,f)^{1/2} \end{aligned} Why L^2 is special. It has an inner product, so we get orthogonality/projection tools.[!definition|1.2.14] Conjugate Spaces L^p and L^q are called conjugated spaces if we have the function f\in L^p(a,b) and g\in L^q(a,b) with  rac{1}{p}+ rac{1}{q}=1 We then have (L)\int_a^b f g\,dx < +\infty \quad 	ext{or}\quad f g \in L^1(a,b) Context. This is the setup for Hölder’s inequality and for defining dual pairings L^q = (L^p)' (for 1<p<\infty).[!remark|1.2.14] L^2 is conjugate with itself We have |(f,g)_{L^2}| \le \|f\|_2\|g\|_2 Comment. This is exactly Cauchy–Schwarz in L^2.0.6 Distributions and weak derivatives0.6.1 Motivation: derivatives that still exist when functions are not smoothIn PDE, solutions may have jumps, corners, or only be L^2. Classical derivatives may not exist, but we still want a “derivative” compatible with integration by parts (weak form). Distributions are the clean framework.[!definition|1.2.15] Dual Spaces The set of linear bounded functionals obtained on a space X is per se a functional space, that we call dual space and denote as X' X' = \left\{\mathcal{F}(f)\ 	ext{for } f\in X,\ 	ext{linear and s.t.}\ \|\mathcal{F}(f)\|\le c\|f\|_Xight\} Interpretation. Elements of X' are “bounded measurements” on X. Boundedness (\|\mathcal{F}(f)\|\le c\|f\|_X) is what makes the functional continuous and stable.[!theorem|1.2.16] Riesz Representation Theorem In L^2, the dual of L^2 is isometric to L^2. (This means that any linear and continuous functional in L^2 corresponds to an element within L^2 itself.)Practical meaning. Every bounded linear functional on L^2 can be written as an L^2 inner product with some g\in L^2: \mathcal{F}(f) = (g,f)_{L^2}. (You don’t need the full proof here; you use it later when deriving weak forms.)[!definition|1.2.17] Support The support of a function is where the function 
e 0 on the interval or region of the domain of definition. In particular, if the support is closed and bounded region, we say the function has compact support.Why compact support matters. It kills boundary terms in integration by parts (no “leakage” at infinity).[!definition|1.2.18] The Space \mathcal{D} \mathcal{D} = \{	ext{functions in } C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)\ (n\ge 1)\ 	ext{with compact support}\} The dual space of \mathcal{D}, \mathcal{D}' is defined in the following notion: \mathcal{D}':\ \langle T,fangle_{\mathcal{D}} \in \mathbb{R},\ 	ext{where } T\in\mathcal{D}'\ 	ext{is linear and continuous and } f\in\mathcal{D} T to be continuous is defined in the following sense: Let \mathrm{supp}(f_n)\subseteq K and f_n	o f and n	o\infty. Then, T is continuous if \langle T,f_nangle 	o \langle T,fangle Interpretation.\mathcal{D} = smooth test functions that vanish outside a bounded set.\mathcal{D}' = all continuous linear functionals acting on \mathcal{D}. These are the “generalized functions”.[!example|1.2.19] A distribution coming from a step function Let H(x) be the step function H(x)=  egin{cases} 0 & 	ext{for } x\le 0 \ 1 & 	ext{for } x>0 \end{cases} Then \langle T,fangle = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} H f\,dx = \int_0^{+\infty} f\,dx The functional \langle T_0,fangle = f(0) belongs to \mathcal{D}' |\langle T_0,fangle| \le \max_{x\in\mathbb{R}} |f(x)| Comment. Two important examples of distributions:f \mapsto \int_0^\infty f (integration against a possibly discontinuous function H),f \mapsto f(0) (evaluation at a point), which is not continuous on many L^p spaces but is meaningful on \mathcal{D}.[!definition|1.2.20] Distributions The objects of \mathcal{D}' are called distributions or generalized functions.0.7 Weak derivative[!theorem|1.2.21] Distributional derivative identity \langle T', fangle = -\langle T, f'angle Meaning. In the distribution sense, differentiating T is defined so that integration by parts is always true (with no boundary term due to compact support of f).Proof 1. Let g\in L^2. Then  egin{aligned} \langle g', fangle &= \int_{\mathbb{R}} g' f \ &= \underbrace{ ig[g f ig]_{-\infty}^{+\infty}}_{=0\ 	ext{since } f\ 	ext{has compact support}} - \int_{\mathbb{R}} g f' \ &= -\langle g, f'angle \end{aligned} Note that  ig[g f ig]_{-\infty}^{+\infty}=0 because \lim_{x	o\infty} f=0, and f has compact support.[!example|1.2.22] Differentiating the step function gives the Dirac impulse Consider H(x)=  egin{cases} 0 & 	ext{for } x\le 0 \ 1 & 	ext{for } x>0 \end{cases} Then, we can differentiate H  egin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} H' f &= -\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} H f' \ &= -\int_0^{+\infty} f' \ &= -[f]_0^{+\infty} \ &= f(0) \ &= \langle T_0, fangle \end{aligned} T_0 is called the Dirac-\delta and it is the mathematical description of an impulse. It is not a function in the traditional sense.Interpretation. H has a jump at 0. Its classical derivative is “zero everywhere except at 0”, which is captured by \delta.[!definition|1.2.23] Dirac-\delta Dirac-\delta is the element in \mathcal{D}' such that \langle \delta,fangle = f(0) We know that H'=\delta.[!theorem|1.2.24] Inclusion into \mathcal{D}' L^2 \subset \mathcal{D}' Comment. Any g\in L^2 defines a distribution by \langle g, fangle := \int_{\mathbb{R}} g f\,dx, so functions can be viewed as a special case of distributions.0.8 Sobolev spaces (the PDE workhorse)0.8.1 Measuring derivatives in L^2Sobolev spaces encode “how many derivatives exist in a weak sense” and how large they are. This is exactly what we need for:weak formulations (existence/uniqueness),regularity,FEM error estimates.[!definition|1.2.25] Sobolev Spaces Space H^k(a,b) (or H^k(\Omega)) is the space of functions f s.t. it belongs to L^2 together with all the derivatives up to the order k H^k(a,b)=\left\{\, f\ 	ext{s.t.}\ f,f',\ldots,f^{(k)}\in L^2 = H^0 ight\} In multiple dimensions, the derivatives are all the derivatives of order k  rac{\partial^{\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\cdots+\alpha_m} f}{\partial x_1^{\alpha_1}\partial x_2^{\alpha_2}\cdots \partial x_m^{\alpha_m}} \in L^2 \quad 	ext{with}\quad \sum_i \alpha_i = k These spaces are called Sobolev spaces. A more generalized definition W^{k,p}=\left\{\, f\ 	ext{s.t.}\ f,f',\ldots,f^{(k)}\in L^p ight\} So, H^k = W^{k,2}.Interpretation.H^0 = L^2.H^1 means f\in L^2 and its weak derivative f'\in L^2.Higher k means more (weak) smoothness.[!theorem|1.2.26] Properties of H^kH^k(a,b) is a Hilbert space with the scalar product (f,g)_{H^k} = \sum_{i=0}^k (f^{(i)},g^{(i)})_{L^2} H^1(a,b) has the norm \|f\|_{H^1}^2 = \|f\|_{L^2}^2 + \|f'\|_{L^2}^2 H^1 \subset L^2. So, \|f\|_{H^1}^2 \ge \|f\|_{L^2}^2 In general, H^{k+1} \subset H^k \subset \cdots \subset L^2 Why this nesting matters. More derivatives in L^2 implies stronger control on the function, hence a “smaller” space.0.9 Boundary values and trace (why H^1 is subtle)[!definition|1.2.27] Trace Operator Trace is an operator that maps a function in H^k to its value of the boundary, and, in general, reduces regularity. \gamma:\ H^k(\Omega)	o H^{k- rac{1}{2}}(\partial\Omega) is the (continuous) trace operator.Interpretation.Functions in H^1(\Omega) may not be classically continuous, yet they have a well-defined boundary value in an appropriate sense.The trace map “costs” a half-derivative of regularity.[!definition|1.2.28] The Space H_0^1 The space H_0^1(\Omega) is the space of H^1 functions with null trace on \partial\Omega.Practical meaning. This is the natural space for homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions u=0 on \partial\Omega.0.10 Poincaré inequality and equivalent norms (the energy norm idea)[!theorem|1.2.29] Poincare Inequality \exists\, c>0 s.t. for f\in H_0^1(\Omega) \|f\|_{L^2} \le c\|
abla f\|_{L^2} Therefore,  egin{aligned} \|
abla f\|_{L^2}^2 &\le \underbrace{\|f\|_{L^2}^2 + \|
abla f\|_{L^2}^2}_{\|f\|_{H_0^1}^2} \le (1+c^2)\|
abla f\|_{L^2}^2 \end{aligned} Hence, in H_0^1(\Omega), the norm of 
abla f in L^2 and of f in H^1 are equivalent. This is also true if the function has only a realization of the boundary (with measure >0) where it vanishes.Interpretation.On H_0^1(\Omega), controlling \|
abla f\|_{L^2} automatically controls \|f\|_{L^2}.So the “energy seminorm” \|
abla f\|_{L^2} is effectively a full norm on H_0^1.[!remark|1.2.29] Equivalent norms (abstract form) \alpha\|u\|_F \le \|u\|_S \le  eta\|u\|_F implies that \|\cdot\|_F and \|\cdot\|_S are equivalent.Why we care. Equivalent norms define the same notion of convergence and stability. In PDE, we often switch between norms that are easier to estimate.[!definition|1.2.30] Dual of H_0^1: H^{-1} H_0^1 \subset L^2 \subset H^{-1} Interpretation.H^{-1} is the dual space of H_0^1 (in a standard identification).Many PDE data terms (like forcing f) naturally live in H^{-1} when solutions live in H_0^1.0.11 Space–time function spaces (for time-dependent PDE)0.11.1 Space-Time Functional SpacesFor time-dependent problems, we have spaces that describe the two dependencies. For instance L^p(0,T;H^k(\Omega)) is the space of functions s.t. \|f\|_{H^k}(t)\in L^p(0,T).Interpretation. You measure spatial regularity in H^k, but that H^k-norm is a function of time, and you require it to be L^p in time.In short, we denote it as L^p(H^k). We will use L^2(H_0^1) and L^\infty(L^2).0.12 Sobolev embeddings (turn derivatives into integrability/continuity)[!theorem|1.2.31] Embedding Theorems If u\in H^s and \Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n0<2s<n:\ H^s\subset L^q, where 1\le q\le q^*=\dfrac{2n}{n-2s} [continuous embedding]2s=n:\ H^s\subset L^q\ \  orall\, q:\ 1\le q<+\infty2s>n:\ H^s\subset C^0(\overline{\Omega})Also, H^s\subset C^n(\overline{\Omega}) if s>n+\dfrac{n}{2}.Interpretation.Enough Sobolev regularity forces better integrability (L^q) and eventually continuity.This is how “weak derivatives” translate into classical-looking properties.[!remark|1.2.31] A boundary constraint can break linear-space structure H^1(\Omega)=\{f\in H^1,\ f(\partial\Omega)=1\} is not a space. In fact f_1,f_2\in H^1 \Longrightarrow f_1+f_2
otin H^1 Reason (intuition). If f_1|_{\partial\Omega}=1 and f_2|_{\partial\Omega}=1, then (f_1+f_2)|_{\partial\Omega}=2, violating the constraint. So affine constraints (fixed nonzero boundary values) create an affine set, not a vector space.

2.4.1 Finite Element: One Possible Choice of X_N[!remark] Remark. What if the problem is non-linear? -\Delta u + u^3 = f \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \int_\Omega 
abla u 
abla v + \int_\Omega u^3 v = f. This problem is WP (although we don’t have symmetry).Solving: linearize, then discretize: \int_\Omega 
abla u^{(k+1)} 
abla v + \int_\Omega  ig(u^{(k)} ig)^2 u^{(k+1)} v = f We can use root finding. For example, Newton’s method.Solving: discretize, then linearize u_N = \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} c_j \varphi_j, \qquad X_N = \mathrm{span}\{\varphi\}_{j=0}^{N-1}. Then, we form a non-linear equation F(c)=0. We can also use Newton’s method.2.4 Finite Element: One Possible Choice of X_NRecall: we need to compute a(\varphi_j,\varphi_i)=\int_\Omega 
abla\varphi_j 
abla\varphi_i.
