title: Diffussion Models — Full ELBO Derivation (compact, rigorous, annotated)
text: Notation (matches your notes):Forward (noising) Markov chain q: q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=\mathcal N\!\big(\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1},\,(1-\alpha_t)I\big), with 0<\alpha_t<1. \beta_t:=1-\alpha_t, \ \bar\alpha_t:=\prod_{s=1}^t\alpha_s. Marginal: q(x_t\mid x_0)=\mathcal N\!\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\,(1-\bar\alpha_t)I\big).Reverse (denoising) model p_\theta: p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t) Gaussian. Prior: p(x_T)=\mathcal N(0,I). Your notation s_\theta(x_t,t) denotes predicted noise (i.e., s_\theta\equiv\varepsilon_\theta).Our goal is a tight, readable derivation of the ELBO, the Gaussian posterior q(x_{t-1}\!\mid x_t,x_0), and the reduction to the standard noise-prediction MSE loss.1 1) ELBO via JensenWe start by inserting the forward chain as an importance distribution and applying Jensen’s inequality: \begin{aligned} \log p_\theta(x_0) &=\log \int \frac{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}{q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)}\,q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)\,dx_{1:T} \\ &\ge \mathbb E_{q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)}\!\left[ \log p_\theta(x_{0:T})-\log q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)\right]. \end{aligned} Factorize the Markov chains (your “Markov chain” line): \begin{aligned} p_\theta(x_{0:T}) &=p(x_T)\,\prod_{t=T}^{2} p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\,\cdot p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1),\\ q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0) &=\prod_{t=1}^{T} q(x_t\mid x_{t-1}). \end{aligned} Expanding the logs: \begin{aligned} \text{ELBO} &= \mathbb E_q\Big[ \log p(x_T) + \sum_{t=2}^T \log p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t) + \log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1) - \sum_{t=1}^T \log q(x_t\mid x_{t-1}) \Big]. \end{aligned} ### 1.a) The “B” telescoping (your blue block)Key identity (Bayes on the forward chain): \boxed{ \log q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)-\log q(x_t\mid x_{t-1}) = \log q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0) - \log q(x_t\mid x_0). } Why: From q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\,q(x_t\mid x_0)=q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\,q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0).Insert and subtract \sum_{t=2}^T \log q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0) inside ELBO, then apply the identity and sum from t=2 to T: \begin{aligned} \sum_{t=2}^T \big(\log q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)-\log q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\big) &= \sum_{t=2}^T \big(\log q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0) - \log q(x_t\mid x_0)\big) \\ &= \log q(x_1\mid x_0) - \log q(x_T\mid x_0) \end{aligned} Use this to cancel the -\log q(x_1\mid x_0) coming from -\sum_{t=1}^T \log q(x_t\mid x_{t-1}). The ELBO becomes$$ $$Equivalently, as a sum of KLs (your red/blue A,B decomposition):Practical notes (matching your margin comments):With p(x_T)=\mathcal N(0,I) and large T, q(x_T\mid x_0)\approx \mathcal N(0,I), so the terminal KL \to 0. The reconstruction term at t=1 is often dropped or replaced by a simple decoder loss. Training focuses on \sum_{t=2}^T KLs.2 2) The forward posterior q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0) (your “part A”)We combine two Gaussians in x_{t-1}: q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)=\mathcal N\!\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_0,\ (1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I\big), \quad q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=\mathcal N\!\big(\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1},\ (1-\alpha_t)I\big). Up to a constant, q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\ \propto\ q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\,q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0). Collect quadratic terms in x_{t-1} (your A,b line): \begin{aligned} &-\frac{1}{2(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}\|x_{t-1}-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0\|^2 -\frac{1}{2(1-\alpha_t)}\|x_t-\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}\|^2 \\ &= -\frac12\,x_{t-1}^\top \underbrace{\Big(\tfrac{1}{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}+\tfrac{\alpha_t}{1-\alpha_t}\Big)}_{A}\,x_{t-1} \ +\ x_{t-1}^\top \underbrace{\Big(\tfrac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}}{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0 +\tfrac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}{1-\alpha_t}x_t\Big)}_{b} \ +\ \text{const}. \end{aligned} Thus the posterior is Gaussian with precision A I and mean A^{-1}b: \boxed{ q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)=\mathcal N\!\big(\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0),\ \tilde\sigma_t^2 I\big),\qquad \tilde\sigma_t^2=A^{-1}=\frac{(1-\alpha_t)(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}=\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\beta_t. } For the mean, simplify A^{-1}b to the standard closed form: \boxed{ \tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0) = \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_t \;+\; \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0. } 2.a) Equivalent “\varepsilon” form (your boxed conversion)Introduce the reparameterization (forward marginal): x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon,\qquad \varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I). Algebra gives an equivalent expression you used on the right board: \boxed{ \tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\varepsilon\right). } (Verify by substituting x_t and collecting terms in x_0 and \varepsilon.)3 3) Turning each KL into a noise-MSE (your red box “Because same variance”)Assume the reverse conditional uses the same variance as the true posterior: p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)=\mathcal N\!\big(\mu_\theta(x_t,t),\ \tilde\sigma_t^2 I\big), and parameterize its mean via predicted noise (your s_\theta): \boxed{ \mu_\theta(x_t,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} \left(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,s_\theta(x_t,t)\right), \qquad s_\theta \approx \varepsilon. } For Gaussians with equal covariance \Sigma=\tilde\sigma_t^2 I, \mathrm{KL}\big(\mathcal N(m_1,\Sigma)\,\|\,\mathcal N(m_2,\Sigma)\big) =\frac{1}{2}\,(m_1-m_2)^\top \Sigma^{-1}(m_1-m_2). Here m_1=\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0), m_2=\mu_\theta(x_t,t). Using the \varepsilon-form above,$$$$Therefore each KL term becomes a weighted MSE on the noise: \boxed{ \mathrm{KL}\!\left(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\,\|\,p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\right) =\underbrace{\frac{1}{2\tilde\sigma_t^2}\cdot\frac{\beta_t^2}{\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)}}_{\displaystyle \lambda_t} \,\big\|s_\theta(x_t,t)-\varepsilon\big\|^2. } With \tilde\sigma_t^2=\dfrac{\beta_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}, this simplifies to \boxed{ \lambda_t =\frac{\beta_t}{2\,\alpha_t\,(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}. } Many implementations use the “simple loss” by dropping \lambda_t and minimizing an unweighted MSE (or a different schedule weighting); that matches your note “in practice only evaluate this”.4 4) Final training objective (your gray box)Sampling x_0\sim\text{data}, t\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\{1,\dots,T\}, \varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I), form x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon. Then \boxed{ \mathcal L_{\text{simple}}(\theta) =\mathbb E\big[\;\|\,\varepsilon - s_\theta(x_t,t)\,\|^2\;\big] \quad\text{(common practical loss)} } and the exact ELBO-consistent, equal-variance objective is \boxed{ \mathcal L_{\text{ELBO}}(\theta) =\sum_{t=2}^T \mathbb E\big[\,\lambda_t\,\|\,\varepsilon - s_\theta(x_t,t)\,\|^2\big] \;+\; \underbrace{\text{(terminal KL)}_{\approx 0}}_{\mathrm{KL}(q(x_T\mid x_0)\,\|\,p(x_T))} \;+\; \underbrace{\text{(reconstruction at }t=1\text{)}}_{\mathrm{KL}(q(x_0\mid x_1)\,\|\,p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1))}. } 5 5) One-line score-matching connection (your last page)Because x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon, predicting \varepsilon is equivalent (up to known scalings) to predicting the score \nabla_{x_t}\log q_t(x_t). This links DDPM training to denoising score matching and to continuous-time score-based SDE formulations.5.1 (Everything above matches your A/B blocks, the telescoping identity, the A^{-1}b,A^{-1} posterior derivation, the \varepsilon substitution, and the final KL→MSE reduction with the explicit weight \lambda_t.)

title: GANs
text:
1 从 VAE 到 GAN1.1 大图景与动机我们要解决什么问题？ 给定真实数据分布 p_{	ext{data}}(x)，学习一个生成模型 G 使其隐变量 z\sim p(z) 下生成 x=G(z) 的分布 p_G(x) 尽可能接近 p_{	ext{data}}(x)。VAE 路线（有log-likelihood）：显式假设 p_	heta(x\mid z)，用变分下界（ELBO）来近似最大化对数似然 \log p_	heta(x)。优点是有概率语义、训练稳定；常见问题是重建模糊（均值化效应）。GAN 路线（无log-likelihood）：不写 p(x\mid z) 的显式密度，直接通过「判别器 vs 生成器」的对抗来最小化两分布的差异。优点是生成锐利；挑战是训练不稳、模式崩塌。VAE 与 ELBO中我们有这些问题：z has smaller dimension.Distribution of z does not guarantee matching the distribution of x.Average training points (blurring effect).于是我们转向 GAN 的minmax问题，推导optimal discrimiator与和 JS 散度的关系，然后讨论 WGAN（Wasserstein-1 距离）、条件 GAN、以及训练层面的问题与缓解策略。1.2 VAE 回顾：从似然最大化到 ELBO1.2.1 潜变量模型与证据下界我们要最大化 \log p_	heta(x)，但边缘化 z 通常不可解：  egin{aligned} \log p_	heta(x) &= \log \int p_	heta(x, z)\,dz = \log \int p_	heta(x\mid z)\,p(z)\,dz. \end{aligned} VAE 以变分分布 q_\phi(z\mid x) 近似后验 p_	heta(z\mid x)。由 Jensen 不等式得 ELBO：  egin{aligned} \log p_	heta(x) &= \log \int q_\phi(z\mid x)\, rac{p_	heta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\,dz \ &\ge \int q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\log  rac{p_	heta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\,dz \;=\; \mathcal{L}(	heta,\phi; x). \end{aligned}展开得  egin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(	heta,\phi;x) &= \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z\mid x)} ig[\log p_	heta(x\mid z) ig] - \mathrm{KL}\! ig(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z) ig). \end{aligned}1.2.2 直觉第一项是重建项：z 下重建 x 的对数似然期望，逼真度。 第二项是正则项：让 q_\phi(z\mid x) 接近先验 p(z)，保证隐空间结构与可采样性。1.2.3 重参数化技巧若 q_\phi(z\mid x)=\mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x),\operatorname{diag}\sigma^2_\phi(x))，令 \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)， egin{aligned} z \;=\; \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x)\odot \varepsilon, \end{aligned} 即可把对 z 的随机性外移到 \varepsilon，使梯度可反传。优点/局限：VAE 有稳定似然学习与编码器-解码器结构，但常出现过度平滑/模糊重建。接下来转入 GAN 的「无似然」思想。1.3 GAN 的极小极大：从判别式学习度量分布差异1.3.1 原始 GAN 目标判别器 D(x)\in(0,1) 估计「来自真实数据的概率」，生成器 G(z) 试图以假乱真： egin{aligned} \min_G \max_D \; V(D,G) &= \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{	ext{data}}} ig[\log D(x) ig] \;+\; \mathbb{E}_{z\sim p(z)} ig[\log (1-D(G(z))) ig]. \end{aligned} ### 1.3.2 固定 G 时的最优判别器 D^* 对每个 x 局部最大化，被积函数为 \;p_{	ext{data}}(x)\log D(x) + p_G(x)\log(1-D(x))。 令导数为 0： egin{aligned}  rac{p_{	ext{data}}(x)}{D(x)} -  rac{p_G(x)}{1-D(x)} = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; D^*(x) =  rac{p_{	ext{data}}(x)}{p_{	ext{data}}(x)+p_G(x)}. \end{aligned}1.3.3 代回得与 JS 散度的关系将 D^* 代回价值函数，得到  egin{aligned} V(D^*,G) &= \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{	ext{data}}}\!\left[\log  rac{p_{	ext{data}}(x)}{p_{	ext{data}}(x)+p_G(x)}ight] + \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_G}\!\left[\log  rac{p_G(x)}{p_{	ext{data}}(x)+p_G(x)}ight] \ &= -\log 4 + 2\,\mathrm{JS}\! ig(p_{	ext{data}} \,\|\, p_G ig). \end{aligned} 因此，在optimal discriminator下，GAN 等价于最小化 \mathrm{JS}(p_{	ext{data}}\|p_G)。直觉：判别器为我们隐式地诱导了一个分布差异度量（JS），无需显式密度函数。1.3.4 非饱和生成器损失原式中 \max_D 的对数项使得当 D(G(z))\approx 0 时梯度饱和。实践中常改用  egin{aligned} \min_G \; 	ilde{J}(G) = - \mathbb{E}_{z\sim p(z)} ig[\log D(G(z)) ig], \end{aligned} 以获得更强梯度信号（同一固定点，不同梯度路径）。1.4 WGAN：引入 Wasserstein-1 距离JS 在「两个distribution不重叠的」时梯度不稳定。WGAN 用地球搬运距离（W_1）替代：  oxed{ egin{aligned} W(p_{	ext{data}},p_	heta) = \inf_{\gamma\in\Pi(p_{	ext{data}},p_	heta)} \;\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\gamma} ig[\|x-y\| ig] \end{aligned}} 其对偶（Kantorovich–Rubinstein）形式：  egin{aligned} W(p_{	ext{data}},p_G) = \sup_{\|f\|_{L}\le 1}\;\Big(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{	ext{data}}}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_	heta}[f(x)]\Big). \end{aligned} WGAN 用一个 1-Lipschitz 的打分函数 f_w（discriminator 	o critic）近似该上确界：  egin{aligned} \max_{w:\|f_w\|_L\le 1}\; \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{	ext{data}}}[f_w(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{z\sim p(z)}[f_w(G(z))]. \end{aligned} 生成器最小化该差值。实践中以权重裁剪或梯度惩罚（WGAN-GP） 来约束 1-Lipschitz：  egin{aligned} \min_G \max_w\;\; &\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{	ext{data}}}[f_w(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{z}[f_w(G(z))] \ &\quad - \lambda \,\mathbb{E}_{\hat x\sim\mathbb{P}_{\hat x}} ig(\|
abla_{\hat x} f_w(\hat x)\|_2 - 1 ig)^2. \end{aligned}直觉：W_1 在分布几乎不重叠时仍给出有意义且连续的梯度，缓解训练不稳与模式崩塌。2 Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)2.1 Forward AnalysisGenerator: G_	heta(z) Input: latent vector z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I) (random noise). Output: generated image.Discriminator: D_\phi(x) Input: real or generated image. Output: scalar in [0,1], probability of being real.Diagrammatically: z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I) \;\; \longrightarrow \;\; G_	heta(z) \;\; \longrightarrow \;\; D_\phi(x) \in [0,1].2.2 Training ObjectiveDiscriminator goal: maximize \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P_{	ext{data}}} \log D(x) > maximize D(x) to correctly classify real images.Generator goal: minimize \mathbb{E}_{z \sim P_z} \log ig(1 - D(G(z)) ig) > fool D into recognizing fake images as real.2.3 Overall Minimax Game\min_G \max_D \Bigg[ \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P_{	ext{data}}} \log D(x) \;+\; \mathbb{E}_{z \sim P_z} \log(1 - D(G(z))) \Bigg] Define the loss as L = - 	ext{goal}.3 Optimal Discriminator[!definition] Optimal Discriminator When fixing the generator G, the optimal discriminator is: D^*(x) =  rac{P_{	ext{data}}(x)}{P_{	ext{data}}(x) + P_G(x)}3.1 Plug Back into GAN Objective egin{aligned} &\quad\,\mathbb{E}_{x \sim P_{	ext{data}}} \log  rac{P_{	ext{data}}(x)}{P_{	ext{data}}(x) + P_G(x)} + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim P_z} \log  rac{P_G(x)}{P_{	ext{data}}(x) + P_G(x)} \[6pt] &= \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P_{	ext{data}}} \log  rac{P_{	ext{data}}(x)}{2m(x)} + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim P_z} \log  rac{P_G(x)}{2m(x)} \[6pt] &= -\log 4 \;+\; KL ig(P_{	ext{data}} \,\|\, m ig) + KL ig(P_G \,\|\, m ig) \end{aligned} where m = 	frac{1}{2} ig(P_{	ext{data}} + P_G ig).3.2 Jensen–Shannon Divergence (JSD)Symmetric divergence: JSD(P \,\|\, Q) = 	frac{1}{2} KL(P \,\|\, m) + 	frac{1}{2} KL(Q \,\|\, m). Thus the GAN loss is: L(G) = 2 \cdot JSD\!\left(P_{	ext{data}} \,\|\, P_Gight) - \log 4.3.3 Issues with GANP_{	ext{data}} and P_G often lie on different manifolds. JSD \approx \log 2 → gradient vanishes for the generator. Leads to mode collapse (many z map to the same G(z)).4 Improvement: Better Metric (Wasserstein Distance)4.1.1 Wasserstein-1 Distance (WGAN)[!definition|*] Wasserstein Distance We define the minimal cost to transport mass from one distribution to another: W(P, Q) = \inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(P,Q)} \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim \gamma} \|x - y\| as the Wasserstein Distance.Symmetry: W(P,Q) = W(Q,P). Referred to as Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD). In WGAN, enforce 1-Lipschitz constraint on D.4.2 Enforcing the 1-Lipschitz Constraint in WGANs4.2.1 Weight Clipping (Original WGAN)Idea: Directly clip critic weights to a fixed range after every update: w \; \leftarrow \; 	ext{clip}(w, -c, c) Ensures the function doesn’t become too steep. Problems: Can lead to capacity underuse and poor critic performance.4.2.2 Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP)Idea: Penalize the critic if its gradient norm deviates from 1.Add a regularization term to the loss: \lambda \, \mathbb{E}_{\widehat{x} \sim p_{\widehat{x}}} \Big[  ig( \|
abla_{\widehat{x}} f(\widehat{x})\|_2 - 1  ig)^2 \Big] where:\widehat{x} is sampled along straight lines between real and generated data\lambda is a penalty coefficientEncourages \|
abla f(\widehat{x})\|_2 \approx 1, enforcing Lipschitz continuity.4.2.3 comparisonMethodProsConsWeight ClippingSimple to implementCan hurt capacity; unstableGradient PenaltyMore stable; widely usedSlightly more computation4.2.4 procedureinterpolation of \widehat{x} between real and fake xcompute gradient norm: g=
abla_{\hat{x}} f(\hat{x}), then \left(\|g\|_2-1ight)^2auto-differentiation w.r.t. \widehat{x}大多数现代 WGAN 实现都采用 WGAN-GP.4.3 Conditional GAN（cGAN）：在标签/条件下生成引入条件 y（如类别/文本），把判别与生成都条件化：  egin{aligned} \min_G \max_D \;\; &\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim p_{	ext{data}}} ig[\log D(x,y) ig] \ &\;+\; \mathbb{E}_{z\sim p(z),\, y\sim p(y)} ig[\log (1 - D(G(z,y),y)) ig]. \end{aligned} 或在 WGAN 中加入条件，critic 学习条件下分布偏差。5 从 VAE 到 GAN的数学与理念的桥梁5.1.1 「likelihood」 vs. 「non-likelihood」VAE：最大化 \log p_	heta(x)，用 ELBO 下界，学习到后验近似 q_\phi(z\mid x)。 GAN：不写likelihood，直接最小化分布差异（JS、Wasserstein 等），通过discriminator/critic 提供信号。5.1.2 两者的互补视角训练信号：VAE 的重建损失在像素域，GAN 的信号在判别器特征域（往往更贴近感知质量）。 多样性 vs. 锐利度：VAE 更多样但模糊；GAN 更锐利但易模式崩塌。 后验推断：VAE 自带编码器；GAN 需借助额外网络（如 BiGAN/ALI）学习逆映射。5.2 训练细节与典型问题5.2.1 模式崩塌（mode collapse）症状：生成样本缺乏多样性，集中到少数模式。 缓解：WGAN/WGAN-GP；使用多判别器或小批次判别（minibatch discrimination）；加入噪声或正则。5.2.2 判别器过强/过弱过强：生成器几乎无梯度；做法：限制判别器训练步数或容量，加入 label smoothing。 过弱：无法提供有信息的梯度；做法：提高判别器更新步、使用谱归一化等。5.2.3 损失选择与指标原始 GAN 损失 vs 非饱和损失；Wasserstein 损失更稳定。 评估：FID、IS、Precision/Recall for GANs 等。

title: NF_transcribed
text:
1 Normalizing Flows (NF) and Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNF)Clean compilation of handwritten lecture notes. Structure and notation preserved.1. Change of Variables in DistributionsLet x = f_	heta(z), with inverse z = f_	heta^{-1}(x).  egin{aligned} p_X(x; 	heta) &= p_Z(f_	heta^{-1}(x)) \left|\det  rac{\partial f_	heta^{-1}(x)}{\partial x}ight|. \end{aligned} In 1D:  egin{aligned} p_X(x; 	heta) &= p_Z(f_	heta^{-1}(x)) \left| rac{d f_	heta^{-1}(x)}{dx}ight|. \end{aligned} For higher dimensions: \;\left|\det J_{f_	heta^{-1}}(x)ight| represents the absolute determinant of the inverse Jacobian.2. Linear Map InterpretationFor a linear map y = f(x) = Jx: J =  rac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \quad \det J 	ext{ = volume scaling factor.} Example in \mathbb{R}^2: If J =  egin{bmatrix}3 & 1\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}, then \det J = 6.3. Nonlinear Case and Local LinearizationFor f: \mathbb{R}^d 	o \mathbb{R}^d, near x_0,  egin{aligned} f(x) \approx f(x_0) + J_f(x_0)(x - x_0), \end{aligned} the first-order Taylor expansion.4. Flow Composition and NotationWe compose multiple invertible mappings: f_	heta = f_K \circ f_{K-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_1. For intermediate states: z_i = f_i(z_{i-1}), \quad z_0 \sim p_0(z_0), \quad z_K = x. Hence p_i(z_i) represents the density at stage i.5. Density Recursion and Change of VariablesIf x = f_	heta(z_0), then z_{i-1} = f_i^{-1}(z_i). By change of variable:  egin{aligned} p_i(z_i) &= p_{i-1}(z_{i-1}) \left|\det  rac{\partial f_i^{-1}(z_i)}{\partial z_i}ight|. \end{aligned} Recursively:  egin{aligned} p_X(x;	heta) &= p_Z(f_	heta^{-1}(x)) \left|\det J_{f_	heta^{-1}}(x)ight| \ &= p_Z(z_0) \prod_{i=1}^K \left|\det  rac{\partial z_{i-1}}{\partial z_i}ight| = p_Z(z_0) \prod_{i=1}^K \left|\det  rac{\partial f_i^{-1}(z_i)}{\partial z_i}ight|. \end{aligned} Or equivalently: p_X(x;	heta) = p_Z(z_0)\prod_{i=1}^{K} \left|\det  rac{\partial f_i(z_{i-1})}{\partial z_{i-1}}ight|^{-1}. Log form:  egin{aligned} \log p_X(x|	heta) = \log p_Z(z_0) - \sum_{i=1}^{K}\log\left|\det  rac{\partial z_i}{\partial z_{i-1}}ight|, \end{aligned} with z_0 = f_	heta^{-1}(x).6. Objective Function \max_	heta \sum_{x\in	ext{data}} \log p_X(x|	heta). 7. Affine Coupling LayersTo ensure invertibility: Split input x = (x_1, x_2),  egin{aligned} y_1 &= x_1,\ y_2 &= x_2 \odot \exp(s(x_1)) + t(x_1), \end{aligned} so y = f(x) = (y_1, y_2).Inverse:  egin{aligned} x_1 &= y_1,\ x_2 &= (y_2 - t(y_1)) \odot \exp(-s(y_1)). \end{aligned} ### Jacobian and DeterminantJacobian: J = , \quad \det J = \exp\!\left(\sum_j s_j(x_1)ight). Hence, computing \log \det J is cheap.8. Neural ODE and Continuous Normalizing Flow (CNF)Limitations of discrete NFs:Fixed K layers, limited approximation.We define the continuous flow:  rac{dz}{dt} = f_	heta(z(t),t), \quad t\in[0,1]. 9. Deriving the CNF EquationDefine probability density p(z,t) and velocity field f_	heta(z,t).Flux through surface: (p f_	heta)\cdot \hat{n}. By divergence theorem: \oint_{\partial V} (p f_	heta)\cdot \hat{n} \, dS = \int_V 
abla_z \cdot (p f_	heta)\,dz. Conservation of probability:  rac{d}{dt}\int_V p\,dz = -\int_V 
abla_z\cdot(p f_	heta)\,dz \Rightarrow  oxed{\partial_t p + 
abla_z\cdot(p f_	heta)=0.} 10. Log-Density DynamicsAlong trajectories:  rac{dz}{dt} = f_	heta(z,t),  rac{d}{dt}p(z(t),t) = \partial_t p + f_	heta \cdot 
abla_z p. Substitute from continuity:  rac{d}{dt}p(z(t),t) = -p\,(
abla_z \cdot f_	heta),  oxed{ rac{d}{dt}\log p = -
abla_z \cdot f_	heta = -\operatorname{Tr}\!\left( rac{\partial f_	heta}{\partial z}ight)}. Hence, \log p_{t_1}(z_{t_1}) = \log p_{t_0}(z_{t_0}) - \int_{t_0}^{t_1}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left( rac{\partial f_	heta}{\partial z}ight)dt. 11. ODE Solver (Runge–Kutta) y(t_1) = y(t_0) + \int_{t_0}^{t_1} f(t,y(t))\,dt. Augmented state: y_t = [z(t), \log p_t], \quad y_0 = [x_	ext{data}, 0]. 12. Hutchinson’s Trick (Trace Estimation) \operatorname{Tr}(J) = \mathbb{E}_{s\sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)}[s^	op J s] \approx s^	op J s. Define scalar S(z) = \langle f_	heta(z), s angle. 
abla_z S(z) = J^	op s. 13. Likelihood Formulation (Backward Integration) \log p_X(x) = \log p_Z(z_0) - \int_0^1 \operatorname{div}f_	heta(z_t,t)\,dt. Alternatively, \log p_Z(z_1) = \log p_X(x) + \int_1^0 \operatorname{Tr}(J_f)\,dt. Training uses negative sign convention.14. Adjoint Method for GradientsAdjoint variable: a_t =  rac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_t}. State evolution: z_{t+\Delta t} = z_t + \int_t^{t+\Delta t} f_	heta(z_	au,	au)\,d	au. Adjoint dynamics: \dot{a}_t = -\left( rac{\partial f_	heta}{\partial z}ight)^	op a_t. Parameter sensitivity:  rac{d}{dt}\left( rac{\partial z_t}{\partial 	heta}ight) =  rac{\partial f_	heta}{\partial z} rac{\partial z_t}{\partial 	heta} +  rac{\partial f_	heta}{\partial 	heta}. Gradient formula:  oxed{ rac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial 	heta} = -\int_{t_1}^{t_0} a_t^	op  rac{\partial f_	heta}{\partial 	heta}(z_t,t)\,dt.} 15. SummaryChange of variables → discrete NF likelihood.Affine coupling → efficient triangular Jacobian.CNF → continuous ODE + log-density ODE.Hutchinson’s trick → efficient trace estimation.Adjoint method → efficient gradient backprop through ODE solver.

title: Normalizing Flows (NF)
text:
1 Change of Variable Theorem1.1 CoV TheoremWe want to push the distribution from z	o x and compute the density of a transformed variable. Let x = f_	heta(z), and z = f_	heta^{-1}(x), then the density transforms as:  egin{aligned} p_X(x;	heta) &= \underbrace{p_Z ig(f_	heta^{-1}(x) ig)}_{\substack{	ext{density of the latent }z=f_	heta^{-1}(x)\	ext{(under the prior)}}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\Bigl|\det rac{\partial f_	heta^{-1}(x)}{\partial x}\Bigr|}_{\substack{	ext{Jacobian det }	ext{of the inverse }f_	heta^{-1}}} \end{aligned} Together, they define the density of x under the flow.1.1.1 One-dimentaionl special case:For 1D case, the determinant vanishes: p_X(x;	heta) = p_Z(f_	heta^{-1}(x)) \cdot \Big| rac{d}{dx} f_	heta^{-1}(x)\Big| ## 1.2 Comparing Base vs. Transformed DistributionsWe start with a simple base distribution: z \sim {N}(0,1) and apply a linear invertible transformation x	o z, where x = f(z) = 2z + 3 By the Change of Variables Theorem: p_X(x) = p_Z(f^{-1}(x)) \cdot \left| rac{d}{dx} f^{-1}(x)ight| we now plot both distributions to see how the transformation shifts and stretches the density.1.2.1 Change of Variables: IntuitionSuppose the transformation: x = \exp(z), \quad z = \ln(x), \quad x > 0 with base distribution z \sim {N}(0,1). By the change of variables theorem:  egin{align} p_X(x) & = p_Z(\ln(x)) \cdot \Big| rac{d}{dx}\ln(x)\Big| \ & = p_Z(\ln(x))\cdot  rac{1}{x} \end{align} This produces a log-normal distribution for x.2 Jacobian Determinant and General Functions2.1 Linear CaseFor a linear map f(x) = Jx, the Jacobian is the constant matrix J: J =  egin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \det(J) = 6. Every region in \mathbb{R}^2 is stretched in area by a factor \det(J)=6.Mass is preserved during Jacobian transformation2.2 General Nonlinear FunctionFor a smooth function f:\mathbb{R}^d 	o \mathbb{R}^d, around a point x_0 we use the first-order Taylor expansion: f(x) \;\approx\; f(x_0) + J_f(x_0)(x - x_0) where J_f(x_0) is the Jacobian matrix of f at x_0.J_f(x_0) is the local linear approximation of f. \det J_f(x_0) measures how f locally stretches (>1) or compresses (<1) volumes near x_0. If \det J_f(x_0) = 0, the map is not locally invertible.2.3 Change of Variables[!theorem|2.3.1] Change of Variables If z \sim p_Z(z) and x = f(z), then p_X(x) = p_Z(f^{-1}(x)) \cdot \left|\det J_{f^{-1}}(x)ight| \det J_f > 1: spreads probability mass (expansion). 0 < \det J_f < 1: concentrates probability mass (compression). \det J_f = 0: collapses space → (not a valid density).3 Interpreting the Jacobian Determinant in ProbabilityThe determinant of the Jacobian tells us how volumes are scaled locally by the transformation f. Since probability mass is preserved under transformation:[!theorem|3.1] probability mass conservation \quad p_Z(z)\,dz = p_X(x)\,dx the density p_X(x) must adjust according to the Jacobian determinant. ## 3.1 Geometric MeaningThe \det J_f(x) is the local volume scaling factor:If \det J_f(x) = 2: a small region doubles in volume. If \det J_f(x) = 0.5: a small region shrinks to half the volume. If \det J_f(x) = 0: the region collapses to lower dimension (area/volume = 0)3.2 Effect on Probability Densities  egin{align} |\det J_f| > 1: \;\quad	ext{expansion} →\qquad\; 	ext{stretch space} & → 	ext{density thins out} \ 0 < |\det J_f| < 1: \;	ext{compression} →\qquad 	ext{squeeze space} & → 	ext{density thickens} \ |\det J_f| = 0: \;\qquad	ext{collapse} → 	ext{a lower dimension} & → 	ext{no density defined} \end{align} 3.3 Examplez \sim {N}(0,1). Transform x = 2z:\det J_f = 2. Distribution is wider and shorter (spread out).Transform x = 0.5z:\det J_f = 0.5. Distribution is narrower and taller (more concentrated).4 Normalizing FlowsDefinition: A Normalizing Flow is a sequence of K invertible transformations:  egin{align} f = f_K \circ f_{K-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_2 \circ f_1 \end{align} and the jacobian reads:  egin{align} J_{f}(z) & =J_{f_{k}}(z_{k-1})J_{f_{k-1}}(z_{k-2})\dots J_{1}(z_{0}) \ \ \Longrightarrow\det J_{f}(z) & = \Pi\det (J_{f_{i}}(z_{i-1}))\ \end{align} Some of the properties we have are:  egin{align} \det J_{f}(z) & =  rac{1}{\det J_{f^{-1}}} \end{align} NF|737x222Change of Variables (composition): If x = f_	heta(z), then: p_X(x;	heta) = p_Z\!\left(f_	heta^{-1}(x)ight) \prod_{i=1}^K \left| \det  rac{\partial f_i^{-1}}{\partial z_i} ight| Equivalently: p_X(x;	heta) = p_Z\!\left(f_	heta^{-1}(x)ight) \prod_{i=1}^K \left| \det  rac{\partial f_i}{\partial z_{i-1}} ight|^{-1} Log-likelihood form (practical for training): \log p_X(x;	heta) = \log p_Z(z_K) - \sum_{i=1}^K \log \left| \det  rac{\partial f_i}{\partial z_{i-1}} ight| where z_K = f_	heta^{-1}(x).4.1.1 Lecture notes  egin{align} y_{2} & =x_{2} \cdot \exp(s(x_{1}))+t(x_{1}) \ x_{2}& =  rac{y_{2} -t(y_{1})}{ \exp(s(x_{1}))} \end{align} J_{f} =  egin{bmatrix} I & 0 \ 	imes & \operatorname{diag}(\exp(s(x_i))) \end{bmatrix} so $$ $$ ### 4.1.2 Key PointsEach transformation f_i must be:InvertibleHave a tractable Jacobian determinantThe base distribution p_Z is usually simple (e.g. standard Gaussian).Training maximizes the exact log-likelihood of data: \max_	heta \sum_{x \in {D}} \log p_X(x;	heta). # 5 Neural ODEs for Continuous Flows Tutorial5.1 Background and Intuition5.1.1 Normalizing Flows (NFs)Goal: Learn a transformation f that maps a simple base distribution (e.g., Gaussian) to a complicated target distribution. Idea: If z_0 \sim p(z_0) and we apply an invertible transformation z_1 = f(z_0), then the new density is given by the change of variables formula: \log p(z_1) = \log p(z_0) - \log \left| \det  rac{\partial f}{\partial z_0} ight| 5.1.2 Limitations of Discrete FlowsEach transformation is a step. To build complex distributions, we often stack many transformations. Computing the Jacobian determinant can be expensive (except for special architectures like coupling layers).5.1.3 Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs)Instead of a finite stack, let’s imagine infinitely many infinitesimal transformations — this leads to a differential equation:  rac{dz}{dt} = f_	heta(z(t), t). Here, f_	heta is a neural network. Now, the change in log-density evolves smoothly over time. Crucial formula (from instantaneous change of variables):  rac{d}{dt} \log p(z(t)) = - 	ext{Tr}\!\left( rac{\partial f_	heta}{\partial z}ight). 👉 This means:To follow how the density changes, we only need the trace of the Jacobian of f_	heta, not the full determinant. This can be approximated with Hutchinson’s trick in high dimensions.5.2 Intuition with a PictureImagine you start with a cloud of Gaussian samples.As time flows (t=0 	o 1), the neural ODE “pushes” each point smoothly along a vector field. This vector field is learned so that by the end (t=1) the cloud matches the target data distribution. The flow is smooth, invertible, and volume-preserving up to the divergence term (controlled by the Jacobian trace).6 🌊 Flux, Net Flow, and the Divergence TheoremLet’s connect the concepts of flux, net flow, and probability conservation using the divergence theorem — a key result you’ve already learned in multivariable calculus.6.1 🔹 1. Local Flow (Flux)Consider a probability density p(z,t) and a velocity field f_	heta(z,t). The quantity p(z,t)\,f_	heta(z,t) is called the probability flux (or flow field). It tells you how much probability mass per unit area per unit time is moving through each point and in what direction.p → how much probability is there f_	heta → how fast and in what direction it moves → Together, p f_	heta describes the local flow rate.6.2 🔹 2. Net Flow Across a RegionNow take any fixed region V in space (with boundary surface \partial V).We can ask: How much total probability is leaving this region per unit time?That’s given by the net outward flux through the boundary: 	ext{Net outflow from } V = \oint_{\partial V} (p f_	heta) \cdot n \, dS, where:n is the unit outward normal to the surface, (p f_	heta) \cdot n is the outward flow rate per unit area, integrating over the boundary adds up all those local flows.This surface integral gives the total rate at which probability exits V.6.3 🔹 3. The Divergence TheoremThe divergence theorem relates a surface integral of flux to a volume integral of divergence: \oint_{\partial V} (p f_	heta) \cdot n \, dS = \int_V 
abla_z \cdot (p f_	heta) \, dz. In words:The total flow leaving a region through its boundary equals the sum of all the local outflows (divergences) inside the region.6.4 Recall: DivergenceWe denote  egin{align} 
abla _{z}\cdot(p(f_{	heta})) & =\sum  rac{\partial p(f_{	heta})}{\partial z_{i}} \ & = \left(  rac{\partial}{\partial z_{1}},  rac{\partial}{\partial z_{2}},\dots  rac{\partial}{\partial z_{k}} ight) \cdot (p(f_{	heta})_{1}, p(f_{	heta})_{2}, \dots,p(f_{	heta})_{k}) \[6pt] & = \operatorname{tr}(J_{pf_{	heta}}(z)) \end{align} 6.5 🔹 4. Conservation of ProbabilityTotal probability inside V at time t is: P_V(t) = \int_V p(z,t)\,dz. The rate of change of this probability is:  rac{dP_V}{dt} = \int_V  rac{\partial p}{\partial t}\,dz. If probability is conserved — meaning no mass is created or destroyed — then any decrease in P_V must come from probability flowing out across the boundary:  rac{dP_V}{dt} = -\oint_{\partial V} (p f_	heta) \cdot n \, dS. 6.6 🔹 5. Substituting the Divergence TheoremUsing the divergence theorem on the right-hand side: \int_V  rac{\partial p}{\partial t}\,dz = -\int_V 
abla_z \cdot (p f_	heta)\,dz. Since this holds for any region V, the integrands themselves must be equal at every point:  oxed{  rac{\partial p}{\partial t} + 
abla_z \cdot (p f_	heta) = 0. } This is the continuity equation — expressing local conservation of probability.6.7 🔹 6. From Density to Log-Density Along a TrajectoryConsider a particle following the deterministic flow:  rac{dz_t}{dt} = f_	heta(z_t, t). The total derivative of the density along that trajectory is:  rac{dp(z_t,t)}{dt} =  rac{\partial p}{\partial t} +  rac{dz_t}{dt} \cdot 
abla_z p =  rac{\partial p}{\partial t} + f_	heta \cdot 
abla_z p. Substitute  rac{\partial p}{\partial t} from the continuity equation:  rac{dp(z_t,t)}{dt} = -p(z_t,t)\,(
abla_z \cdot f_	heta). Divide both sides by p(z_t,t):  rac{1}{p} rac{dp}{dt} = -
abla_z \cdot f_	heta. Recognize that the left-hand side is the derivative of the log-density:  rac{d}{dt}\log p(z_t) = -
abla_z \cdot f_	heta = -\operatorname{Tr}\!\left( rac{\partial f_	heta}{\partial z_t}ight). ✅ Final Result  oxed{  rac{d}{dt}\log p(z_t) = -\operatorname{Tr}\!\left( rac{\partial f_	heta}{\partial z_t}ight). } This equation tells us that the log-density decreases in proportion to how much the local flow expands (positive divergence) or contracts (negative divergence) the space.6.7.1 💬 InterpretationIf 
abla_z \cdot f_	heta > 0: trajectories diverge → space expands → density decreases. If 
abla_z \cdot f_	heta < 0: trajectories converge → space contracts → density increases. The trace of the Jacobian \operatorname{Tr}(\partial f_	heta / \partial z_t) quantifies this local volume change.This is the continuous-time form of the change of variables formula used in normalizing flows and probability flow ODEs in diffusion models.6.8 SetupThe latent variable evolves continuously by an ODE:  rac{dz}{dt} = f(z_t, t). Here, f is a vector field: it tells us how each point z_t moves in space as time increases.6.9 Jacobian of the Vector FieldThe matrix  rac{\partial f}{\partial z_t} is the Jacobian of f with respect to z_t.Each entry is a partial derivative:  igg[ rac{\partial f}{\partial z_t} igg]_{ij} =  rac{\partial f_i}{\partial z_j}. The trace of this Jacobian is the divergence of f: \mathrm{div}\,f(z_t) = \sum_{i=1}^d  rac{\partial f_i}{\partial z_i}. 6.10 Why the Trace MattersIn discrete flows, we use the Jacobian determinant to measure how much a transformation stretches or compresses volume.In continuous flows, we look at the instantaneous rate of change of volume.This rate is exactly the trace of the Jacobian.6.11 Intuition: Expansion vs CompressionThink of probability density as an incompressible fluid flowing through space.The divergence tells us what happens locally:Positive divergence (>0):The flow pushes space outward.A small region expands.Same mass over larger volume \;\Rightarrow\; density decreases.Negative divergence (<0):The flow pulls space inward.A small region contracts.Same mass in smaller volume \;\Rightarrow\; density increases.Zero divergence:Flow is volume-preserving.Density stays constant.6.12 Example in 1DLet  rac{dz}{dt} = f(z) = az. Jacobian:  rac{\partial f}{\partial z} = a.Trace = a.Then:  rac{d}{dt}\log p(z_t) = -a. If a > 0: the system expands exponentially, so density decays. If a < 0: the system contracts, so density grows. If a = 0: density is unchanged.6.13 SummaryThe formula  rac{d}{dt}\,\log p(z_t) = - \mathrm{Tr}\!\left( rac{\partial f}{\partial z_t}ight) is the continuous analogue of the change-of-variables theorem.Discrete flows: multiply Jacobian determinants across layers. Continuous flows: integrate the divergence of f over time. This guarantees that probability mass is preserved as the distribution evolves.7 🧠 Continuous Normalizing Flows — What’s Really Implemented7.1 The Core ODE SystemCNFs model data as the solution of an ODE:  rac{dz_t}{dt} = f_	heta(z_t, t), \qquad  rac{d\,\log p(z_t)}{dt} = -\operatorname{Tr}\!\left( rac{\partial f_	heta}{\partial z_t}ight). Both z_t and its log-density evolve together. We integrate these two coupled ODEs using a numerical solver (e.g. torchdiffeq.odeint).7.2 Forward vs. Backward IntegrationPurposeDirectionKnown QuantityWhat You ComputeSamplingForward (0→1)z_0 \sim N(0,I)z_1 in data spaceTraining / LikelihoodBackward (1→0)z_1 = x_{	ext{data}}z_0 and \log p(z_0)So during training we start from data and integrate backward to base space, while during sampling we start from the base and integrate forward.7.3 ⚙️ Understanding the ODE Solver in Continuous Normalizing FlowsContinuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs) rely on a numerical ODE solver (e.g., torchdiffeq.odeint) to integrate both the state z_t and the log-density \log p(z_t) over time.7.3.1 🔹 Inputs to the ODE Solverfunc(t, y) — the ODE function Defines  rac{dy}{dt} for the current time t and state y. In CNFs, we augment the state as y = [z_t, \log p(z_t)] and evolve both:  rac{dz_t}{dt} = f_	heta(z_t, t), \qquad  rac{d\log p(z_t)}{dt} = -	ext{div}\,f_	heta(z_t, t). y0 — initial condition The starting point of the ODE.For sampling (forward): y0 = [z0, log p(z0)] with z_0 \sim N(0,I). For training (backward): y0 = [x_{	ext{data}}, 0], we accumulate the log-density change.tspan — time interval A 1-D tensor specifying the integration direction:Forward: [0.0, 1.0] Backward: [1.0, 0.0]7.3.2 🔹 What the ODE Solver DoesThe solver numerically integrates: y(t_1) = y(t_0) + \int_{t_0}^{t_1} f(t, y)\,dt using adaptive methods (e.g., Runge–Kutta). It repeatedly calls func(t, y) to estimate derivatives and update the state.You can think of it as a black-box integrator that returns the trajectory of y at all requested times.7.3.3 🔹 Output of the ODE Solver in Continuous Normalizing FlowsWhen you integrate the augmented ODE (for both z_t and \log p_t) backward in time, you typically call:Here:y0 is the initial condition at t = 1.0, containing both data and initial log-density: y_0 = [x_{	ext{data}}, 0]. The solver integrates backward from t = 1.0 to t = 0.0.After integration:Each state in zT includes both the position and the log-density accumulator: y_t = [z_t, \log p_t]. Thus, the final outputs are obtained by slicing:7.3.4 Interpretationsz0 → latent variable in the base space (the transformed version of the data). logp_change → accumulated integral of -	ext{div}\, f_	heta, representing the total log-volume change (the continuous-time Jacobian term).

title: Score Matching
text:
1 What is the “Score”?1.1 Definition of Score[!definition] Score The score of a probability distribution is the gradient of its log-likelihood: s(x) = 
abla_x \log p(x) It tells us the direction in which p(x) increases the fastest — that is, the direction pointing toward regions of higher data density.1.2 Intuition of Score functionThe score function s(x):points toward more likely samples. shows how to “move” a noisy sample back to data.In diffusion models, the network learns to approximate this function. Knowing s(x) is almost as good as knowing p(x) itself. We can:infer the geometry and shape of the data distribution even without explicitly computing p(x)and also (implicitly) recover the underlying probability density  oxed{
abla_x \log p(x) = s(x) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \log p(x) = \int s(x) \, dx + C} 1.3 Sampling from the Implicit DistributionIf we know the true score s(x), we can generate new samples from the corresponding distribution by following the reverse of the diffusion (noising) process - or equivalently, by running a Langevin dynamics update:[!definition] Langevin Dynamics x_{i+1} = x_i + \epsilon \, 
abla_x \log p(x_i) + \sqrt{2\epsilon}\, z_i, \quad z_i \sim {N}(0, I) where\epsilon: small step size (learning rate) z_i: Gaussian noise (same dimension as x)Langevin|840x840 2D2 Why Estimate the Score Instead of the Probability Density?2.1 Density Functions Are Hard to ModelProbability density can be complex, high-dimensional, and multimodal, so directly parameterizing p(x) is hard in high dimension because we always need:positive everywhereintegrate to 1 (for normalization) \int p(x) d x=1 For example, notice that the partition function for energy-based model E_{	heta}(x), Z=\int e^{-E_	heta(x)}dx is intractable for high dimensional x \in R^D. However, the gradients of the log-density cancel Z: 
abla_x \log p_	heta(x) = 
abla_x ig(-E_	heta(x)-\log Z ig) = -
abla_x E_	heta(x). Hence learning the score avoids normalizing constants.2.2 The Score Is Simpler and UnconstrainedThe score function s(x) = 
abla_x \log p(x) only depends on relative changes in p(x), not on its absolute scale.tells us where and how fast p(x) increases or decreases. no need to ensure normalization or positivity. score can take any real value 	o much easier for a neural network to approximate.Score # 3 How to Estimate the Score?3.1 The Idea of Score MatchingWe want the learned score network to approximate the true score 
abla_x \log p(x). s_	heta(x)\approx \underbrace{
abla_x \log p(x)}_{	ext{true score}} Formally, we simply minimize the difference between them  oxed{	ext { minimize the expected squared error } \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \min _	heta \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}\left[\left\|s_	heta(x)-
abla_x \log p(x)ight\|^2ight]} However, the term 
abla_x \log p(x) is NOT computable directly, so we have to find another surrogate objective (computed using data samples \left\{x_iight\}_{i=1}^n only). To do this, we introduce the noisy version of this matching, Denoising Score Matching (DSM).3.2 Using noisy score instead of the true data scoreGiven that we want a network s_	heta(x) to approximate the score of the real data distribution, what should the loss be? \;\mathcal L_{	ext{SM}}(	heta) = \mathbb E_{x\sim p_{	ext{data}}} ig\|s_	heta(x)-
abla_x\log p_{	ext{data}}(x) ig\|_2^2\ ### 3.2.1 Problem on the data manifoldHowever, here \min_	heta\; \mathbb E_{x\sim p_{	ext{data}}} ig\|s_	heta(x)-
abla_x\log p_{	ext{data}}(x) ig\|^2 is ill-defined because p_{	ext{data}} is supported on a thin manifold (score is undefined off-manifold).[!theorem] p_{	ext {data }}(x)=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad	ext { outside of manifold } Therefore, this means \log p_{	ext {data }}=	ext { undefined }, which is problematic.3.3 Solution: DenoiseWe introduce Gaussian corruption:  oxed{	ilde x = x+\sigma\varepsilon,\quad	ext{where } \varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)} and hence we have \quad oxed{p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)=\mathcal N(x,\sigma^2 I)} This process corresponds to convolving the data density: p_\sigma(	ilde x)=\int p_{	ext{data}}(x)\,\underbrace{p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)}_{ \mathcal N(	ilde x\mid x,\sigma^2 I)}\,dx which has full support (non-zero almost everywhere). We cannot compute p_\sigma(	ilde x) in closed form(why?), but p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x) is tractable and will be enough. Then  egin{align} \log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)= & C -  rac{\|	ilde x-x\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\ \Longrightarrow \quad
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)= & - rac{	ilde x-x}{\sigma^2} \ = & - rac{\varepsilon }{\sigma} \end{align} The noisy regression form:  oxed{\; \mathbb E_{x,	ilde x} ig\|s_	heta(	ilde x)-
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x) ig\|_2^2 + C = \mathbb E_{x,\varepsilon}\Big\|s_	heta(x+\sigma\varepsilon)+	frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma}\Big\|_2^2 + C\;} 3.4 Relation Between Marginal and Conditional ScoresIf we smooth the data with Gaussian corruption p_\sigma(	ilde x)=\int \underbrace{p(x)}_{	ext{intractable}}\,\underbrace{p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)}_{\mathcal N(x,\sigma^2 I).}\,dx then, notice p(x) is independent of 	ilde x, hence  egin{aligned}  oxed{
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x)} &= rac{ 
abla_{	ilde x} p_\sigma(	ilde x)}{ p_\sigma(	ilde x)} = rac{1}{\;p_\sigma(	ilde x)\;} \int p(x)\; \underbrace{
abla_{	ilde x} p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)}_{	ext{(use } 
abla u = u 
abla \log u	ext{)}}\,dx \[6pt] &= rac{1}{p_\sigma(	ilde x)} \int p(x)\; \underparen{p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)\, 
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)}dx \[10pt] &= rac{1}{p_\sigma(	ilde x)} \int \underbrace{p(x)\,p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)}_{	ext{joint }p(x,	ilde x)}\; 
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)\,dx \[8pt] &=\cancel{ rac{1}{p_\sigma(	ilde x)}} \int \underbrace{p(x, 	ilde{x})}_{\substack{	ext{Bayes: }\ p(x,	ilde x)=p(x\mid	ilde x)\,\cancel{p_\sigma(	ilde x)}}}\; 
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)\,dx \[6pt] &=\int \underbrace{p(x\mid 	ilde x)}_{	ext{posterior weight}}\; \underbrace{
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)}_{	ext{local score}}\,dx \[4pt] &= oxed{\ \mathbb E_{x\sim p(x\mid 	ilde x)}  ig[\,
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)\, ig]\ } \end{aligned} 3.5 Gaussian checkFor p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)=\mathcal N(x,\sigma^2 I), we have \underbrace{
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)}_{	ext{score of the conditional}} = - rac{	ilde x-x}{\sigma^2}. Therefore, 
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x) = \mathbb E_{x\mid 	ilde x}\!\left[- rac{	ilde x-x}{\sigma^2}ight] =  rac{\mathbb E[x\mid 	ilde x]-	ilde x}{\sigma^2}, which also implies Tweedie’s denoising identity (idk what this is) \ \mathbb E[x\mid 	ilde x]=	ilde x+\sigma^2
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x)3.6 Expanding the ideal loss and isolating the constant  egin{aligned}  oxed{L_{	ext{ideal}}(	heta)} &=\mathbb{E}_{	ilde x\sim p_\sigma}\!\left[\left\|\,s_	heta(	ilde x) -
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x)\,ight\|^2ight] \[6pt] &=\mathbb{E}_{	ilde x}\!\left[\left\|\,s_	heta(	ilde x) -\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p(x\mid 	ilde x)}  ig[
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x) ig]}_{	ext{posterior expectation identity}}ight\|^2ight] \[6pt] &\overset{\|a-b\|^2}{=} \mathbb{E}_{	ilde x}\!\Big[\|s_	heta(	ilde x)\|^2 -2\,s_	heta(	ilde x)^	op \mathbb{E}_{x\mid 	ilde x}\![
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)] + ig\|\mathbb{E}_{x\mid 	ilde x}\![
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)] ig\|^2\Big] \[6pt] &=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{	ilde x}\!\left[\|s_	heta(	ilde x)\|^2ight]}_{	ext{depends on }	heta} -2\,\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{x,	ilde x}\!\left[s_	heta(	ilde x)^	op 
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)ight]}_{	ext{swap } \mathbb{E}_{	ilde x}\mathbb{E}_{x\mid	ilde x}} +\underbrace{\color{red}{\mathbb{E}_{	ilde x}\!\left[\left\|\mathbb{E}_{x\mid 	ilde x}\![
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)]ight\|^2ight]}}_{	ext{no }	heta} \[6pt] &=\mathbb{E}_{x,	ilde x}\!\left[\|s_	heta(	ilde x)\|^2-2\,s_	heta(	ilde x)^	op 
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)ight] +\color{red}{C_0} \[4pt] \overset{\substack{	ext{complete-}\	ext{the-square}}}{\Rightarrow}\;&=\mathbb{E}_{x,	ilde x}\!\left[\|s_	heta(	ilde x)-
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)\|^2ight] +\underbrace{\Big(\color{red}{C_0}-\mathbb{E}_{x,	ilde x}\!\left[\|
abla_{	ilde x}\log p_\sigma(	ilde x\mid x)\|^2ight]\Big)}_{\displaystyle \color{red}{=:C}\ 	ext{no }	heta} \[6pt] &\equiv  oxed{L_{	ext{DSM}}(	heta)}+\color{red}{C} \end{aligned} where on line (3) you may recall that  egin{align} \|a-b\|^2 & =(a+b)^	op(a-b) \ & =a^Ta-2a^	op b+b^Tb\ & =\|a\|^2-2a^	op b+\|b\|^2 \end{align} which gives the same constant C as above. Therefore, eventually we have:  oxed{L_{D S M}(	heta)=\mathbb{E}_{x, \widetilde{x}}\left[\left\|s_	heta(\widetilde{x})-
abla_{\widetilde{x}} \log p(\widetilde{x} \mid x)ight\|^2ight] }3.7 Final denoising score matching (DSM) objectiveFor Gaussian noise p(\widetilde{x}\mid x) = {N}(\widetilde{x}; x, \sigma^2 I), 
abla_{\widetilde{x}}\log p(\widetilde{x}\mid x) = - rac{\widetilde{x}-x}{\sigma^2} which gives the standard denoising score matching loss:  oxed{ {L}_{DSM}(	heta) = \mathbb{E}_{x,\epsilon} \left[ \left\|\, s_	heta(x + \sigma \epsilon) +  rac{\epsilon}{\sigma}\, ight\|^2 ight], \quad \epsilon \sim {N}(0, I) } 4 Side note: relation to DDPMIn DDPM, for each noise level t, x_t=\sqrt{ ar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1- ar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I), and training often minimizes \mathbb E ig\|\varepsilon_	heta(x_t,t)-\varepsilon ig\|_2^2, which is equivalent to DSM at scale \sigma_t=\sqrt{1- ar\alpha_t} via s_	heta(x_t,t)\;\approx\;- rac{1}{\sigma_t}\,\varepsilon_	heta(x_t,t) \quad(	ext{up to known weights}).

title: 4.1 Polarization
text: 4.1.1 Dielectircsmost everyday objects belong to one of two large classes: conductors and insulators (dielectrics)In dielectrics, unlike conductors that has unlimited supply of electrons to move around, all charges are attached to specific atoms or molecules.The electrons can only: \begin{align} \text{ move a bit \textit{within} the atom} & \to \text{cumulative effects} \end{align} which accounts for characteristics behaviors.4.1.2 Induced Dipoles for Neutral AtomThe electrons and the nucleus inside a neutral atom experience:electric field \mathbf{E} pulling them apartmutual attraction (what force?) drawing them back The resulted equilibrium leaves the atom polarized.In particular, for dipoles for Atom, the slightly shifted charges: \qquad+\leftleftarrows\qquad \rightrightarrows - lead to a tiny dipole moment \mathbf{p} in the same direction as \mathbf{E}.[!claim|*] The induced dipole moment is approximately proportional to the field \mathbf{p}=\alpha \mathbf{E} where \alpha = 4\pi \epsilon_{0}a^{3}=3\epsilon_{0}v is the atomic polarizability,Dipoles for Moleculesmore complicated than atom due to particular angles of polarization that occurs more readily than others.induced dipole moment may not be in the same direction as \mathbf{E}molecules may be asymmatrical (polarizability tensor \alpha_{ij} is needed)4.1.3 Alignment of Polar Moleculessome molecules have permanent, built-in dipole momentsuniform field cancels the force (+q\mathbf{E}-q\mathbf{E}=0), but the torque remains…4.1.4 PolarizationRecall:Consider external electric field onatommoleculeThe main question we ask is:What happens to a piece of dielectric material when it is placed in an electric field?[!definition] The material becomes polarized if a lot of little dipoles pointing along the direction of the field, and we write polarization as \mathbf{P}\equiv \text{dipole moment / unit volume}
