title: 4.4 Linear Dielectrics
text:
4.4.1 Susceptibility, Permittivity, Dielectric ConstantWe dealt with the effect of the polarization \mathbf{P}, but what about the cause?This set of notes transitions between Chapter 4 (Linear Dielectrics) and Chapter 5 (Magnetostatics). It covers how electric fields behave in matter and then introduces the fundamental laws governing magnetic fields from steady currents.4.4 Linear Dielectrics (Electrostatics)In many substances, the polarization \mathbf{P} is directly proportional to the total electric field \mathbf{E}, provided the field is not too strong. These are called linear dielectrics.1. Susceptibility and PermittivityThe proportionality is defined using the electric susceptibility (\chi_e): \mathbf{P} = \epsilon_0 \chi_e \mathbf{E}This allows us to write the electric displacement (\mathbf{D}) in terms of the field alone:  egin{aligned} \mathbf{D} &= \epsilon_0 \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P} \ &= \epsilon_0(1 + \chi_e)\mathbf{E} \ &= \epsilon \mathbf{E} \end{aligned} [!definition] Constants of Linear MediaPermittivity (\epsilon): \epsilon \equiv \epsilon_0(1 + \chi_e)Relative Permittivity (\epsilon_r): \epsilon_r \equiv 1 + \chi_e = \epsilon / \epsilon_0 (also called the dielectric constant).2. Physical EffectsField Reduction: In a homogeneous linear dielectric that fills all space, the electric field is reduced by a factor of 1/\epsilon_r compared to the vacuum field (\mathbf{E} =  rac{1}{\epsilon_r} \mathbf{E}_{	ext{vac}}).Shielding: The polarization of the medium shields embedded charges by surrounding them with bound charge of the opposite sign.Crystals: In anisotropic materials like crystals, susceptibility is a tensor, meaning \mathbf{P} might not point in the same direction as \mathbf{E}.4.4.2 Boundary Value Problems with Linear DielectricsThe introduction of linear media simplifies boundary value problems significantly. In a homogeneous linear dielectric, the bound charge density (ho_b) is directly proportional to the free charge density (ho_f).1. Bound vs. Free ChargeWithin a dielectric, the bound charge density is given by:  egin{aligned} ho_b &= -
abla \cdot \mathbf{P} = -
abla \cdot \left( \epsilon_0  rac{\chi_e}{\epsilon} \mathbf{D} ight) \ &= -\left(  rac{\chi_e}{1 + \chi_e} ight) ho_f \end{aligned} [!important] The Zero Rule Unless free charge is actually embedded in the material (ho_f 
eq 0), the total volume charge density ho is zero. This means within the dielectric, the potential V still obeys Laplace’s equation (
abla^2 V = 0).2. Boundary ConditionsWhen solving for V at the interface between two media, we use the following conditions:VariableBoundary ConditionNotesPotential (V)V_{	ext{above}} = V_{	ext{below}}Potential is always continuous.Electric Field (\mathbf{E})\epsilon_{	ext{above}} E_{	ext{above}}^{\perp} - \epsilon_{	ext{below}} E_{	ext{below}}^{\perp} = \sigma_fAccounts for free surface charge.In terms of V\epsilon_{	ext{above}}  rac{\partial V_{	ext{above}}}{\partial n} - \epsilon_{	ext{below}}  rac{\partial V_{	ext{below}}}{\partial n} = -\sigma_fDerivative w.r.t. the normal vector.4.4.3 Energy in Dielectric SystemsHow much work does it take to charge up a system when dielectrics are present? The answer depends on what you mean by energy.1. The Capacitor CaseIf a capacitor is filled with a linear dielectric, its capacitance increases: C = \epsilon_r C_{	ext{vac}} Consequently, the work required to charge it to a specific voltage V increases by the same factor: W =  rac{1}{2} CV^2 This extra work is necessary because you must overcome the field produced by the bound charges that are trying to cancel out your efforts.2. General Energy FormulaFor a linear dielectric system, the total work done to assemble the free charge is:  oxed{W =  rac{1}{2} \int \mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{E} d	au}3. Two Ways to Count EnergyGriffiths highlights a subtle distinction in what we call the energy of a system:Total Energy (Eq. 2.45): W =  rac{\epsilon_0}{2} \int E^2 d	au. This represents the work to assemble every charge (free and bound) piece by piece. It does not include the energy stored in the molecular springs (the stretching/twisting of atoms).Free Charge Energy (Eq. 4.58): W =  rac{1}{2} \int \mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{E} d	au. This represents the work to bring in the free charges only, allowing the dielectric to polarize naturally. This does include the energy stored in the molecular springs.[!warning] Linearity Required Eq. 4.58 (W =  rac{1}{2} \int \mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{E} d	au) is only valid for linear dielectrics. If the system is non-linear or dissipative (like an electret with frozen-in polarization), the work done depends on the path taken, and the simple integral fails.4.4.3.4 Summary ChecklistBoundary Conditions: Use D for free charge and V for continuity.Energy: Use  rac{1}{2} \mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{E} if you only care about the work done on free charges.Homogeneity: If ho_f = 0 in the bulk, ho_b = 0 in the bulk too! All charge resides on the surface.4.4 Linear DielectricsIn the previous sections, we analyzed the effects of polarization (\mathbf{P}) without committing to its cause. In this section, we assume the polarization is sustained by an applied electric field and is proportional to that field.4.4.1 Susceptibility, Permittivity, and Dielectric ConstantFor many substances, the polarization is proportional to the total field \mathbf{E}, provided the field is not too strong:\mathbf{P} = \epsilon_0 \chi_e \mathbf{E}[!definition] Electric Susceptibility (\chi_e) \chi_e is a dimensionless constant of proportionality that depends on the microscopic structure of the substance and external conditions like temperature.1. The Displacement Field (D)In linear media, the displacement field \mathbf{D} is also proportional to \mathbf{E}:  egin{aligned} \mathbf{D} &= \epsilon_0 \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P} \ &= \epsilon_0 \mathbf{E} + \epsilon_0 \chi_e \mathbf{E} \ &= \epsilon_0(1 + \chi_e)\mathbf{E} \ &= \epsilon \mathbf{E} \end{aligned} [!definition] Permittivity and Dielectric ConstantPermittivity (\epsilon): Defined as \epsilon \equiv \epsilon_0(1 + \chi_e).Relative Permittivity (\epsilon_r): Also called the dielectric constant, defined as \epsilon_r \equiv 1 + \chi_e = \epsilon/\epsilon_0.2. Anisotropy and the Susceptibility TensorIn crystals, it is often easier to polarize the material in certain directions. In such cases, the linear relation is replaced by a general tensor relation: P_i = \epsilon_0 \sum_{j} \chi_{eij} E_j The nine coefficients \chi_{exx}, \chi_{exy}, \dots constitute the susceptibility tensor.4.4.2 Boundary Value Problems with Linear DielectricsIn a homogeneous isotropic linear dielectric, the bound charge density ho_b is proportional to the free charge density ho_f: ho_b = -
abla \cdot \mathbf{P} = -
abla \cdot \left( \epsilon_0  rac{\chi_e}{\epsilon} \mathbf{D} ight) = -\left(  rac{\chi_e}{1 + \chi_e} ight) ho_fKey Implication: Unless free charge is embedded in the material, ho_b = 0 in the bulk. Any net charge must reside on the surface. Within the dielectric, the potential obeys Laplace’s equation (
abla^2 V = 0).1. Boundary ConditionsThe conditions for solving the potential V are expressed in terms of free charge:Potential Continuity: V_{	ext{above}} = V_{	ext{below}}Field Jump (Normal): \epsilon_{	ext{above}} E_{	ext{above}}^{\perp} - \epsilon_{	ext{below}} E_{	ext{below}}^{\perp} = \sigma_fPotential Derivative: \epsilon_{	ext{above}}  rac{\partial V_{	ext{above}}}{\partial n} - \epsilon_{	ext{below}}  rac{\partial V_{	ext{below}}}{\partial n} = -\sigma_f4.4.3 Energy in Dielectric SystemsTo calculate the work done in charging a system with dielectrics, we must account for the work done on the free charges while the dielectric responds.1. General Derivation for WorkTo increase the free charge by an amount \Delta ho_f, the work done is: \Delta W = \int (\Delta ho_f)V d	au Since 
abla \cdot \mathbf{D} = ho_f, then \Delta ho_f = 
abla \cdot (\Delta \mathbf{D}):  egin{aligned} \Delta W &= \int [
abla \cdot (\Delta \mathbf{D})]V d	au \ &= \int 
abla \cdot [(\Delta \mathbf{D})V] d	au + \int (\Delta \mathbf{D}) \cdot \mathbf{E} d	au && 	ext{\scriptsize (Integration by parts)} \end{aligned} The first term vanishes as a surface integral over all space. For linear media, (\Delta \mathbf{D}) \cdot \mathbf{E} =  rac{1}{2} \Delta (\mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{E}).[!important] Total Stored Energy Integrating from zero to the final configuration:  oxed{W =  rac{1}{2} \int \mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{E} d	au}Equation 2.45 vs 4.58: Eq 2.45 (W =  rac{\epsilon_0}{2} \int E^2 d	au) counts the work to assemble all charges (free and bound). Eq 4.58 includes the spring energy stored in the polarized molecules because it accounts for the work done on the free charges as they stretch those molecular springs.4.4.4 Forces on DielectricsA dielectric is attracted into an electric field. In a parallel-plate capacitor, this is caused by the fringing field—the non-uniform field at the edges of the plates.1. Force Calculation (Energy Method)If the dielectric is pulled out by dx, the work done is dW = F_{	ext{me}} dx. The electrical force is F = -dW/dx.Constant Charge (Q): W =  rac{1}{2}  rac{Q^2}{C} F = - rac{dW}{dx} =  rac{1}{2}  rac{Q^2}{C^2}  rac{dC}{dx} =  rac{1}{2} V^2  rac{dC}{dx}Constant Potential (V): dW = F_{	ext{me}} dx + V dQ. This yields the same result for F but requires accounting for the work done by the battery.[!important] Result for a Slab For a slab of width w and thickness d inserted a distance x: F = - rac{\epsilon_0 \chi_e w}{2d} V^2 The negative sign indicates the dielectric is pulled into the capacitor.

title: 5.1 The Lorentz Force Law
5.2 The Biot–Savart Law
text: This section bridges the gap between individual moving charges and the constant fields we study in Magnetostatics. Just as Electrostatics deals with charges that don’t move, Magnetostatics deals with currents that don’t change.5.2.1 Steady Currents1. Defining the RegimeThe transition from electricity to magnetism follows a perfect parallel logic. In both cases, we are looking for equilibrium states where the fields themselves do not fluctuate with time.RegimeSourceField ResultElectrostaticsStationary ChargesConstant Electric Field (\mathbf{E})MagnetostaticsSteady CurrentsConstant Magnetic Field (\mathbf{B})[!definition] Steady Current A steady current is a continuous flow of charge that has been going on forever, without change and without charge piling up anywhere.2. Formal Conditions of MagnetostaticsTo keep the fields constant in time, the sources (charge density and current density) must themselves be independent of time at every point in space.[!Remark] The Mathematical Conditions Formally, magnetostatics is the regime where: \boxed{\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} = 0} \quad \text{and} \quad \boxed{\frac{\partial \mathbf{J}}{\partial t} = \mathbf{0}}\partial \rho / \partial t = 0: Charge density at any fixed point remains constant.\partial \mathbf{J} / \partial t = \mathbf{0}: The flow rate at any fixed point remains constant.3. The Point Charge HeadacheGriffiths points out a major difference between how we teach Electrostatics and Magnetostatics:In Electrostatics: we start with a point charge at rest, which produces a static field.In Magnetostatics: we cannot start with a single moving point charge.Why? Because a moving point charge is the opposite of steady. If a charge is at position A at time t_1, and at position B at t_2, then \rho at those points is changing violently over time. A single moving point charge does not produce a static magnetic field. Therefore, we must deal with extended current distributions (like wires or loops) right from the start.4. Conservation of Charge: Continuity EquationIn magnetostatics, the fact that charge does not pile up has a specific mathematical consequence for the Divergence of the current density.Derivation of the Magnetostatic Continuity Equation: \begin{aligned} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{J} &= -\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} && \text{\scriptsize starting from the general Continuity Equation} \\ &= 0 && \text{\scriptsize since } \partial \rho / \partial t = 0 \text{ in magnetostatics} \end{aligned}[!definition] Magnetostatic Continuity In the steady current regime, the current density is divergenceless: \boxed{\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J} = 0} This implies that for a steady current in a wire, the magnitude I must be the same all along the line.5.2.2 The Magnetic Field of a Steady CurrentThis section introduces the Biot-Savart Law, which serves as the fundamental empirical law of magnetostatics, analogous to Coulomb’s law in electrostatics.1. The Biot-Savart Law for Line CurrentsThe magnetic field produced by a steady line current I follows an inverse-square relationship with the separation distance, with a direction governed by the cross product.[!definition] Biot-Savart Law (Line Current) The magnetic field \mathbf{B} at a point \mathbf{r} due to a steady current I is: \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} I \int \frac{d\mathbf{l}' \times \hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}{\boldsymbol{r}^2}d\mathbf{l}': Element of length along the wire, pointing in the direction of current.\boldsymbol{r}: The separation vector from the source (d\mathbf{l}') to the field point (\mathbf{r}).\mu_0: Permeability of free space, defined as \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \text{ N/A}^2.2. Units and ComparisonThe magnetic field is measured in Teslas (T). According to the Lorentz force law, the dimensions are: 1 \text{ T} = 1 \text{ N}/(\text{A} \cdot \text{m})FeatureCoulomb’s LawBiot-Savart LawSourceStationary charge (dq)Steady current (I d\mathbf{l}')Dependence1/\boldsymbol{r}^21/\boldsymbol{r}^2DirectionRadial (along \hat{\boldsymbol{r}})Perpendicular to d\mathbf{l}' and \hat{\boldsymbol{r}}3. Generalization to Continuous DistributionsUsing the dictionary from Section 5.1.3 (I d\mathbf{l}' \sim \mathbf{K} da' \sim \mathbf{J} d\tau'), we extend the law to surface and volume currents.Derivation of Surface and Volume Fields: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}) &= \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \int \frac{\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{r}') \times \hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}{\boldsymbol{r}^2} da' && \text{\scriptsize for surface currents } \mathbf{K} \\ &= \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \int \frac{\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{r}') \times \hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}{\boldsymbol{r}^2} d\tau' && \text{\scriptsize for volume currents } \mathbf{J} \end{aligned} 4. Important Principles and Warnings[!Remark] The Point Charge Error It is tempting to write the field of a moving point charge as: \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \frac{q\mathbf{v} \times \hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}{\boldsymbol{r}^2} \quad \text{(INCORRECT)} Griffiths emphasizes that this is simply wrong. A moving point charge does not constitute a steady current, and the Biot-Savart law applies strictly to the steady-state regime.The Superposition Principle: Magnetic fields obey the superposition principle. If you have a collection of source currents, the net field is the vector sum of the fields due to each source: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{B}_{\text{net}} &= \mathbf{B}_1 + \mathbf{B}_2 + \dots && \text{\scriptsize summation of individual fields} \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{B}_i && \text{\scriptsize discrete sources} \\ &= \int d\mathbf{B} && \text{\scriptsize continuous distribution} \end{aligned} 5.2.2.5 Summary ChecklistInverse-Square: Field strength drops with 1/\boldsymbol{r}^2.Geometry: d\mathbf{l}' \times \hat{\boldsymbol{r}} ensures the field circles the wire (Right-Hand Rule).Steady state: The law only works if \partial \mathbf{J}/\partial t = 0.

title: 5.3 The Divergence and Curl of B 227
6.1 Magnetization
text:
6.1.1 Diamagnets, Paramagnets, FerromagnetsIn classical electrodynamics, all magnetic phenomena are due to electric charges in motion.[!definition] Magnetization Magnetization is the process of inducing a net alignment of magnetic dipoles within a medium.If we examine magnetic materials at the atomic scale, we find tiny currents caused by two primary motions:Orbital Motion: Electrons orbiting around the nuclei.Spin: Electrons spinning about their own axes.6.1.1.1 Classification of Magnetic MaterialsUnlike electric polarization (which is in the same direction as the electric field \mathbf{E}), the response of a material to a magnetic field \mathbf{B} depends on its internal structure. Materials are classified into three main categories:Material TypeResponse to Applied Field \mathbf{B}Key CharacteristicsParamagnetsmagnetization parallel to \mathbf{B}.caused by the torque of the external field.Diamagnetsmagnetization opposite to \mathbf{B}.resulted by the changes in orbital speeds (Lenz’s law analogy).Ferromagnetsretain magnetization even after \mathbf{B} is removed.defined by the “history” of the object; the most complex type.6.1.2 Torques and Forces on Magnetic Dipoles6.1.2.1 Torque on a Rectangular LoopWe use a rectangular loop of sides a and b carrying current I to represent a simplified model for atom for mathematical convenience.The torque \mathbf{N} on , tilted at an angle 	heta in a uniform field \mathbf{B} = B \hat{\mathbf{z}}, is derived as:  egin{aligned} \mathbf{N} &= {a F \sin 	heta}\hat{\mathbf{x}} && 	ext{\scriptsize lever arm $	imes$ force} \ &= a ({I b B}) \sin 	heta \hat{\mathbf{x}} && \scriptsize F = IbB 	ext{ on vertical segments} \ &= \underbrace{I a b}_{m} B \sin 	heta \hat{\mathbf{x}} && \ &= m B \sin 	heta \hat{\mathbf{x}} && 	ext{\scriptsize applying the magnitude of the dipole moment} \ &= \mathbf{m} 	imes \mathbf{B} && 	ext{\scriptsize vector cross product form (Eq. 6.1)} \end{aligned}[!definition] Torque on a Dipole A magnetic dipole in a uniform magnetic field experiences a torque that tries to line it up parallel to the field:  oxed{\mathbf{N} = \mathbf{m} 	imes \mathbf{B}} This is mathematically identical to the electrical analog: \mathbf{N} = \mathbf{p} 	imes \mathbf{E}.6.1.2.2 Qualitative Origin of ParamagnetismThe torque \mathbf{N}=\mathbf{m} 	imes \mathbf{B} is what accounts for paramagnetism:The Mechanism: The torque acts in such a direction as to line the dipole up parallel to the field.The Constraint: While every electron is a magnetic dipole (a tiny spinning charged sphere), the Pauli exclusion principle usually locks electrons into pairs with opposing spins, neutralizing the torque.The Result: Paramagnetism occurs primarily in atoms with an odd number of electrons, where an extra unpaired member is subject to the magnetic torque.6.1.2.3 Forces in Non-Uniform Fields3. Force on a Magnetic DipoleHow a dipole moves linearly depends entirely on whether the external magnetic field is uniform or not.6.1.2.4.1 A. In a Uniform FieldIf the external field \mathbf{B} is constant everywhere, the net force on any closed current loop is exactly zero.Proof:  egin{aligned} \mathbf{F} &= I \oint (d\mathbf{l} 	imes \mathbf{B}) && 	ext{\scriptsize integrating the magnetic force around the loop} \ &= I \left( \oint d\mathbf{l} ight) 	imes \mathbf{B} && 	ext{\scriptsize pulling the constant } \mathbf{B} 	ext{ outside the integral} \ &= \mathbf{0} && 	ext{\scriptsize the net displacement of any closed loop is zero} \end{aligned} 6.1.2.4.2 B. In a Nonuniform FieldIf the external magnetic field is changing (like the fringing field at the end of a solenoid), the field lines have a radial component. This radial component exerts a net force on the loop, pulling it toward regions of stronger field.Example: The Fringing Field Suppose a circular wire ring of radius R, carrying a current I, is suspended above a short solenoid. Because \mathbf{B} flares outward, there is a net downward force on the loop:  egin{aligned} F &= \underbrace{I (2\pi R)}_{I 	imes 	ext{circumference}} B \cos 	heta && 	ext{\scriptsize Net downward force (Eq. 6.2)} \end{aligned} The General Formula We can generalize this for any infinitesimal loop with dipole moment \mathbf{m} in a non-uniform field \mathbf{B}. The exact force is the gradient of the dot product:  egin{aligned} \mathbf{F} &= 
abla (\underbrace{\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{B}}_{-U}) && 	ext{\scriptsize Force as the negative gradient of interaction energy} \end{aligned} > [!remark] > Just as in electrostatics where \mathbf{F} = 
abla(\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{E}), the magnetic formula tells us that the dipole seeks out the region of lowest potential energy (where \mathbf{m} and \mathbf{B} are parallel and \mathbf{B} is strongest).For an infinitesimal loop with dipole moment \mathbf{m}, the exact force is: > [!definition] Force on a Dipole >  oxed{\mathbf{F} = 
abla(\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{B})} > Again, this perfectly mirrors the electrical formula: \mathbf{F} = 
abla(\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{E}).4. The Two Models Warning: Gilbert vs. AmpèreBecause the formulas for magnetic dipoles (\mathbf{m}) so perfectly match those for electric dipoles (\mathbf{p}), early physicists developed a model of magnetism that assumed it worked exactly like electricity.ModelThe Physical PictureGriffiths’ VerdictThe Gilbert ModelMagnetic dipoles are made of positive and negative magnetic charges (North and South poles) separated by a distance.Bad Physics, but Useful Math. It yields the correct field far away and the correct torque, but fails completely up close because monopoles don’t exist.The Ampère ModelMagnetism is strictly due to moving electric charges (current loops).Physically Correct. If you break a magnet, you just get two smaller current loops, not isolated poles.Griffiths’ Advice: You can use the Gilbert model to get a quick intuitive feel for a problem by swapping \mathbf{p} 	o \mathbf{m}, 1/\epsilon_0 	o \mu_0, and \mathbf{E} 	o \mathbf{B}. But never rely on it for quantitative results when dealing with the close-up features of a dipole, because the two models yield strikingly different answers at the origin.6.1.3 Effect of a Magnetic Field on Atomic OrbitsWhile electrons have intrinsic spin, they also revolve around the nucleus. This orbital motion creates a second contribution to the magnetic properties of matter, known as diamagnetism.1. The Orbital Dipole MomentFor an electron revolving in a circle of radius R with speed v, the period is T = 2\pi R / v. This constitutes a steady current I = -e/T.[!definition] Orbital Dipole Moment The magnetic dipole moment associated with this orbit is: \mathbf{m} = I\mathbf{a} = \left( - rac{ev}{2\pi R} ight) \pi R^2 \hat{\mathbf{z}} =  oxed{- rac{1}{2}evR\hat{\mathbf{z}}}2. The Mechanism of DiamagnetismWhen an external magnetic field \mathbf{B} is turned on, it exerts an additional force -e(\mathbf{v} 	imes \mathbf{B}) on the electron. This force doesn’t change the radius of the orbit (in this simplified classical model) but it changes the speed of the electron.Derivation of the change in speed (\Delta v): Suppose \mathbf{B} is perpendicular to the plane of the orbit. The centripetal acceleration must now be sustained by both electrical and magnetic forces:  egin{aligned}  rac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} rac{e^2}{R^2} + e ar{v}B &= m_e  rac{ ar{v}^2}{R} && 	ext{\scriptsize new force balance with magnetic field on} \ \underbrace{m_e  rac{v^2}{R}}_{F_{elec}} + e ar{v}B &= m_e  rac{ ar{v}^2}{R} && 	ext{\scriptsize substituting the original orbital condition} \ e ar{v}B &=  rac{m_e}{R}( ar{v}^2 - v^2) && 	ext{\scriptsize rearranging to isolate the change} \ e ar{v}B &=  rac{m_e}{R}( ar{v} + v)( ar{v} - v) && 	ext{\scriptsize factoring the difference of squares} \end{aligned} Assuming the change \Delta v =  ar{v} - v is small, we let  ar{v} \approx v:  egin{aligned} e v B &\approx  rac{m_e}{R}(2v)\Delta v && 	ext{\scriptsize applying the small-change approximation} \ \Delta v &=  rac{eRB}{2m_e} && 	ext{\scriptsize solving for the speed increment (Eq. 6.7)} \end{aligned} 3. The Induced Dipole MomentThe change in speed leads directly to a change in the dipole moment:  egin{aligned} \Delta \mathbf{m} &= - rac{1}{2}e(\Delta v)R\hat{\mathbf{z}} && 	ext{\scriptsize from the definition of orbital moment} \ &= - rac{1}{2}e\left(  rac{eRB}{2m_e} ight)R\hat{\mathbf{z}} && 	ext{\scriptsize substituting } \Delta v \ &=  oxed{- rac{e^2 R^2}{4m_e} \mathbf{B}} && 	ext{\scriptsize (Eq. 6.8)} \end{aligned} [!important] The Core Principle of Diamagnetism The change in dipole moment \Delta \mathbf{m} is always opposite to the direction of \mathbf{B}. This induced effect is universal to all atoms, but it is typically much weaker than paramagnetism and is only clearly observed in atoms with even numbers of electrons where paramagnetism is absent.6.1.4 MagnetizationNow that we have analyzed the two microscopic mechanisms (spin alignment for paramagnetism and orbital speed changes for diamagnetism), we need a macroscopic variable to describe the state of magnetic polarization in a chunk of matter.[!definition] Magnetization (\mathbf{M}) Magnetization is defined as the magnetic dipole moment per unit volume:  oxed{\mathbf{M} \equiv  rac{d\mathbf{m}}{d	au}}Units: Amperes per meter (A/m).Role: It is the magnetic analog to the polarization \mathbf{P} in electrostatics.6.1.4.1 Summary of Magnetic Effects in MatterEffectPhysical MechanismAlignmentStrengthParamagnetismTorque on electron spinsParallel to \mathbf{B}WeakDiamagnetismChange in orbital speedsOpposite to \mathbf{B}Very WeakFerromagnetismQuantum domain alignmentParallel (very strong)ExtremeNote on Strength: In a non-uniform field, paramagnets are attracted into the field, while diamagnets are repelled. However, both forces are pitifully weak compared to ferromagnets like iron, which can be 10^4 to 10^5 times stronger. This is why we can often ignore magnetization when calculating fields for ordinary copper wires.

title: 6.2 The Field of a Magnetized Object 276
6.2 The Field of a Magnetized
text:
6.2 The Field of a Magnetized ObjectThis section explores how to calculate the magnetic field produced by a magnetized material. The key theoretical breakthrough is showing that a magnetized object can be replaced by an equivalent distribution of bound currents.6.2.1 Bound CurrentsIf the magnetization \mathbf{M} (dipole moment per unit volume) of an object is known, we can find the total vector potential \mathbf{A} by integrating the contributions from all infinitesimal dipoles d\mathbf{m} = \mathbf{M} d	au'.Derivation of the Potential from Magnetization:  egin{aligned} \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}) &=  rac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \int  rac{\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}') 	imes \hat{ oldsymbol{r}}}{ oldsymbol{r}^2} d	au' && 	ext{\scriptsize starting from the potential of a single dipole (Eq. 6.11)} \ &=  rac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \int \left[ \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}') 	imes \left( 
abla'  rac{1}{ oldsymbol{r}} ight) ight] d	au' && 	ext{\scriptsize utilizing the identity }  rac{\hat{ oldsymbol{r}}}{ oldsymbol{r}^2} = 
abla'  rac{1}{ oldsymbol{r}} \ &=  rac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \left\{ \int  rac{1}{ oldsymbol{r}} [
abla' 	imes \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}')] d	au' - \int 
abla' 	imes \left[  rac{\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}')}{ oldsymbol{r}} ight] d	au' ight\} && 	ext{\scriptsize applying vector product rule 7} \ &=  rac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \int  rac{1}{ oldsymbol{r}} [
abla' 	imes \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}')] d	au' +  rac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \oint  rac{1}{ oldsymbol{r}} [\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}') 	imes d\mathbf{a}'] && 	ext{\scriptsize converting second volume integral to surface integral} \ &= \underbrace{ rac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \int  rac{\mathbf{J}_b(\mathbf{r}')}{ oldsymbol{r}} d	au'}_{	ext{potential of volume current}} + \underbrace{ rac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \oint  rac{\mathbf{K}_b(\mathbf{r}')}{ oldsymbol{r}} da'}_{	ext{potential of surface current}} && 	ext{\scriptsize substituting bound current definitions (Eq. 6.15)} \end{aligned} [!definition] Bound Current Densities The field of a magnetized object is identical to the field produced by a specific distribution of bound currents:Bound Volume Current:  oxed{\mathbf{J}_b = 
abla 	imes \mathbf{M}}Bound Surface Current:  oxed{\mathbf{K}_b = \mathbf{M} 	imes \hat{\mathbf{n}}}6.2.2 Physical Interpretation of Bound CurrentsThese currents are not free to move through the material; they represent the macroscopic average of billions of tiny atomic current loops.1. Surface Current (\mathbf{K}_b)In a uniformly magnetized material, the internal current loops of adjacent atoms cancel one another out. However, at the surface, the loops are uncompensated, resulting in a net current flowing around the boundary.Relation to Magnetization: Consider a slab of thickness t. The dipole moment of a single loop is m = I a, where a is the area. The total magnetization is M = m / (at) = I/t. Thus, the current per unit length is K_b = I/t = M. The vector form \mathbf{K}_b = \mathbf{M} 	imes \hat{\mathbf{n}} accounts for the orientation relative to the surface normal.2. Volume Current (\mathbf{J}_b)If the magnetization is non-uniform, the internal cancellation is no longer perfect. The mismatch between adjacent loops creates a net current in the bulk of the material, described by the curl of \mathbf{M}.6.2.3 The Magnetic Field inside MatterThe microscopic magnetic field inside a material fluctuates violently at the atomic scale. When we talk about the field in matter, we mean the macroscopic field: the average over a region large enough to contain many atoms.[!important] Magnetization effects are typically much weaker than fields from free currents in ordinary conductors (like copper). We only consider \mathbf{M} significant when dealing with magnetic materials (like iron) or permanent magnets.6.2.1.4 Summary Dictionary for Chapter 6QuantitySymbolDefinition / RelationMagnetization\mathbf{M}Dipole moment per unit volumeBound Volume Current\mathbf{J}_b
abla 	imes \mathbf{M}Bound Surface Current\mathbf{K}_b\mathbf{M} 	imes \hat{\mathbf{n}}Total Potential\mathbf{A}Sum of potentials from \mathbf{J}_b and \mathbf{K}_b

title: 7.1 Electromotive Force
text:
7.1.1 Chapter 7.1 — Exam Notes7.1.1 Ohm’s Law7.1.2 Electromotive Force7.1.3 Motional Emf7.1.1.4 Big pictureChapter 7.1 answers one practical question:What actually drives charges around a circuit?The structure is:Local material response: how current density \mathbf J responds to force per unit charge \mathbf fCircuit-level driving: how a source produces an emf \mathcal EMotion in a magnetic field: how moving conductors generate emf even when the “source” is magneticFor exams, the main skill is to know which formula belongs to which physical mechanism.7.1.1 Ohm’s Law7.1.1.5.1 Core formulas7.1.1.5.1.1 Most general local form in this section \mathbf J=\sigma \mathbf f Meaning:\mathbf J = current density\sigma = conductivity\mathbf f = force per unit chargeThis is the real starting point.7.1.1.5.1.2 Electromagnetic driving force \mathbf J=\sigma(\mathbf E+\mathbf v	imes \mathbf B) Use this when the current is driven by electromagnetic forces and the charges may be moving through a magnetic field.7.1.1.5.1.3 Ordinary Ohm’s law \mathbf J=\sigma \mathbf E Use this when the magnetic term is negligible, which is the standard case in ordinary conductors/circuits.This is the formula most problems mean by “Ohm’s law,” but the book emphasizes that it is really a special case of the more general relation above.7.1.1.5.1.4 Resistivity ho= rac{1}{\sigma} Be careful:here ho means resistivitynot charge density7.1.1.5.1.5 Circuit form of Ohm’s law V=IR This is the global/circuit version.Meaning:V = potential difference between electrodes/endsI = total currentR = resistance7.1.1.5.1.6 Current from current density I=\int \mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf a Use this whenever the current density is known, or when symmetry makes \mathbf J easy to integrate.7.1.1.5.1.7 Resistance of a uniform cylindrical resistorFor a resistor of length L, cross-sectional area A, conductivity \sigma: I=\sigma  rac{A}{L}V so R= rac{L}{\sigma A} This is the standard “wire resistor” formula.Use when:material is homogeneouscross section is constantfield/current is uniform along the wire7.1.1.5.1.8 Resistance of coaxial cylindrical geometryFor two coaxial cylinders of radii a,b, length L, conductivity \sigma: I= rac{2\pi \sigma L}{\ln(b/a)}V so R= rac{\ln(b/a)}{2\pi \sigma L} Use when current flows radially through the material between coaxial conductors.This is an exam favorite because it tests whether you recognize that the area for current flow changes with radius.7.1.1.5.1.9 Steady current in uniform ohmic mediumFor steady currents and uniform conductivity, 
abla\cdot \mathbf E= rac{1}{\sigma}
abla\cdot \mathbf J=0 So inside a homogeneous ohmic material carrying steady current:
abla\cdot \mathbf E=0charge density in the bulk is zeroany excess charge lives on the surfaceHence the potential satisfies Laplace’s equation: 
abla^2 V=0 This is extremely important for solving conductor/current problems with boundary conditions.7.1.1.5.1.10 Joule heating law P=VI=I^2R Also, P= rac{V^2}{R} Use this whenever the problem asks about:heat dissipatedpower delivered to a resistorenergy loss in a resistive element7.1.1.5.2 What Ohm’s law means physicallyA constant electric field does not make the current grow forever because charges collide repeatedly inside the material.So:microscopic motion is accelerated between collisionsmacroscopic result is a steady drift velocitytherefore \mathbf J can be proportional to \mathbf EThe book’s rough Drude-style estimate gives \mathbf J = \left(  rac{nf\lambda q^2}{2mv_{	ext{thermal}}} ight)\mathbf E Do not usually use this formula computationally unless explicitly asked. What it is good for:explaining why conductivity increases with charge-carrier densityexplaining why conductivity typically decreases as temperature rises7.1.1.5.3 What to do on an examIf you see a conduction problem, ask:7.1.1.5.3.1 Case 1: Is this a local-material law problem?Then start from \mathbf J=\sigma \mathbf E or \mathbf J=\sigma(\mathbf E+\mathbf v	imes \mathbf B) 7.1.1.5.3.2 Case 2: Is this a geometry-to-resistance problem?Then:find \mathbf E or Vget \mathbf J=\sigma \mathbf Ecompute I=\int \mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf a identify R= rac{V}{I} 7.1.1.5.3.3 Case 3: Is this a steady-current boundary value problem?Then use:
abla\cdot \mathbf J=0uniform \sigma \Rightarrow 
abla\cdot \mathbf E=0\mathbf E=-
abla Vtherefore 
abla^2 V=0 This lets you use all the Chapter 3 Laplace-equation machinery.7.1.1.5.4 Example logic you should remember7.1.1.5.4.1 Example 7.1: uniform cylindrical resistorBecause the ends are equipotentials and the geometry is uniform, the field inside is uniform: \mathbf E=- rac{V_0}{L}\hat{\mathbf z} and so I=\sigma  rac{A}{L}V 7.1.1.5.4.2 Example 7.2: coaxial cylindersUse radial electrostatic field and integrate current across a cylindrical surface: I=\int \mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf a Then relate \lambda to V using the potential difference.7.1.1.5.4.3 Example 7.3: proving the field is uniformTechnique:use 
abla^2 V=0 impose boundary conditions on the ends and side wallguess the simple linear solutioninvoke uniqueness theoremThat is a very exam-worthy solution style.7.1.2 Electromotive Force7.1.1.6.1 Core ideaIn a real circuit, current is uniform all the way around, even though the obvious “source” may only be inside the battery.Why?Because charge pileups create an electrostatic field that rapidly adjusts the flow until the current becomes uniform.So there are two forces per unit charge in the circuit: \mathbf f=\mathbf f_s+\mathbf E where:\mathbf f_s = source force per unit charge\mathbf E = electrostatic force per unit charge from redistributed charge7.1.1.6.2 Definition of emf \mathcal E \equiv \oint \mathbf f\cdot d\mathbf l = \oint \mathbf f_s\cdot d\mathbf l Why can we replace \mathbf f by \mathbf f_s?Because for electrostatic fields, \oint \mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l=0 So only the non-electrostatic source part contributes to the loop integral.7.1.1.6.3 What emf means\mathcal E is not a force.It is:line integral of force per unit charge around the circuitoften interpreted as work done per unit charge by the sourceSo dimensions: [\mathcal E]=	ext{volts} not newtons.7.1.1.6.4 Ideal source relationInside an ideal source, such as an ideal battery, the net force on charges is zero, so \mathbf E=-\mathbf f_s Then the terminal voltage is V=-\int_a^b \mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l = \int_a^b \mathbf f_s\cdot d\mathbf l = \oint \mathbf f_s\cdot d\mathbf l = \mathcal E So for an ideal battery: V=\mathcal E That is the clean relation to remember.7.1.1.6.5 Meaning in circuit languageA battery does two things:inside the battery, non-electrostatic forces push charges “uphill” in potentialoutside the battery, the electrostatic field drives current through the rest of the circuitSo:inside source: \mathbf f_s is essentialoutside source: \mathbf E usually does the pushing7.1.1.6.6 Exam traps7.1.1.6.6.1 Trap 1: emf is not the same thing as electric field\mathcal E is a loop integral. \mathbf E is a field.Do not confuse \mathcal E \quad 	ext{with} \quad \mathbf E 7.1.1.6.6.2 Trap 2: current uniformity comes from small surface charge rearrangementsIf a problem asks > Why is the current the same everywhere in the loop?the answer is:transient charge buildup creates an electrostatic fieldthat field redistributes the driving so the current equalizes7.1.1.6.6.3 Trap 3: a purely electrostatic arrangement does not produce emf around a closed loopBecause \oint \mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l=0 So if a loop is partly inside a capacitor field and partly outside, the net emf around the whole closed loop is still \mathcal E=0 This is exactly the kind of “trick question” the book warns about.7.1.1.6.7 How to use emf on an examIf the problem asks for emf from a battery/source:identify the non-electrostatic driving regioncompute \mathcal E=\oint \mathbf f_s\cdot d\mathbf l if resistance is given, then use circuit Ohm’s law I= rac{\mathcal E}{R} For an ideal battery, you can usually jump directly to: V=\mathcal E 7.1.3 Motional Emf7.1.1.7.1 Core ideaA conductor moving through a magnetic field can develop an emf.This is the generator idea.The charges in the moving conductor feel magnetic force, which separates charge and drives current.7.1.1.7.2 Basic motional-emf formula \mathcal E=\oint \mathbf f_{	ext{mag}}\cdot d\mathbf l where \mathbf f_{	ext{mag}} is the magnetic force per unit charge on the mobile charges.In simple rigid-wire problems, \mathbf f_{	ext{mag}}=\mathbf v	imes \mathbf B for the moving segment.More generally, if the charge has actual velocity \mathbf w, \mathbf f_{	ext{mag}}=\mathbf w	imes \mathbf B 7.1.1.7.3 Standard rectangular-loop resultFor a bar/segment of length h moving with speed v perpendicular to a uniform B: \mathcal E=vBh Use this immediately when:one segment of length h cuts magnetic field linesmotion is perpendicular to both the wire segment and \mathbf B7.1.1.7.4 Magnetic flux \Phi\equiv \int \mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf a 7.1.1.7.5 Flux rule for motional emf \mathcal E=- rac{d\Phi}{dt} This is the major shortcut formula.Use it when:there is a single, well-defined loopthe loop moves, rotates, stretches, or distorts continuouslyyou can compute the changing magnetic flux more easily than the magnetic force integral7.1.1.7.6 Sign conventionThere are two sign choices:direction around loop in \oint \cdots d\mathbf lorientation of d\mathbf a in the fluxThey must be connected by the right-hand rule:fingers curl in positive loop directionthumb gives positive area directionIf you compute \mathcal E<0 it means the current flows opposite to your chosen positive loop direction.7.1.1.7.7 Extremely important conceptual pointThe magnetic force sets up the emf, but 	ext{magnetic forces do no work} So who supplies the energy?The external agent pulling the loop.That is why generators require mechanical work input.7.1.1.7.8 Work/emf subtletyThe book stresses a subtle but important distinction:7.1.1.7.8.1 To compute emfyou integrate around the loop at one instant of time \mathcal E=\oint \mathbf f_{	ext{mag}}\cdot d\mathbf l 7.1.1.7.8.2 To compute actual work done on a chargeyou follow the charge around its true pathThese are not the same path.Yet in the rectangular-loop example, the work per unit charge done by the external pulling force turns out to equal the emf.This is exam-worthy as a conceptual explanation.7.1.1.7.9 Standard rectangular-loop formulasIf the loop width inside the field is x, height is h, and field is uniform B, then \Phi=Bhx As the loop moves out of the field,  rac{d\Phi}{dt}=-Bhv So \mathcal E=- rac{d\Phi}{dt}=vBh If the total circuit resistance is R, then I= rac{\mathcal E}{R}= rac{vBh}{R} 7.1.1.7.10 Faraday disk / Faraday dynamoFor a rotating conducting disk of radius a, angular speed \omega, in uniform vertical field B: v=\omega s so \mathbf f_{	ext{mag}}=\mathbf v	imes \mathbf B=\omega sB\,\hat{\mathbf s} Then \mathcal E=\int_0^a f_{	ext{mag}}\,ds = \omega B\int_0^a s\,ds =  rac{\omega B a^2}{2} Hence I= rac{\mathcal E}{R} =  rac{\omega B a^2}{2R} This example matters because:it does have motional emfbut the flux rule is not convenient/directly applicable, since current spreads over the disk and there is no single simple wire pathSo this is a classic example of:use direct motional-emf integral, not flux rule7.1.1.7.11 When the flux rule is safeUse \mathcal E=- rac{d\Phi}{dt} when the current path is a single loop and remains well defined.7.1.1.7.12 When the flux rule is dangerousBe cautious if there are:switchessliding contactsmultiple possible current pathsextended conductors where current spreads through a 2D regionstrange geometries like the Faraday diskThe book explicitly warns that flux can change without there being a motional emf, if no conductor is actually moving through the magnetic field in the required way.7.1.1.8 One-page exam checklist7.1.1.8.1 If you see a resistor/material problemStart from \mathbf J=\sigma\mathbf E then use I=\int \mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf a and V=IR 7.1.1.8.2 If you see a “why is current the same everywhere?” questionAnswer with:transient surface charge buildupinduced electrostatic fieldself-correcting redistribution until 
abla\cdot \mathbf J=07.1.1.8.3 If you see a battery/source problemUse \mathcal E=\oint \mathbf f_s\cdot d\mathbf l and for an ideal battery V=\mathcal E 7.1.1.8.4 If you see a moving rod/loop in a magnetic fieldFirst think: \mathcal E=\oint \mathbf f_{	ext{mag}}\cdot d\mathbf l If geometry is simple: \mathcal E=vBh If flux is easier: \mathcal E=- rac{d\Phi}{dt} 7.1.1.8.5 If you see a power/heating questionUse P=VI=I^2R= rac{V^2}{R} 7.1.1.9 High-yield distinctions to memorize1. Local vs circuit Ohm’s lawLocal: \mathbf J=\sigma\mathbf E Circuit: V=IR 2. emf vs voltageVoltage = potential difference between two pointsemf = loop integral of source force per unit chargeFor an ideal battery they are equal: V=\mathcal E 3. Electrostatic emf vs motional emfElectrostatic field alone satisfies \oint \mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l=0 Motional emf comes from moving conductors in magnetic field: \mathcal E=\oint \mathbf f_{	ext{mag}}\cdot d\mathbf l 4. Magnetic force vs energy transfermagnetic force establishes charge separation/current directionexternal mechanical agent supplies the energy

title: 7.3 Maxwell’s Equations
text:
Chapter 7.3 is the point where electrodynamics becomes a complete field theory. Before Maxwell, we had Gauss’s law, 
abla \cdot B = 0, Faraday’s law, and the old Ampère law. The problem was that the old Ampère law fails for time-dependent situations, especially when charge accumulates, such as in a charging capacitor. Maxwell fixed this by adding the displacement current term. The result is the full set of Maxwell’s equations.7.3.1 Electrodynamics before MaxwellThe pre-Maxwell equations were:  egin{aligned} 
abla \cdot E &=  rac{ho}{\epsilon_0} &&	ext{(Gauss's law)},\ 
abla \cdot B &= 0,\ 
abla 	imes E &= - rac{\partial B}{\partial t} &&	ext{(Faraday's law)},\ 
abla 	imes B &= \mu_0 J &&	ext{(old Ampère law)}. \end{aligned} 7.3.1.1 Why this is inconsistentTake the divergence of the curl equations. For Faraday:  egin{aligned} 
abla \cdot (
abla 	imes E) &= 
abla \cdot \left(- rac{\partial B}{\partial t}ight)\ 0 &= - rac{\partial}{\partial t}(
abla \cdot B), \end{aligned} which is fine because 
abla \cdot B = 0. But for old Ampère:  egin{aligned} 
abla \cdot (
abla 	imes B) &= \mu_0 
abla \cdot J,\ 0 &= \mu_0 
abla \cdot J. \end{aligned} So this would force 
abla \cdot J = 0, which is only true for steady currents. Hence the old Ampère law cannot be correct in general time-dependent electrodynamics.7.3.1.2 Capacitor paradoxFor a charging capacitor, if we apply Ampère’s law in integral form, \oint B \cdot dl = \mu_0 I_{	ext{enc}}, then the answer depends on which surface spans the same loop:a flat surface cutting the wire gives I_{	ext{enc}} = I,a bulging surface between capacitor plates gives I_{	ext{enc}} = 0.So the old Ampère law makes I_{	ext{enc}} surface-dependent, which is unacceptable.7.3.2 How Maxwell fixed Ampère’s lawUse charge conservation: 
abla \cdot J = - rac{\partial ho}{\partial t}. Then use Gauss’s law: ho = \epsilon_0 
abla \cdot E. So  egin{aligned} 
abla \cdot J &= - rac{\partial}{\partial t}(\epsilon_0 
abla \cdot E)\ &= -
abla \cdot \left(\epsilon_0  rac{\partial E}{\partial t}ight). \end{aligned} This suggests correcting Ampère’s law by replacing J with J + \epsilon_0  rac{\partial E}{\partial t} Therefore the corrected equation is 
abla 	imes B = \mu_0 J + \mu_0 \epsilon_0  rac{\partial E}{\partial t}. This extra term is called the displacement current density: J_d \equiv \epsilon_0  rac{\partial E}{\partial t}. #### Integral formThe corrected Ampère-Maxwell law is \oint B \cdot dl = \mu_0 I_{	ext{enc}} + \mu_0 \epsilon_0 \int  rac{\partial E}{\partial t} \cdot da. This resolves the charging capacitor paradox:on the wire-cutting surface, the conduction current contributes;on the balloon surface between the plates, the displacement current contributes.Both surfaces give the same magnetic field.7.3.2.1 Key ideaFaraday says: 	ext{changing } B \Rightarrow 	ext{induces } E. Maxwell’s correction says: 	ext{changing } E \Rightarrow 	ext{induces } B. This symmetry is one of the deep structural ideas of electrodynamics.[!remark] In some time-dependent situations, a nonzero conduction current can be exactly canceled by displacement current, so the magnetic field can still be zero by symmetry.7.3.3 Maxwell’s equationsThe finished Maxwell equations are:  egin{aligned} 
abla \cdot E &=  rac{ho}{\epsilon_0}, \ 
abla \cdot B &= 0, \ 
abla 	imes E &= - rac{\partial B}{\partial t}, \ 
abla 	imes B &= \mu_0 J + \mu_0 \epsilon_0  rac{\partial E}{\partial t}. \end{aligned} 	ag{Maxwell} Together with the Lorentz force law, F = q(E + v 	imes B), they summarize classical electrodynamics.7.3.3.1 Continuity equation from MaxwellApplying 
abla \cdot to Ampère-Maxwell gives  egin{aligned} 0 &= \mu_0 
abla \cdot J + \mu_0 \epsilon_0  rac{\partial}{\partial t}(
abla \cdot E)\ &= \mu_0 
abla \cdot J + \mu_0  rac{\partial ho}{\partial t}, \end{aligned} hence 
abla \cdot J = - rac{\partial ho}{\partial t}. So charge conservation is built into Maxwell’s equations.7.3.3.2 Alternative source-emphasizing formIt is often conceptually cleaner to write all field terms on the left and all source terms on the right:  egin{aligned} 
abla \cdot E &=  rac{ho}{\epsilon_0}, \ 
abla \cdot B &= 0, \ 
abla 	imes E +  rac{\partial B}{\partial t} &= 0, \ 
abla 	imes B - \mu_0 \epsilon_0  rac{\partial E}{\partial t} &= \mu_0 J. \end{aligned} This emphasizes that the ultimate sources are ho and J.7.3.4 Magnetic chargeIn vacuum, where ho = 0 and J = 0, Maxwell’s equations look very symmetric:  egin{aligned} 
abla \cdot E &= 0, & 
abla 	imes E &= - rac{\partial B}{\partial t}, \ 
abla \cdot B &= 0, & 
abla 	imes B &= \mu_0 \epsilon_0  rac{\partial E}{\partial t}. \end{aligned} This suggests asking: what if magnetic charge existed? Then one would write  egin{aligned} 
abla \cdot E &=  rac{1}{\epsilon_0}ho_e, \ 
abla \cdot B &= \mu_0 ho_m, \ 
abla 	imes E &= -\mu_0 J_m -  rac{\partial B}{\partial t}, \ 
abla 	imes B &= \mu_0 J_e + \mu_0 \epsilon_0  rac{\partial E}{\partial t}. \end{aligned} Then both electric and magnetic charges would satisfy continuity equations:  egin{aligned} 
abla \cdot J_e &= - rac{\partial ho_e}{\partial t}, \ 
abla \cdot J_m &= - rac{\partial ho_m}{\partial t}. \end{aligned} [!remark] Physical conclusion This would be mathematically elegant, but experimentally no magnetic monopoles have been found. So, as far as classical electrodynamics goes, ho_m = 0, \qquad J_m = 0. That is why electric fields have monopole sources, but magnetic fields do not.7.3.5 Maxwell’s equations in matterInside matter, it is useful to separate free charge/current from bound charge/current.7.3.4.1.1 Bound sourcesElectric polarization P produces bound charge density ho_b = -
abla \cdot P. Magnetization M produces bound current density J_b = 
abla 	imes M. If the polarization changes with time, there is also a polarization current J_p =  rac{\partial P}{\partial t}. This is important: J_p is not the same thing as J_b.J_b comes from magnetization,J_p comes from changing electric polarization.7.3.4.1.2 Total charge and currentThus, ho = ho_f + ho_b = ho_f - 
abla \cdot P, and J = J_f + J_b + J_p = J_f + 
abla 	imes M +  rac{\partial P}{\partial t}. 7.3.4.1.3 Define D and HIntroduce the auxiliary fields D \equiv \epsilon_0 E + P, and H \equiv  rac{1}{\mu_0}B - M. Then Maxwell’s equations become  egin{aligned} 
abla \cdot D &= ho_f, \ 
abla \cdot B &= 0, \ 
abla 	imes E &= - rac{\partial B}{\partial t}, \ 
abla 	imes H &= J_f +  rac{\partial D}{\partial t}. \end{aligned} These are not more fundamental than the vacuum-style equations; they are just more convenient in matter because they isolate the free sources.7.3.4.1.4 Linear mediaFor linear materials, P = \epsilon_0 \chi_e E, \qquad M = \chi_m H. Therefore, D = \epsilon E, \qquad H =  rac{1}{\mu} B, where \epsilon = \epsilon_0(1+\chi_e), \qquad \mu = \mu_0(1+\chi_m). In this context, one also writes the displacement current as J_d \equiv  rac{\partial D}{\partial t}. 7.3.6 Boundary conditionsAt an interface between two media, or across a surface carrying free surface charge density \sigma_f or free surface current density K_f, the fields may jump.Notation:\perp means component normal to the boundary,\parallel means component tangent to the boundary,“above” and “below” refer to the two sides of the interface,\hat n is the unit normal pointing from below to above.7.3.6.1 General boundary conditionsFrom Maxwell’s equations in matter: $$ $$ These are the basic jump conditions.7.3.6.2 In linear mediaUsing D=\epsilon E and H=B/\mu, these become  egin{align} \epsilon_{	ext{above}} E_{\perp}^{	ext{above}} - \epsilon_{	ext{below}} E_{\perp}^{	ext{below}} & = \sigma_f, \ B_{\perp}^{	ext{above}} - B_{\perp}^{	ext{below}} & = 0, \ E_{\parallel}^{	ext{above}} - E_{\parallel}^{	ext{below}} & = 0, \  rac{1}{\mu_{	ext{above}}}B_{\parallel}^{	ext{above}} -  rac{1}{\mu_{	ext{below}}}B_{\parallel}^{	ext{below}} & = K_f 	imes \hat n. \end{align} 7.3.6.2.1 If there is no free surface charge or currentIf \sigma_f = 0 and K_f = 0, then \epsilon_{	ext{above}} E_{\perp}^{	ext{above}} = \epsilon_{	ext{below}} E_{\perp}^{	ext{below}}, B_{\perp}^{	ext{above}} = B_{\perp}^{	ext{below}}, E_{\parallel}^{	ext{above}} = E_{\parallel}^{	ext{below}},  rac{1}{\mu_{	ext{above}}}B_{\parallel}^{	ext{above}} =  rac{1}{\mu_{	ext{below}}}B_{\parallel}^{	ext{below}}. These are the boundary conditions used later for reflection and refraction.7.3.7 What to remember most1. The old Ampère law fails in time-dependent situationsThe inconsistency is 
abla \cdot (
abla 	imes B) = 0 \quad 	ext{but} \quad 
abla \cdot J 
eq 0 in general.2. Maxwell’s correction is \mu_0 \epsilon_0  rac{\partial E}{\partial t}. 3. The full Maxwell system is  egin{aligned} 
abla \cdot E &=  rac{ho}{\epsilon_0}, \ 
abla \cdot B &= 0, \ 
abla 	imes E &= - rac{\partial B}{\partial t}, \ 
abla 	imes B &= \mu_0 J + \mu_0 \epsilon_0  rac{\partial E}{\partial t}. \end{aligned} 4. In matter, use D = \epsilon_0 E + P, \qquad H =  rac{1}{\mu_0}B - M. 5. In matter, Maxwell becomes  egin{aligned} 
abla \cdot D &= ho_f, \ 
abla \cdot B &= 0, \ 
abla 	imes E &= - rac{\partial B}{\partial t}, \ 
abla 	imes H &= J_f +  rac{\partial D}{\partial t}. \end{aligned} 6. Boundary conditions are indispensableThey tell you exactly which components jump and by how much at interfaces.7.3.8 One-line intuitionElectrostatics and magnetostatics are not separate worlds anymore. In full electrodynamics, 	ext{changing } B \leftrightarrow 	ext{induces } E, \qquad 	ext{changing } E \leftrightarrow 	ext{induces } B, and Maxwell’s equations are the compact mathematical statement of that mutual coupling.

title: 7.4 The Field of a Rotating Magnet

abla\cdot \mathbf B=0Faraday’s lawAmpère’s law in magnetostaticsThe problem was that old Ampère’s law failed for nonsteady current.Maxwell fixed that by adding the displacement current term, and then everything became consistent:charge conservation workscapacitor problems workelectromagnetic waves become possibleSo for exams, the main goals are:know the four Maxwell equationsknow why the displacement-current term is neededknow when to use the vacuum form vs the matter formknow the boundary conditionsknow how to read physical information from divergence/curl equations7.3.1 Electrodynamics before Maxwell1.10 What you had before the correctionThe old set was essentially: 
abla\cdot \mathbf E =  rac{ho}{\epsilon_0} 
abla\cdot \mathbf B = 0 
abla	imes \mathbf E = - rac{\partial \mathbf B}{\partial t} 
abla	imes \mathbf B = \mu_0 \mathbf J \qquad 	ext{(old Ampère law)} This last equation works in magnetostatics, where currents are steady.1.11 Exact exam trigger: when old Ampère’s law is safeUse 
abla	imes \mathbf B = \mu_0 \mathbf J only when the situation is genuinely steady current / magnetostatics, meaning:currents are time-independentcharge is not piling up anywherecapacitor charging is not happening\partial ho/\partial t = 0equivalently, 
abla\cdot \mathbf J = 0If any current is changing with time, or charge is accumulating, the old form is no longer reliable.1.12 The capacitor paradoxThis is the key warning example.If a capacitor is charging, current flows in the wire, but no conduction current crosses the gap between the plates.Now take an Ampèrian loop around the wire.If you use one spanning surface, the wire pierces it, so you get enclosed current I.If you use a different bulging surface through the capacitor gap, no wire pierces it, so you get enclosed current 0.So old Ampère’s law gives two different answers for the same loop.That is impossible.1.12.1 What condition should you look for on an exam?If the problem has:a charging capacitortime-varying currenta loop where different surfaces give different enclosed conduction currentcharge buildup on plates or surfacesthen the old Ampère law is wrong, and you must use Ampère-Maxwell law.7.3.2 How Maxwell Fixed Ampère’s Law1.14 The key inconsistencyTake divergence of old Ampère law: 
abla\cdot(

abla\cdot \mathbf J But 
abla\cdot(

abla\cdot \mathbf J=0 But in electrodynamics, continuity says 
abla\cdot \mathbf J = - rac{\partial ho}{\partial t} So if ho changes in time, then 
abla\cdot \mathbf J
eq 0, and old Ampère law fails.1.15 Maxwell’s fixUsing Gauss’s law, ho=\epsilon_0 
abla\cdot \mathbf E so

abla	imes \mathbf B = \mu_0 \mathbf J + \mu_0\epsilon_0  rac{\partial \mathbf E}{\partial t} } 1.16 Displacement currentMaxwell called  oxed{ \mathbf J_d \equiv \epsilon_0  rac{\partial \mathbf E}{\partial t} } the displacement current densitySo the corrected Ampère law can be written as 
abla	imes \mathbf B = \mu_0(\mathbf J+\mathbf J_d) 1.17 What displacement current meansIt is not ordinary charge flow through matter.It is not conduction current.It is the extra term required so that a changing electric field can act as a source of magnetic field.1.18 Exact exam trigger: when to use displacement current explicitlyUse \mathbf J_d=\epsilon_0  rac{\partial \mathbf E}{\partial t} when the problem gives:a capacitor gaptime-varying electric field between platesasks for “displacement current density” or “total displacement current”compares conduction current with displacement currentasks you to repair the Ampère-law paradox1.19 Concrete pattern to look forIf the problem gives:capacitor plate area Aelectric field E(t) between platesthen \mathbf J_d = \epsilon_0  rac{\partial \mathbf E}{\partial t} and the total displacement current is I_d = \int \mathbf J_d\cdot d\mathbf a If \mathbf J_d is uniform over the plate area, I_d = \epsilon_0 A  rac{dE}{dt} This is the exact quantity that replaces the missing conduction current in the capacitor gap.1.20 Physical sentence to memorizeA changing magnetic field induces an electric field, and a changing electric field induces a magnetic fieldThat is the symmetry Maxwell restored.7.3.3 Maxwell’s Equations1.22 The four equations in vacuum  oxed{ 
abla\cdot \mathbf E =  rac{ho}{\epsilon_0} } \qquad 	ext{(Gauss's law)}  oxed{ 
abla\cdot \mathbf B = 0 }  oxed{

abla	imes \mathbf B = \mu_0 \mathbf J + \mu_0\epsilon_0  rac{\partial \mathbf E}{\partial t} } \qquad 	ext{(Ampère-Maxwell law)} Together with the Lorentz force law,  oxed{ \mathbf F = q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v	imes \mathbf B) } they summarize classical electrodynamics.1.23 Griffiths’ source-first formGriffiths also likes writing them as  oxed{ 
abla\cdot \mathbf E =  rac{ho}{\epsilon_0}, \qquad

abla\cdot \mathbf J = - rac{\partial ho}{\partial t} } This is not separate new physics here; it follows from Maxwell’s equations.1.25 Exact exam trigger: when to start from the full Maxwell equationsUse the full set when the problem mentions:time-dependent electric and magnetic fieldscapacitor charginginduced fieldswave propagationmatter response with \mathbf D,\mathbf Hboundary jumps across surfacesIf the problem is purely electrostatics or magnetostatics, you usually only need the reduced subset.1.26 How to read each equation physically1. abla	imes \mathbf E = - rac{\partial \mathbf B}{\partial t} Look for this when:changing magnetic field induces electric fieldinduced electric field loopstangential \mathbf E relation at boundariesChapter 7.2 style induction problemsMeaning:time-changing \mathbf B creates circulating \mathbf E4. Ampère-Maxwell law

abla\cdot \mathbf E =  rac{ho_e}{\epsilon_0} 
abla\cdot \mathbf B = \mu_0 ho_m 
abla	imes \mathbf E = -\mu_0 \mathbf J_m -  rac{\partial \mathbf B}{\partial t} 
abla	imes \mathbf B = \mu_0 \mathbf J_e + \mu_0\epsilon_0  rac{\partial \mathbf E}{\partial t} But physically, as far as the textbook is concerned, ho_m = 0, \qquad \mathbf J_m = 0 So in actual classical electrodynamics, magnetic monopoles are absent.1.31 Exact exam triggerUsually this subsection is conceptual, not computational.If the exam asks:Why is 
abla\cdot \mathbf B=0 special?Why are \mathbf E and \mathbf B not fully symmetric?What would Maxwell’s equations look like with magnetic charge?then this is the section.The one thing to remember: > electric charges exist as isolated sources; magnetic charges do not, in standard theory7.3.5 Maxwell’s Equations in Matter1.33 Why rewrite them?Inside matter, you have polarization and magnetization, so total charge/current split into free and bound parts.The key decompositions are:  oxed{ ho = ho_f + ho_b = ho_f - 
abla\cdot \mathbf P }  oxed{ \mathbf J = \mathbf J_f + \mathbf J_b + \mathbf J_p = \mathbf J_f + 
abla	imes \mathbf M +  rac{\partial \mathbf P}{\partial t} } where:ho_f,\mathbf J_f = free charge/currentho_b = bound charge\mathbf J_b = magnetization current\mathbf J_p = polarization current1.34 Definitions of \mathbf D and \mathbf H  oxed{ \mathbf D \equiv \epsilon_0 \mathbf E + \mathbf P }  oxed{ \mathbf H \equiv  rac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf B - \mathbf M } 1.35 Maxwell equations in matter  oxed{ 
abla\cdot \mathbf D = ho_f }  oxed{ 
abla\cdot \mathbf B = 0 }  oxed{ 
abla	imes \mathbf E = - rac{\partial \mathbf B}{\partial t} }  oxed{ 
abla	imes \mathbf H = \mathbf J_f +  rac{\partial \mathbf D}{\partial t} } 1.36 Exact exam trigger: when to use the matter formUse \mathbf D,\mathbf H when the problem gives:dielectric or magnetic mediumfree charge density ho_ffree current density \mathbf J_fpolarization \mathbf Pmagnetization \mathbf Msusceptibility/permittivity/permeabilityboundary between mediaIf the problem explicitly distinguishes free vs bound charges/currents, you should almost certainly use \mathbf D and \mathbf H.1.37 When not to use the matter formIf the problem is just vacuum, air, or ordinary source charges/currents without material response, the vacuum form is usually cleaner.Also, Griffiths emphasizes that the \mathbf D,\mathbf H version is not “more general.” It is just a useful regrouping.1.38 Linear media relationsFor linear media, \mathbf P = \epsilon_0 \chi_e \mathbf E \mathbf M = \chi_m \mathbf H so  oxed{ \mathbf D = \epsilon \mathbf E }  oxed{ \mathbf H =  rac{1}{\mu}\mathbf B } with \epsilon = \epsilon_0(1+\chi_e), \qquad \mu = \mu_0(1+\chi_m) 1.39 Displacement current in matterIn matter form, the displacement current density is  oxed{ \mathbf J_d \equiv  rac{\partial \mathbf D}{\partial t} } This is the version you use in materials.1.40 Exact exam trigger: how to know whether to use \epsilon_0  rac{\partial \mathbf E}{\partial t} \quad 	ext{or} \quad  rac{\partial \mathbf D}{\partial t} 1.40.1 Use \epsilon_0  rac{\partial \mathbf E}{\partial t} in vacuum form1.40.2 Use  rac{\partial \mathbf D}{\partial t} in matter form, especially when medium properties are givenIf the problem gives \epsilon,\mu,\chi_e,\chi_m, it is signaling the matter form.7.3.6 Boundary ConditionsThis is one of the highest-yield exam parts of the chapter.1.42 The four boundary conditionsAcross an interface:1.42.1 Normal component of \mathbf D  oxed{ D_{\perp,	ext{above}} - D_{\perp,	ext{below}} = \sigma_f } 1.42.2 Normal component of \mathbf B  oxed{ B_{\perp,	ext{above}} - B_{\perp,	ext{below}} = 0 } 1.42.3 Tangential component of \mathbf E  oxed{ \mathbf E_{\parallel,	ext{above}} - \mathbf E_{\parallel,	ext{below}} = 0 } 1.42.4 Tangential component of \mathbf H  oxed{ \mathbf H_{\parallel,	ext{above}} - \mathbf H_{\parallel,	ext{below}} = \mathbf K_f 	imes \hat{\mathbf n} } where:\sigma_f = free surface charge density\mathbf K_f = free surface current density\hat{\mathbf n} = unit normal from “below” to “above”1.43 Exact exam trigger: when to use each one1.43.1 Use D_{\perp,	ext{above}} - D_{\perp,	ext{below}} = \sigma_f when:problem gives free surface charge densityasks for normal electric-field jump across interfacedielectric boundary problemIf medium is linear and isotropic, translate with \mathbf D=\epsilon \mathbf E.1.43.2 Use B_{\perp,	ext{above}} - B_{\perp,	ext{below}} = 0 when:asked whether normal B changes at boundarymagnetic interface questionschecking consistency of a proposed fieldThis one is always continuous because 
abla\cdot \mathbf B=0.1.43.3 Use \mathbf E_{\parallel,	ext{above}} = \mathbf E_{\parallel,	ext{below}} when:you need tangential electric field at boundarydielectric interfaceelectromagnetic wave boundary matchingconductor surface limitThis one is continuous in the infinitesimal-loop limit.1.43.4 Use \mathbf H_{\parallel,	ext{above}} - \mathbf H_{\parallel,	ext{below}} = \mathbf K_f	imes \hat{\mathbf n} when:a surface current density is presentcurrent sheetmagnetic-field jump at conducting sheetwave/interface problems with sheet currentIf there is no free surface current, \mathbf H_{\parallel,	ext{above}} = \mathbf H_{\parallel,	ext{below}} 1.44 Very important special cases1.44.1 No free surface chargeIf \sigma_f=0, then D_{\perp,	ext{above}} = D_{\perp,	ext{below}} 1.44.2 No free surface currentIf \mathbf K_f=0, then \mathbf H_{\parallel,	ext{above}} = \mathbf H_{\parallel,	ext{below}} These are the versions used most often.1.45 Converting to \mathbf E and \mathbf B in linear mediaIf the media are linear, \mathbf D = \epsilon \mathbf E, \qquad \mathbf H =  rac{1}{\mu}\mathbf B So the boundary conditions become:1.45.1 Normal electric condition  oxed{ \epsilon_1 E_{1\perp} - \epsilon_2 E_{2\perp} = \sigma_f } If \sigma_f=0:  oxed{ \epsilon_1 E_{1\perp} = \epsilon_2 E_{2\perp} } 1.45.2 Tangential magnetic condition  oxed{  rac{\mathbf B_{1\parallel}}{\mu_1} -  rac{\mathbf B_{2\parallel}}{\mu_2} = \mathbf K_f 	imes \hat{\mathbf n} } If \mathbf K_f=0:  oxed{  rac{\mathbf B_{1\parallel}}{\mu_1} =  rac{\mathbf B_{2\parallel}}{\mu_2} } 1.46 Exact exam trigger: pillbox vs loopWhen deriving or choosing boundary conditions:1.46.1 Use a thin pillbox when the quantity is a divergence lawThat means:Gauss for \mathbf DGauss for \mathbf BSo pillbox gives normal-component jumps.1.46.2 Use a thin loop when the quantity is a curl lawThat means:Faraday for \mathbf EAmpère-Maxwell for \mathbf HSo loop gives tangential-component jumps.This is a very common conceptual exam question.1.47 High-yield strategy summary1.48 If problem asks “which field component is continuous?”Remember:divergence equations control normal componentscurl equations control tangential componentsSo:
abla\cdot \mathbf D gives jump in D_\perp
abla\cdot \mathbf B gives continuity of B_\perp
abla	imes \mathbf E gives continuity of E_\parallel
abla	imes \mathbf H gives jump in H_\parallel1.49 If problem involves a charging capacitorThink immediately:old Ampère law failsuse displacement currentin vacuum: \mathbf J_d=\epsilon_0 rac{\partial \mathbf E}{\partial t} total Ampère-Maxwell source is conduction plus displacement current1.50 If problem gives medium data like \epsilon,\mu,\chi_e,\chi_mThink immediately:use \mathbf D,\mathbf Hmaybe convert with \mathbf D=\epsilon \mathbf E,\qquad \mathbf H= rac{1}{\mu}\mathbf B 1.51 If problem asks whether some proposed fields satisfy MaxwellChecklist:1.51.1 Check Gauss-electric:

title: 9.2 Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum
text:
9.2.1 Big pictureThe goal of this section is to show that, in empty space, Maxwell’s equations imply self-propagating waves of \mathbf E and \mathbf B. The key consequences are:both \mathbf E and \mathbf B satisfy the wave equation,the propagation speed is c= rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon_0\mu_0}}, electromagnetic waves are transverse,for a plane monochromatic wave, \mathbf E, \mathbf B, and the propagation direction are mutually perpendicular,the wave carries energy and momentum.9.2.1 The wave equation for \mathbf E and \mathbf BIn vacuum, where there is no charge and no current, Maxwell’s equations are  egin{aligned} 
abla\cdot \mathbf E &= 0, \ 
abla\cdot \mathbf B &= 0, \ 
abla	imes \mathbf E &= - rac{\partial \mathbf B}{\partial t}, \ 
abla	imes \mathbf B &= \mu_0\epsilon_0  rac{\partial \mathbf E}{\partial t}. \end{aligned} These are coupled first-order PDEs. To decouple them, take the curl of Faraday’s law and of Ampère–Maxwell’s law.9.2.1.1 Derivation for \mathbf E  egin{aligned} 
abla	imes(
abla	imes \mathbf E) &= 
abla(
abla\cdot \mathbf E)-
abla^2\mathbf E \ &= 
abla	imes\left(- rac{\partial \mathbf B}{\partial t}ight) \ &= - rac{\partial}{\partial t}(
abla	imes \mathbf B) \ &= -\mu_0\epsilon_0  rac{\partial^2 \mathbf E}{\partial t^2}. \end{aligned} Since 
abla\cdot \mathbf E=0,  oxed{
abla^2\mathbf E=\mu_0\epsilon_0 rac{\partial^2 \mathbf E}{\partial t^2}}. 9.2.1.2 Derivation for \mathbf B  egin{aligned} 
abla	imes(
abla	imes \mathbf B) &= 
abla(
abla\cdot \mathbf B)-
abla^2\mathbf B \ &= 
abla	imes\left(\mu_0\epsilon_0 rac{\partial \mathbf E}{\partial t}ight) \ &= \mu_0\epsilon_0 rac{\partial}{\partial t}(
abla	imes \mathbf E) \ &= -\mu_0\epsilon_0 rac{\partial^2 \mathbf B}{\partial t^2}. \end{aligned} Since 
abla\cdot \mathbf B=0,  oxed{
abla^2\mathbf B=\mu_0\epsilon_0 rac{\partial^2 \mathbf B}{\partial t^2}}. Thus each Cartesian component satisfies the 3D wave equation 
abla^2 f= rac{1}{v^2} rac{\partial^2 f}{\partial t^2}, with wave speed  oxed{v= rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon_0\mu_0}}=3.00	imes 10^8\ 	ext{m/s}}. So in vacuum,  oxed{c= rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon_0\mu_0}}}. 9.2.1.3 Conceptual pointThis is the central result: empty space itself supports electromagnetic disturbances that travel at speed c. This is why light can be understood as an electromagnetic wave.9.2.2 Monochromatic plane waves9.2.2.1 SetupRestrict attention to sinusoidal waves of angular frequency \omega. For a wave traveling in the z direction, with no x or y dependence, take 	ilde{\mathbf E}(z,t)=	ilde{\mathbf E}_0 e^{i(kz-\omega t)}, \qquad 	ilde{\mathbf B}(z,t)=	ilde{\mathbf B}_0 e^{i(kz-\omega t)}, where 	ilde{\mathbf E}_0 and 	ilde{\mathbf B}_0 are complex amplitudes, and \omega=ck. These are called plane waves because the fields are uniform on each plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation.9.2.2.2 TransversalityFrom 
abla\cdot \mathbf E=0 and 
abla\cdot \mathbf B=0,  oxed{(	ilde{\mathbf E}_0)_z=0,\qquad (	ilde{\mathbf B}_0)_z=0}. So electromagnetic waves are transverse: both fields are perpendicular to the propagation direction.9.2.2.3 Relation between \mathbf E and \mathbf BUse Faraday’s law: 
abla	imes \mathbf E=- rac{\partial \mathbf B}{\partial t}. For the plane-wave ansatz, this gives  egin{aligned} -k(	ilde E_0)_y &= \omega (	ilde B_0)_x, \ k(	ilde E_0)_x &= \omega (	ilde B_0)_y. \end{aligned} Equivalently,  oxed{	ilde{\mathbf B}_0= rac{k}{\omega}\left(\hat{\mathbf z}	imes 	ilde{\mathbf E}_0ight)}. Hence:\mathbf E \perp \mathbf B,\mathbf E \perp \hat{\mathbf z},\mathbf B \perp \hat{\mathbf z}.Also, the fields are in phase, and their amplitudes satisfy  oxed{B_0= rac{k}{\omega}E_0= rac{1}{c}E_0}. So the electric and magnetic fields are locked together.9.2.2.4 Standard example: propagation in +\hat{\mathbf z}If \mathbf E points in the x direction, then \mathbf B points in the y direction: 	ilde{\mathbf E}(z,t)=	ilde E_0 e^{i(kz-\omega t)}\hat{\mathbf x}, \qquad 	ilde{\mathbf B}(z,t)= rac{1}{c}	ilde E_0 e^{i(kz-\omega t)}\hat{\mathbf y}. Taking the real part,  oxed{  egin{aligned} \mathbf E(z,t) &= E_0\cos(kz-\omega t+\delta)\,\hat{\mathbf x}, \ \mathbf B(z,t) &=  rac{1}{c}E_0\cos(kz-\omega t+\delta)\,\hat{\mathbf y}. \end{aligned}} This is the basic model of a monochromatic plane wave.9.2.2.5 PolarizationBy convention, polarization is specified by the direction of \mathbf E. So the wave above is polarized in the x direction.9.2.2.6 General propagation directionIntroduce the propagation vector \mathbf k, with magnitude k and direction \hat{\mathbf k}.Then  oxed{ 	ilde{\mathbf E}(\mathbf r,t)=	ilde E_0 e^{i(\mathbf k\cdot \mathbf r-\omega t)}\hat{\mathbf n}} and  oxed{ 	ilde{\mathbf B}(\mathbf r,t)= rac{1}{c}	ilde E_0 e^{i(\mathbf k\cdot \mathbf r-\omega t)}(\hat{\mathbf k}	imes \hat{\mathbf n}) = rac{1}{c}\hat{\mathbf k}	imes 	ilde{\mathbf E}}. Here \hat{\mathbf n} is the polarization vector, and because the wave is transverse,  oxed{\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot \hat{\mathbf k}=0}. The corresponding real fields are  oxed{  egin{aligned} \mathbf E(\mathbf r,t) &= E_0\cos(\mathbf k\cdot \mathbf r-\omega t+\delta)\,\hat{\mathbf n}, \ \mathbf B(\mathbf r,t) &=  rac{1}{c}E_0\cos(\mathbf k\cdot \mathbf r-\omega t+\delta)\,(\hat{\mathbf k}	imes \hat{\mathbf n}). \end{aligned}} 9.2.3 Energy and momentum in electromagnetic wavesThe fields do not just oscillate; they transport energy and momentum.9.2.3.1 Energy densityFrom the general field-energy formula, u= rac{1}{2}\left(\epsilon_0 E^2+ rac{1}{\mu_0}B^2ight). For a monochromatic plane wave, B^2= rac{1}{c^2}E^2=\mu_0\epsilon_0 E^2, so the electric and magnetic parts are equal. Therefore,  oxed{u=\epsilon_0 E^2} and specifically,  oxed{u=\epsilon_0 E_0^2\cos^2(kz-\omega t+\delta)}. So in an EM plane wave, energy is equally shared between the electric and magnetic fields.9.2.3.2 Energy flux: Poynting vectorThe energy flux density is the Poynting vector \mathbf S= rac{1}{\mu_0}(\mathbf E	imes \mathbf B). For a monochromatic plane wave propagating in the z direction,  oxed{\mathbf S=c\,u\,\hat{\mathbf z}} or explicitly,  oxed{\mathbf S=c\epsilon_0 E_0^2\cos^2(kz-\omega t+\delta)\,\hat{\mathbf z}}. So \mathbf S points in the propagation direction, and its magnitude is energy density times wave speed.9.2.3.3 Momentum densityFrom the field-momentum formula, \mathbf g= rac{1}{c^2}\mathbf S. Hence for a monochromatic plane wave,  oxed{\mathbf g= rac{1}{c}u\,\hat{\mathbf z}} or  oxed{\mathbf g= rac{1}{c}\epsilon_0 E_0^2\cos^2(kz-\omega t+\delta)\,\hat{\mathbf z}}. So electromagnetic waves carry momentum in the same direction as energy flow.9.2.4 Time averages over a cycleBecause optical frequencies are extremely high, most measurements see cycle averages rather than the instantaneous oscillation.Using \langle \cos^2(\cdots)angle= rac{1}{2}, we get  oxed{\langle uangle= rac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E_0^2}  oxed{\langle \mathbf Sangle= rac{1}{2}c\epsilon_0 E_0^2\,\hat{\mathbf z}}  oxed{\langle \mathbf gangle= rac{1}{2c}\epsilon_0 E_0^2\,\hat{\mathbf z}} 9.2.5 IntensityThe average power per unit area carried by the wave is the intensity:  oxed{I\equiv \langle Sangle= rac{1}{2}c\epsilon_0 E_0^2}. This is one of the most useful formulas in applications.9.2.6 Radiation pressureWhen light strikes a perfect absorber normally, it transfers momentum to the surface. The resulting average pressure is  oxed{P= rac{I}{c}}. For a perfect reflector, the momentum reverses direction, so the pressure doubles:  oxed{P_{	ext{reflector}}= rac{2I}{c}}. 9.2.7 Summary sheet9.2.7.1 Vacuum wave equations  oxed{ 
abla^2\mathbf E=\mu_0\epsilon_0 rac{\partial^2 \mathbf E}{\partial t^2}, \qquad
